entries.title: Two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → Quarkus AmbiguousResolutionException, not Unsatisfied
entries.body:
Two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → Quarkus AmbiguousResolutionException, not Unsatisfied

## What happened

Two `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` implementations of the same SPI type appeared on the CDI
classpath simultaneously (one from a platform mock library, one from a persistence testing module).
Quarkus reported **"Ambiguous dependencies"** and refused to start — even though both beans
explicitly said "I am a default, defer to anyone else".

## Why this is non-obvious

`@DefaultBean` is documented as "yield to any other bean of the same type". With two
`@DefaultBean` beans and no non-default implementation, neither bean yields — the contract
("yield to someone else") cannot resolve because there IS no "someone else" with higher
precedence. The error message is **Ambiguous** (same as two regular `@ApplicationScoped`
beans conflicting), not **Unsatisfied** (what you'd expect if both were supposedly yielding).
Developers often assume two `@DefaultBean` beans resolve cleanly because they both "opt in"
to being overridden.

## Root cause

CDI/ARC `@DefaultBean` semantics: a default bean is only eligible when no other bean at
the same or higher priority is eligible. With two `@DefaultBean` beans and no higher-priority
bean, the tie-break is undefined — ARC treats this as an ambiguous injection point.

## Fix

Exclude the unwanted `@DefaultBean` implementation via `application.properties`:
```properties
quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.platform.mock.MockCurrentPrincipal,\
  io.casehub.platform.mock.MockGroupMembershipProvider,\
  io.casehub.platform.mock.MockPreferenceProvider
```

This removes the conflicting bean from CDI discovery entirely, leaving the desired
`@DefaultBean` as the sole implementation. Prefer excluding the one that returns null or
uninitialized values rather than the one with correct sentinel behaviour.

### Why this fix

`@Alternative @Priority(N)` would also work, but requires activating it via
`selected-alternatives` — that is a heavier configuration change and makes the
intent less clear. `exclude-types` is surgical: "this specific class should not
participate in CDI at all in this context."

### Alternative — use `Instance<T>` with `isUnsatisfied()` to avoid the conflict entirely

Rather than excluding a conflicting bean after the fact, don't provide a competing `@DefaultBean` in the extension at all. Inject `Instance<T>` and check `isUnsatisfied()` at call time:

```java
@Inject Instance<PreferenceProvider> preferenceProviderInstance;

int threshold;
if (preferenceProviderInstance.isUnsatisfied()) {
    threshold = DEFAULT_VALUE;  // no provider on classpath
} else {
    threshold = preferenceProviderInstance.get().resolve(...).getOrDefault(KEY).value();
}
```

`Instance<T>` always satisfies its own injection point (the container injects the `Instance` holder, not `T` directly). When zero beans of type `T` exist, `isUnsatisfied()` returns `true`; when one is active, `.get()` returns it. No `@DefaultBean` is added to the extension, so no conflict can arise.

**Best for:** library/extension authors who control their own code and want to make a platform SPI optional without contributing a competing `@DefaultBean`.

**Limitation:** requires call-site guards (`isUnsatisfied()` before `.get()`); callers that inject `T` directly still get an ambiguous point if two `@DefaultBean` beans exist from other sources.

## Constraints

Applies when both `@DefaultBean` implementations reach the CDI container's scanning phase
(i.e. both are indexed via `quarkus.index-dependency` or are in the app's own sources).
In two-repo / multi-module projects, platform library JARs can silently contribute
`@DefaultBean` mocks that conflict with internal no-ops.

## Alternatives considered

- Mark one bean `@Alternative @Priority(1)` instead of `@DefaultBean` — works but changes
  the semantics of the "winning" bean and requires `selected-alternatives` configuration.
- Remove one of the `@DefaultBean` implementations from the classpath entirely — clean, but
  may not be possible if it comes from a third-party dependency.

## Invalidation triggers

Would change if Quarkus ARC adds a deterministic tie-break for two `@DefaultBean` beans
(e.g. favour the one in the current module's sources). Track Quarkus changelog for ARC
`@DefaultBean` resolution changes.

**See also:** [GE-20260515-fd3156](GE-20260515-fd3156.md) — @DefaultBean must be on @Produces method not on the class | [GE-20260529-ab148d](GE-20260529-ab148d.md) — multiple CDI constructors without @Inject → UnsatisfiedResolutionException | [GE-20260601-848232](GE-20260601-848232.md) — exclude-types silently does nothing for Jandex-indexed JARs

**See also:** [GE-20260604-2f0889](GE-20260604-2f0889.md) — @Alternative @Priority(N) stubs appear in @All List<T> alongside original bean

**See also:** [GE-20260609-26ffa5](GE-20260609-26ffa5.md) — @ApplicationScoped POJO + @Produces for same type causes CDI ambiguous bean resolution

**See also:** [GE-20260515-99cf39](GE-20260515-99cf39.md) — config-driven @Produces @DefaultBean for engine-internal strategy selection

**See also:** [GE-20260614-337397](GE-20260614-337397.md) — quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel, clashing with @DefaultBean fallback | [GE-20260604-b3d2ef](GE-20260604-b3d2ef.md) — quarkus-flow CDI extension already registers WorkflowApplication — adding @Produces causes ambiguity

**See also:** [GE-20260615-6c4767](../casehub-engine/GE-20260615-6c4767.md) — adding custom CDI qualifier to @ApplicationScoped removes @Default

**See also:** GE-20260627-51e402 — @Alternative totally suppresses @DefaultBean (not just deprioritized, gone from container)

entries.title: quarkus.arc.exclude-types resolves @DefaultBean ambiguity between two Jandex-indexed framework JARs
entries.body:
quarkus.arc.exclude-types resolves @DefaultBean ambiguity between two Jandex-indexed framework JARs

## Context

Two Jandex-indexed framework JARs both provide `@DefaultBean` implementations for the same SPI type. Both are on the test classpath. Quarkus CDI augmentation reports ambiguous dependencies:

```
Ambiguous dependencies for type io.example.SomeProvider and qualifiers [@Default]
  - CLASS bean [...DefaultImpl...] (jar-a)
  - CLASS bean [...MockImpl...] (jar-b)
```

Changing scope or modifying either JAR is not an option. The less-capable no-op implementation should lose.

## Technique

Add the less-capable bean to `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` in the test `application.properties`. Quarkus removes it from CDI scanning entirely, leaving the more-capable implementation as the sole `@DefaultBean`:

```properties
# src/test/resources/application.properties
quarkus.arc.exclude-types=\
  io.example.NoOpSomeProvider,\
  io.example.AnotherNoOpBean
```

Multiple types are comma-separated with backslash continuation. Each entry is a fully-qualified class name. Excluded types are invisible to CDI — the remaining `@DefaultBean` wins without ambiguity.

## Why this is non-obvious

The natural responses to a CDI ambiguity are: change scope, add `@Priority`, or use `beans.xml` alternatives. `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` is a Quarkus-specific property that completely removes a class from CDI scanning — it doesn't just lower priority, it makes the class invisible. Most developers don't reach for it because the Quarkus docs present it as a workaround for scheduler-incompatible beans (a different use case), not as a general CDI conflict resolver.

**See also:** [GE-20260601-848232](GE-20260601-848232.md) — quarkus.arc.exclude-types silently does nothing for beans from Jandex-indexed JARs (contradicts this entry — verify your scenario) | [GE-20260601-81be07](GE-20260601-81be07.md) — resolve ambiguity by introducing a concrete non-default bean

entries.title: @DefaultBean on @Produces method makes the produced bean default — placing it on the class does not
@Alternative @Priority(n) in CDI 4.0/Quarkus globally activates the alternative — causes AmbiguousResolutionException
entries.body:
@Alternative @Priority(n) in CDI 4.0/Quarkus globally activates the alternative — causes AmbiguousResolutionException

## @Alternative @Priority(n) in CDI 4.0/Quarkus globally activates the alternative — causes AmbiguousResolutionException

### Stack
Quarkus 3.31.1, CDI 4.0

### Symptom
Multiple beans implement the same SPI interface. Each alternative is annotated with
`@Alternative @Priority(10)` as well as `@ApplicationScoped`. On Quarkus startup, the
application fails with `AmbiguousResolutionException` — all implementations are active
simultaneously.

```
AmbiguousResolutionException: Ambiguous dependencies for type ContextDiffStrategy
and qualifiers [@Default]: [TopLevelContextDiffStrategy, JsonPatchContextDiffStrategy, 
NoOpContextDiffStrategy]
```

### Context
SPI pattern where one default bean and two `@Alternative` beans implement an interface.
The intent was to activate one alternative at a time via
`quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` in `application.properties`.

### What was tried
Adding `@Priority(10)` alongside `@Alternative` — expected this to be a ranking hint
that would help CDI resolve ambiguity. Instead, `@Priority` on an `@Alternative` is what
globally activates the bean in CDI 4.0, making all three implementations simultaneously
active and causing the ambiguous resolution error.

### Root cause
In CDI 4.0 (Jakarta EE 10), `@Alternative @Priority(n)` is a shorthand for globally
activating an alternative across the entire application — no `beans.xml` or
`selected-alternatives` config needed. When ALL alternatives carry this annotation,
they are ALL active, which breaks injection points expecting a single bean.

### Solution 1 — Remove @Priority, use selected-alternatives config
**Approach:** Strip `@Priority` from all alternatives; activate one via config.
**Pros:** Per-profile/per-module control without code changes; the intended Quarkus mechanism for SPI switching.
**Cons:** Requires a config entry per activation; all alternatives default to inactive.

Remove `@Priority` from all `@Alternative` beans. Activate a specific alternative only
via `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` in `application.properties`:

```java
// WRONG — @Priority globally activates the alternative in CDI 4.0
@Alternative
@Priority(10)
@ApplicationScoped
public class MyAlternativeImpl implements MyInterface { ... }

// CORRECT — @Alternative only; activation controlled by config
@Alternative
@ApplicationScoped
public class MyAlternativeImpl implements MyInterface { ... }
```

```properties
# application.properties — activate the desired alternative
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=com.example.MyAlternativeImpl
```

### Solution 2 — Use different @Priority values to establish precedence
**Approach:** Keep `@Alternative @Priority` but assign distinct priority values; CDI resolves to the highest.
**Pros:** No config entry needed; the default (lowest priority) is always active, the override (highest priority) wins when present on the classpath. Works naturally for optional-module patterns where a higher-capability implementation should auto-replace the baseline.
**Cons:** All alternatives are always globally active (the core CDI 4.0 behaviour). The "default" must have the lowest priority; adding a third implementation requires careful priority assignment.

```java
// Default — always active; lowest priority loses when a higher one is present
@Alternative
@Priority(0)
@ApplicationScoped
public class ClaimFirstStrategy implements WorkerSelectionStrategy { ... }

// Override — higher priority wins; active only when on the classpath
@Alternative
@Priority(1)
@ApplicationScoped
public class SemanticWorkerSelectionStrategy implements WorkerSelectionStrategy { ... }
```

CDI injects the `@Priority(1)` bean when both are present; falls back to `@Priority(0)` when only
the default module is on the classpath. No `beans.xml` or `selected-alternatives` required.

**When to choose Solution 2 over Solution 1:** When the override is an optional module (not always
on the classpath) and the default must always be present. Config-based activation (Solution 1)
requires an explicit entry even for the default case; priority-based resolution (Solution 2) makes
the default zero-configuration.

### Why this is non-obvious
The `@Priority` annotation is commonly used alongside `@Alternative` in CDI tutorials
and examples from the CDI 2.x era, where `@Priority` on an alternative was a *ranking*
hint. In CDI 4.0 the semantics changed — `@Priority` on an `@Alternative` is now an
*activation* mechanism (equivalent to listing it in `beans.xml` with a priority). The
Quarkus docs for `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` don't warn about this interaction.

### Why this fix
`quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` gives per-profile/per-module control via config,
which is the intended Quarkus mechanism for SPI switching (same as how `PanningStrategyLoopControl`
and other engine SPIs are activated). It doesn't require code changes to switch backends.

**See also:** GE-20260422-ebb91d — AmbiguousResolutionException from multiple unqualified @ApplicationScoped beans

**See also:** GE-20260427-97650e "CDI ambiguity when adding second implementation of a quarkus-ledger repository interface"
**See also:** GE-20260427-62d3ab — use @Alternative @Priority(1) inner beans in @QuarkusTest to spy on SPI call sites
**See also:** [GE-20260427-c2b84f — @Alternative @Priority(1) beans in a test-helper jar are invisible to downstream @QuarkusTest — no Jandex index](GE-20260427-c2b84f.md)

### Update — Test-refactoring trap: two classes declaring the same @Alternative

During a test refactoring, if two `@QuarkusTest` classes *simultaneously* declare an
`@Alternative @Priority(2)` inner class implementing the same type, Quarkus boot fails
with `AmbiguousResolutionException` even though `mvn test-compile` passes cleanly. The
compile succeeds because both classes are syntactically valid; the CDI conflict only
surfaces at application startup.

entries.title: Resolve CDI ambiguity between two competing @DefaultBean implementations by introducing a concrete non-default bean
entries.body:
Resolve CDI ambiguity between two competing @DefaultBean implementations by introducing a concrete non-default bean

## Context

Two `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` beans from different JARs both implement the same interface. CDI can't resolve which to use and throws `AmbiguousResolutionException`. Standard approaches don't help:

- `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` is silently ignored for beans from Jandex-indexed JARs (see GE-20260601-848232)
- Marking one as `@Alternative` requires changes to a JAR you don't own
- `@Priority` on `@Alternative` has CDI 2.0 global-scope problems

## Technique

Add a concrete `@ApplicationScoped` bean to your project (production or test sources as appropriate) that implements the conflicting interface:

```java
@ApplicationScoped
public class ProjectGroupMembershipProvider implements GroupMembershipProvider {
    @Override
    public Set<GroupMember> membersOf(String groupName) {
        return Set.of(); // or delegate to preferred implementation
    }
}
```

CDI selects the most-specific non-default bean. Since your bean is NOT `@DefaultBean`, it wins over both competing `@DefaultBean` implementations and the `AmbiguousResolutionException` is resolved. No changes to any JAR required.

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

Most developers reach for `exclude-types` first (fails silently for Jandex-indexed JARs), then try `@Priority` on one of the `@DefaultBean` beans (requires modifying third-party JARs), then consider `@Alternative` + `selected-alternatives` (same problem). The CDI suppression rule — "a non-default bean beats all @DefaultBean candidates for the same type" — is the correct lever, and a thin adapter class is the minimal mechanism that activates it without touching any dependency.

**See also:** [GE-20260601-848232](GE-20260601-848232.md) — exclude-types silently does nothing for Jandex JARs | [GE-20260601-3dbc80](GE-20260601-3dbc80.md) — exclude-types as technique for @DefaultBean ambiguity

**See also:** [GE-20260601-7a3b38](GE-20260601-7a3b38.md) — @DefaultBean invisible when supertype JAR has no Jandex index

**See also:** [GE-20260616-d70e7e](GE-20260616-d70e7e.md) — selected-alternatives silently accepts non-@Alternative beans

entries.title: CDI AmbiguousResolutionException when multiple @ApplicationScoped beans implement the same SPI interface
entries.body:
CDI AmbiguousResolutionException when multiple @ApplicationScoped beans implement the same SPI interface

## Symptom

`@QuarkusTest` fails at boot with `AmbiguousResolutionException: Ambiguous dependencies for type X`. The production code compiles and the beans look correct.

## Context

Defining multiple `@ApplicationScoped` implementations of the same SPI interface (e.g. three `SkillProfileProvider` implementations) so users can choose which to activate. All three are unqualified, so CDI cannot resolve which one to inject at a single injection point.

## What was tried

Adding all three as `@ApplicationScoped` beans, assuming CDI would pick the first one or throw a clear build-time error.

## Root cause

CDI requires exactly one unambiguous bean per injection type when no qualifier is used. Multiple unqualified `@ApplicationScoped` beans implementing the same interface all compete — CDI cannot resolve the injection point and throws at container startup, not at compile time.

## Fix

Designate exactly one implementation as the default (leave it unqualified `@ApplicationScoped`). Mark all others with `@Alternative`:

```java
// Default — CDI injects this when no override is present
@ApplicationScoped
public class WorkerProfileSkillProfileProvider implements SkillProfileProvider { ... }

// Not active by default — user activates via @Alternative @Priority(1)
@ApplicationScoped
@Alternative
public class CapabilitiesSkillProfileProvider implements SkillProfileProvider { ... }

@ApplicationScoped
@Alternative
public class ResolutionHistorySkillProfileProvider implements SkillProfileProvider { ... }
```

Users override the default at their own application level:

```java
@ApplicationScoped
@Alternative
@Priority(1)
public class MyCustomProvider implements SkillProfileProvider { ... }
```

## Why this is non-obvious

The error only appears at `@QuarkusTest` boot — compile succeeds silently. The fix (marking non-default implementations `@Alternative`) is easy once known, but the CDI resolution rules around `@Alternative` vs unqualified beans are non-obvious. The natural instinct is to let the user pick via config, not via CDI qualifiers.

**See also:** GE-20260415-884e48 — @Alternative @Priority(n) globally activates the alternative in CDI 4.0 | GE-20260417-c59817 — quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives activates @Alternative beans in application.properties | GE-20260421-1cfae6 — @Produces @DefaultBean provides consumer-replaceable CDI defaults without @Alternative

**See also:** [GE-20260428-9311f8](GE-20260428-9311f8.md) — casehub-engine @ApplicationScoped no-op SPI beans collide with consumer implementations when engine is indexed | [GE-20260427-97650e](GE-20260427-97650e.md) — CDI ambiguity when adding second implementation of a quarkus-ledger repository interface

**See also:** GE-20260427-62d3ab "Use @Alternative @Priority(1) inner beans in @QuarkusTest to spy on SPI call sites without Mockito"
**See also:** GE-20260427-c2b84f — @Alternative @Priority(1) beans in test-helper jar are invisible without Jandex index

## Update — Variant: two @DefaultBean impls for the same type

`@DefaultBean` in Quarkus Arc means "use this if no non-default bean for this type exists."
When **two** `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` beans implement the same interface, Arc cannot
resolve the injection point — both are default, neither wins — and throws
`AmbiguousResolutionException` as soon as any production bean injects that type. The symptom
only surfaces once an `@Inject` for the interface is added; before that the ambiguity exists
silently in the CDI container.

**Scenario:** Two library modules each provide a `@DefaultBean CurrentPrincipal` for
"uncontested" environments (`MockCurrentPrincipal` from casehub-platform, `QhorusInboundCurrentPrincipal`
from casehub-qhorus). Adding `@Inject CurrentPrincipal` to any production bean in the app
module triggers the error — the injection point forces CDI to resolve and it finds two equals.

**Fix — exclude one at application level:**

```properties
# application.properties — exclude the stub; the runtime principal wins
quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.platform.mock.MockCurrentPrincipal
```

**Test fix — use quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives to force a third, definitive impl:**

```properties
# src/test/resources/application.properties
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=io.casehub.platform.testing.FixedCurrentPrincipal
```

**Why @DefaultBean differs from @Alternative:** `@DefaultBean` is not in the CDI spec — it is
a Quarkus Arc extension that says "this bean loses to any explicit non-default bean." But when
two `@DefaultBean` beans compete, there is no winner — Arc throws rather than picking arbitrarily.
The `@Alternative` pattern (one winner, rest marked alternative) is the correct SPI design for
exactly-one-at-a-time. `@DefaultBean` is for extension-provided stubs that yield to consumer
overrides, not for multiple peers. Two `@DefaultBean` peers should be refactored so that only one
module provides the default; the other moves to `@Alternative`.

entries.title: @DefaultBean lives in io.quarkus.arc, not jakarta.enterprise.inject
entries.body:
@DefaultBean lives in io.quarkus.arc, not jakarta.enterprise.inject

## Symptom

```
error: cannot find symbol
  symbol: class DefaultBean
  location: package jakarta.enterprise.inject
```

The error gives no hint that the annotation exists — just that it doesn't exist
in the package you reached for.

## Context

When writing a `@DefaultBean` CDI bean in a Quarkus extension or application.
`@DefaultBean` marks a bean as the fallback when no higher-priority bean is
present — the Quarkus Arc equivalent of Spring's `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`.

## Root cause

`@DefaultBean` is a Quarkus Arc-specific annotation. It is not part of the
Jakarta CDI spec, so it doesn't live in `jakarta.enterprise.inject`. It lives
in `io.quarkus.arc`.

## Fix

```java
// Wrong — jakarta CDI doesn't have this
import jakarta.enterprise.inject.DefaultBean;

// Right — Quarkus Arc annotation
import io.quarkus.arc.DefaultBean;
```

## Why this is non-obvious

If you know CDI, `jakarta.enterprise.inject` is the natural package to reach for.
The compile error only says the class doesn't exist there — not that it exists
somewhere else. Easy to waste time searching for a CDI spec addition that never
happened.

**See also:** GE-20260427-543663 — @Produces @DefaultBean for library-level overridable CDI defaults (correct usage)

**See also:** [GE-20260515-fd3156](GE-20260515-fd3156.md) — @DefaultBean on @Produces method makes the produced bean default (related annotation gotcha)

**See also:** [GE-20260601-fcf0d9](GE-20260601-fcf0d9.md) — two @DefaultBean beans for same type → AmbiguousResolutionException

**See also:** [GE-20260604-81a6a6](GE-20260604-81a6a6.md) — @DefaultBean @Unremovable required when injection point is in a different Maven module

**See also:** [GE-20260609-18a0b1](GE-20260609-18a0b1.md) — quarkus.index-dependency for a JAR with jandex.idx double-scans it

entries.title: @Typed required when CDI bean implements a framework-owned interface to prevent AmbiguousResolutionException
entries.body:
@Typed required when CDI bean implements a framework-owned interface to prevent AmbiguousResolutionException

### Symptom

Quarkus fails to start with:

```
AmbiguousResolutionException: Ambiguous dependencies for type com.framework.SomeInterface
```

Occurs when a custom CDI bean implements an interface that a framework component already
provides a bean for.

### Context

Implementing a framework SPI interface (e.g. `AgentChannelBackend` in casehub-qhorus)
to create a custom backend or handler. The framework ships its own `@ApplicationScoped`
implementation of the same interface.

### Root cause

CDI sees two beans satisfying the same interface type — the framework's default bean and
the custom implementation. Without disambiguation, CDI cannot choose. Unlike `@DefaultBean`
(which requires the custom bean to displace it), `@Typed` restricts which types the custom
bean is visible as, removing it from contention for the framework's injection point.

### Fix

Add `@Typed` to the custom bean, listing only the interfaces it should be discoverable as:

```java
// ❌ CDI sees this as AgentChannelBackend — conflicts with framework's QhorusChannelBackend
@Dependent
public class PushAgentDispatch implements AgentDispatchMechanism, AgentChannelBackend {
    // ...
}

// ✅ CDI only sees this as AgentDispatchMechanism and PushAgentDispatch
@Dependent
@Typed({AgentDispatchMechanism.class, PushAgentDispatch.class})
public class PushAgentDispatch implements AgentDispatchMechanism, AgentChannelBackend {
    // ...
}
```

Always include the concrete class itself in `@Typed` to preserve direct-type injection.

### Why this is non-obvious

The error message names the interface type but gives no hint that `@Typed` exists or
would fix it. Developers typically try `@Alternative`, `@DefaultBean`, or `@Priority`
— all wrong in this case. `@Typed` is rarely needed in application code (it's mainly
a framework-authoring tool) and doesn't appear in most Quarkus tutorials. The Java
`implements` declaration is the cause: removing one interface from `implements` would
fix it, but `@Typed` does this at the CDI level without changing the implementation
hierarchy.

**See also:** [GE-20260531-1ec900](GE-20260531-1ec900.md) — Quarkus ARC registers non-CDI abstract class as @Dependent bean when it declares @Observes and implements a CDI SPI

entries.title: @DefaultBean + plain @ApplicationScoped enables CDI layer displacement without config switches or @Alternative @Priority
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives silently accepts non-@Alternative beans, leaving CDI ambiguity unresolved
entries.body:
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives silently accepts non-@Alternative beans, leaving CDI ambiguity unresolved

### Symptom

27 "Ambiguous dependencies for type `CurrentPrincipal`" ARC deployment errors at `quarkus:build`. Three `@Default` beans competing; you have the problematic one in `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives`. Build broken.

### Context

Multiple `@Default` beans satisfy the same injection type. You add the "intended winner" to `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` expecting it to take priority. The entry is accepted silently — no warning, no error — but the ambiguity persists exactly as before.

### What was tried

Added the non-`@Alternative` class to `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives`. Quarkus did not reject the entry; the config appeared correct. But all 27 errors remained on the next build.

### Root cause

`quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` is designed for beans annotated `@Alternative`. For non-`@Alternative` beans, Quarkus accepts the config entry silently (no validation, no warning) but does nothing with it — the bean is already active as a `@Default` and needs no "selection." The other `@Default` competitors are unaffected. Since CDI ambiguity requires exactly one unambiguous `@Default` winner, adding the non-`@Alternative` to `selected-alternatives` achieves nothing.

### Fix

Do not put non-`@Alternative` beans in `selected-alternatives`. To resolve `@Default` ambiguity when you cannot change the competing beans' annotations (they live in upstream dependency JARs), add the losing beans to `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` instead:

```properties
quarkus.arc.exclude-types=\
  io.example.CompetingBeanA,\
  io.example.CompetingBeanB
```

The intended winner survives; excluded beans are not visible to CDI at all.

### Why this is non-obvious

`selected-alternatives` is the documented mechanism for activating a preferred CDI bean. Nothing in the Quarkus docs or ARC error output warns that the listed class must itself be `@Alternative`. The config entry is accepted, the bean is already live, so the fix "looks applied" — yet the 27 errors persist unchanged.

**See also:** [GE-20260524-2b587e](GE-20260524-2b587e.md) — `selected-alternatives` does not activate `@Alternative` beans during `quarkus:build` (related but distinct failure mode)

**See also:** [GE-20260616-036128](GE-20260616-036128.md) — casehub-ledger JpaActorTrustScoreRepository is @Alternative — must be explicitly selected

@DefaultBean @Unremovable required when injection point lives in a different Maven module
entries.body:
@DefaultBean @Unremovable required when injection point lives in a different Maven module

### Symptom

`jakarta.enterprise.inject.UnsatisfiedResolutionException` at augmentation time when using a Quarkus library module that defines a `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` SPI implementation. The exception says no bean is available for the injection type — but the bean class is clearly on the classpath and CDI-annotated.

No warning is emitted that the bean was eliminated. The error looks identical to a missing implementation.

### Context

A library is split across two Maven modules:

- `core` defines a SPI interface (`Foo`) and a `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped NoOpFoo implements Foo` default
- `mcp` depends on `core` and contains the only `@Inject Foo` injection point in the consuming app

An application adds both `core` and `mcp` as dependencies. Augmentation fails.

Concrete case: `casehub-connectors-core` defines `ConnectorMeshBridge` SPI and `NoOpConnectorMeshBridge @DefaultBean`. The injection point `@Inject ConnectorMeshBridge` lives only in `casehub-connectors-mcp` tool classes. Without `@Unremovable`, augmentation of an app using both modules throws `UnsatisfiedResolutionException`.

### Root cause

Quarkus ARC performs unused-bean elimination at build time. It scans for injection points within the module being augmented, but `@DefaultBean` implementations that have no injection point visible within the defining module itself are treated as unused and eliminated. ARC does not traverse sibling modules to discover injection points — it only sees what is compiled together in the augmentation classpath at that moment.

The result: the `@DefaultBean` bean is removed before the consuming app can inject it.

### Fix

Add `@Unremovable` to the `@DefaultBean` class:

```java
@DefaultBean
@Unremovable   // ← required: injection point is in a different Maven module (mcp)
@ApplicationScoped
public class NoOpConnectorMeshBridge implements ConnectorMeshBridge {
    @Override
    public void notifyDelivered(String connectorId, String destination, String content) {}
}
```

`@Unremovable` instructs ARC to retain the bean in the CDI graph regardless of whether a visible injection point is found.

### Why this is non-obvious

The `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` error message is identical whether the bean is absent from the classpath or has been eliminated by ARC. Nothing in the error output mentions bean removal. Developers familiar with `@Unremovable` associate it with extension-published beans (where the Quarkus docs describe it explicitly) — not with plain `@DefaultBean` library beans whose injection point happens to be in a sibling module.

The protocol `quarkus-extension-unremovable-consumer-beans.md` covers the extension case; this gotcha surfaces the same issue in non-extension library modules where the split is a Maven module boundary rather than an extension deployment boundary.

**See also:** [GE-20260531-9118e7](GE-20260531-9118e7.md) — runtime Maven scope on shared mock library silently expands CDI scan, breaking @DefaultBean suppression | [GE-20260515-ffde26](GE-20260515-ffde26.md) — optional Quarkus features: Jandex library module pattern | [GE-20260422-e48245](GE-20260422-e48245.md) — @DefaultBean lives in io.quarkus.arc | [GE-20260603-268164](GE-20260603-268164.md) — quarkus:build on library JAR forces CDI validation on compile-scope only

entries.title: Quarkus augmentation cache masks @DefaultBean CDI conflicts — only surfaces on clean builds or targeted test runs
entries.body:
Quarkus augmentation cache masks @DefaultBean CDI conflicts — only surfaces on clean builds or targeted test runs

## Symptom

`mvn verify` passes (all tests run, CDI starts cleanly), but running a single test class with `-Dtest=SpecificTest` fails at CDI augmentation:

```
jakarta.enterprise.inject.spi.DeploymentException: Found 1 deployment problems:
  Ambiguous dependencies for type io.example.SomeProvider and qualifiers [@Default]
```

The conflict is real — two `@DefaultBean` implementations are both on the classpath. Yet the full build doesn't surface it.

## Root Cause

`mvn verify` reuses the Quarkus augmented bytecode from a **previous** build run that was produced when one of the conflicting JARs was absent (e.g., before a dependency was added, or before an embedded Jandex index was introduced into a library). The cached augmented bytecode does not include the conflicting bean, so CDI sees only one `@DefaultBean` and starts cleanly.

A targeted `mvn test -Dtest=X` or `mvn clean verify` triggers **fresh augmentation** from the current classpath, which now includes both conflicting beans — surfacing the real CDI state.

## Fix

1. Run `mvn clean verify` to force fresh augmentation and surface all real CDI conflicts.
2. Resolve the ambiguity by excluding the less-capable bean via `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` in `application.properties` (test scope):

```properties
quarkus.arc.exclude-types=\
  io.example.NoOpSomeProvider,\
  io.example.OtherConflictingBean
```

## Why this is non-obvious

The full CI build passes. The stale cache provides false confidence. The conflict only appears when the build artifact cache is invalid — which happens ad-hoc (after `mvn clean`, first run after adding a dependency, or targeted `-Dtest=` runs). There is no warning that cached augmentation is being reused.

### Alternatives considered

- **Scope isolation** — changing one conflicting bean's JAR to `test` scope may not be feasible if the JAR is also needed at augmentation time for other beans
- **`beans.xml` alternatives section** — verbose and less targeted than `exclude-types`

entries.title: @DefaultBean implementations invisible to CDI when their supertype JAR has no Jandex index
entries.body:
@DefaultBean implementations invisible to CDI when their supertype JAR has no Jandex index

### Symptom

CDI reports "Unsatisfied dependency for type `Foo`" even though:
- A `@ApplicationScoped @DefaultBean` implementation of `Foo` is on the compile classpath
- The implementing JAR contains a valid `META-INF/jandex.idx`
- The implementing class is listed in that index

### Context

A library JAR (`impl-lib`) provides `@DefaultBean class NoOpFoo implements Foo`. A separate JAR (`api-lib`) defines the `Foo` interface. `api-lib` ships without a Jandex index. A downstream module depends on both (directly or transitively).

Quarkus ARC processes the Jandex index of `impl-lib` and finds `NoOpFoo`. When it tries to validate the bean — checking the type hierarchy, qualifiers, and injection points — it needs to read metadata about `Foo` from its defining JAR. Because `api-lib` has no Jandex index, ARC cannot resolve the supertype and silently discards `NoOpFoo` from the CDI graph.

### Root cause

Quarkus ARC bean discovery is index-driven. All types involved in a bean's type hierarchy must be present in **some** Jandex index for the bean to be fully resolved. It is not sufficient for the implementing JAR to have an index — the interface-defining JAR must also be indexed.

### Fix

Add the Jandex plugin to the API JAR's build:

```xml
<plugin>
  <groupId>io.smallrye</groupId>
  <artifactId>jandex-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <id>make-index</id>
      <goals><goal>jandex</goal></goals>
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>
```

Or, if you cannot modify the API JAR, force-index it in the consuming module's test config:

```properties
quarkus.index-dependency.my-api.group-id=com.example
quarkus.index-dependency.my-api.artifact-id=my-api
```

Note: `quarkus.index-dependency` is a build-time property and must be set in `application.properties`, not via `QuarkusTestResourceLifecycleManager`.

### Why this is non-obvious

The error message ("Unsatisfied dependency") points at the missing bean, not at the missing index. The implementing class is visually present in the JAR, correctly annotated, and listed in that JAR's Jandex index — all the obvious checks pass. The missing piece is in a completely different JAR.

### Alternative root cause — stale SNAPSHOT cache

The same symptom appears when the API JAR **does** have a Jandex index but the locally cached SNAPSHOT predates the commit that added the new types. This happens when:

1. `api-lib` is updated to add new interface types and a CI run publishes a fresh SNAPSHOT
2. A consuming module refreshes its SNAPSHOT dependency (e.g. `casehub-ledger`) but not `api-lib`
3. The local cache holds an old `api-lib` SNAPSHOT whose index doesn't yet list the new types

**Diagnosis:** check the JAR timestamp in `~/.m2/repository/`. If it's older than the CI run that added the types, refresh:
```bash
mvn install -DskipTests -f ~/path/to/api-lib/pom.xml
```

When refreshing a SNAPSHOT dependency chain (e.g. `casehub-ledger`), always refresh its upstreams (e.g. `casehub-platform`) if the ledger has added dependencies on new platform types.

**See also:** [GE-20260523-afab1d](GE-20260523-afab1d.md) — @ApplicationScoped bean in JAR bytecode invisible to Quarkus ARC without Jandex index | [GE-20260523-20046c](GE-20260523-20046c.md) — %prod.quarkus.index-dependency limits JAR indexing to production

**See also:** [GE-20260609-18a0b1](GE-20260609-18a0b1.md) — quarkus.index-dependency for a JAR with jandex.idx double-scans it (the reverse problem)

**See also:** [GE-20260610-204ddb](GE-20260610-204ddb.md) — stale core module jar breaks CDI resolution — symptom mimics missing @DefaultBean

Stale core module jar breaks CDI resolution — symptom mimics missing @DefaultBean but root cause is outdated Jandex index in .m2
entries.body:
Stale core module jar breaks CDI resolution — symptom mimics missing @DefaultBean but root cause is outdated Jandex index in .m2

## Symptom

`mvn clean test -pl runtime` reports multiple `Unsatisfied dependency` errors:

```
[1] Unsatisfied dependency for type io.casehub.work.api.ClaimSlaPolicy and qualifiers [@Default]
[2] Unsatisfied dependency for type io.casehub.work.core.strategy.WorkBroker and qualifiers [@Default]
```

All missing beans are `@ApplicationScoped` classes in the `core` module — not `@DefaultBean`, not `@Alternative`. They should be discovered automatically via Jandex.

## Context

Multi-module Quarkus extension project. `runtime` depends on `core` at compile scope. `core` has its own Jandex index. After `mvn clean -pl runtime`, Maven resolves `core` from `.m2/repository` (the installed jar), not from the reactor.

The installed `core` jar was built before recent commits added the `@ApplicationScoped` beans (e.g. `WorkBroker`, `ClaimFirstStrategy`). The jar's Jandex index doesn't list them. Quarkus augmentation reads the Jandex index from the jar → beans not found → `Unsatisfied dependency`.

## What was tried (didn't work)

- Checking for `@DefaultBean` annotations — none missing; the beans are plain `@ApplicationScoped`
- Checking `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` — irrelevant, beans aren't alternatives
- Running the specific test class with `-Dtest=` — same failure (augmentation is per-JVM, not per-test)

## Root cause

The `casehub-work-core` jar in `.m2/repository` was installed by a previous build that predates the `@ApplicationScoped` beans. Its `META-INF/jandex.idx` doesn't include them. Quarkus CDI resolution uses the Jandex index from the jar, not source scanning. When the index is stale, beans that exist in source are invisible to CDI.

## Fix

Reinstall the upstream module before running downstream tests:

```bash
mvn install -pl core -DskipTests
mvn test -pl runtime -Dtest=SomeTest
```

Or use the reactor to include the dependency:

```bash
mvn test -pl runtime -am -Dtest=SomeTest
```

The `-am` (also-make) flag builds `core` from source before testing `runtime`, ensuring the Jandex index is current.

## Why this is non-obvious

The error message says "Unsatisfied dependency for type X" — the natural diagnosis is a missing bean declaration, a missing `@DefaultBean`, or a CDI scope issue. Nothing in the error points to a stale Jandex index in a dependency jar. The beans exist in source, they compile, and `test-compile` succeeds — the failure is purely at Quarkus augmentation time when it reads the installed jar's Jandex index.

### Alternatives considered

- Adding `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` — wrong diagnosis; the beans aren't alternatives
- Adding `@DefaultBean` no-op implementations — masks the real problem and adds unnecessary code

**See also:** [GE-20260515-ffde26](GE-20260515-ffde26.md) — optional Quarkus features: Jandex library module pattern | [GE-20260609-18a0b1](GE-20260609-18a0b1.md) — quarkus.index-dependency double-scans JAR with jandex.idx | [GE-20260522-adb5cd](GE-20260522-adb5cd.md) — moving @ApplicationScoped bean to library breaks CDI | [GE-20260601-7a3b38](GE-20260601-7a3b38.md) — @DefaultBean invisible when supertype JAR lacks Jandex index

entries.title: JPA JOINED inheritance field shadowing + Hibernate bytecode enhancement: base class NOT NULL fails despite subclass field being set
entries.body:
JPA JOINED inheritance field shadowing + Hibernate bytecode enhancement: base class NOT NULL fails despite subclass field being set

### Symptom

`org.hibernate.PropertyValueException: not-null property references a null or transient value for entity CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId`

The test code explicitly sets `cle.tenancyId = "test-tenant"`. Java field access confirms the value is set. The error is impossible — except it isn't.

### Context

JPA JOINED inheritance with a base class (`LedgerEntry`) and subclass (`CaseLedgerEntry`). Both declare a `tenancyId` field with `@Column(name = "tenancy_id", nullable = false)`. In JOINED inheritance, these map to separate columns on separate tables (`ledger_entry.tenancy_id` and `case_ledger_entry.tenancy_id`).

### What was tried (didn't work)

1. Setting `tenancyId` on the entity before calling `save()` — still fails
2. Using `em.persist()` directly instead of the repository's `save()` — still fails
3. Setting the base field via reflection workaround — works but is wrong
4. Clean rebuild (`mvn clean`) to rule out stale bytecode — still fails

### Root cause

Java field shadowing creates two separate fields: `LedgerEntry.tenancyId` and `CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId`. They share the same name but are different fields in the JVM.

Hibernate bytecode enhancement (active by default in Quarkus 3.x) intercepts field access on entity classes. When code does `cle.tenancyId = "value"`, the enhancement transparently routes to the subclass field. When code does `((LedgerEntry) cle).tenancyId`, the enhancement ALSO routes to the subclass field — making the shadowing invisible to Java code.

But `em.persist()` reads field values via reflection on the actual declared fields. `LedgerEntry.class.getDeclaredField("tenancyId")` reads the base class field — which was never set (all writes were routed to the subclass by enhancement). The `nullable = false` constraint on the base table column fires.

### Diagnostic

```java
CaseLedgerEntry cle = new CaseLedgerEntry();
cle.tenancyId = "from-subclass";

// Java access (enhanced — both route to subclass):
cle.tenancyId                           → "from-subclass"
((LedgerEntry) cle).tenancyId           → "from-subclass"

// Reflection (raw — reveals the actual field state):
CaseLedgerEntry.class.getDeclaredField("tenancyId").get(cle) → "from-subclass"
LedgerEntry.class.getDeclaredField("tenancyId").get(cle)     → null  // THE BUG
```

### Fix

Remove the shadowing field from the subclass. JPA JOINED inheritance maps the base class field to the base table automatically — the subclass does not need its own declaration.

```java
// BEFORE (broken):
public class CaseLedgerEntry extends LedgerEntry {
    @Column(name = "tenancy_id", nullable = false)
    public String tenancyId;  // SHADOWS LedgerEntry.tenancyId
}

// AFTER (correct):
public class CaseLedgerEntry extends LedgerEntry {
    // tenancyId inherited from LedgerEntry — no shadowing
}
```

Migration: drop the `tenancy_id` column from the join table (it's redundant with `ledger_entry.tenancy_id`).

### Why this is non-obvious

Hibernate's bytecode enhancement makes the shadowing completely invisible to Java code. Both `cle.tenancyId` and `((LedgerEntry) cle).tenancyId` return the same value. The error message names the subclass entity but the actual null is on the base class — and you can't see it without reflection. The symptom appears impossible: "the field is null but I literally just set it."

### Why this fix

Removing the shadowing field is the only correct fix. Workarounds (setting the base field via reflection, using a special save method) are fragile — they couple application code to JPA internals and break when the entity hierarchy changes. The field belongs on the base class; the subclass inherits it.

### Alternatives considered

- **Reflection workaround in test helpers** — sets the base field directly. Works but couples tests to the field shadowing structure and masks the underlying design bug.
- **Setting both fields explicitly** — impossible via normal Java code because enhancement intercepts the access. Would require reflection on every write path.
- **Hibernate `@Access(AccessType.PROPERTY)` with getter/setter** — might route correctly but changes the access strategy for all fields and is a much larger change.

### Caveats

- This only triggers when bytecode enhancement is active. Without enhancement (e.g. plain Hibernate outside Quarkus), both `cle.tenancyId` and `((LedgerEntry) cle).tenancyId` access their respective declared fields — the shadowing is visible and the developer would naturally set both.
- The fix requires a Flyway migration to drop the redundant column from the join table.

**See also:** [GE-20260609-58e5d9](GE-20260609-58e5d9.md) — JPA JOINED inheritance: child entity redeclaring parent field shadows the parent mapping

entries.title: JPA JOINED inheritance: child entity redeclaring parent field shadows the parent mapping — setting child field leaves parent nullable=false column null
entries.body:
JPA JOINED inheritance: child entity redeclaring parent field shadows the parent mapping — setting child field leaves parent nullable=false column null

## Context

A JPA JOINED inheritance hierarchy where the child entity redeclares a field already declared in
the parent entity — both with `@Column(nullable = false)`. The child table gets a denormalized copy
of the column (e.g. for a local index to avoid joins). This pattern is intentional for performance
but creates a hidden trap for external writers.

Example from casehub platform:
- `LedgerEntry.tenancyId @Column(name="tenancy_id", nullable=false)` — in `ledger_entry` table
- `CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId @Column(name="tenancy_id", nullable=false, length=64)` — in `case_ledger_entry` table

## Symptom

```
org.hibernate.PropertyValueException: not-null property references a null or transient value
  for entity io.casehub.ledger.model.CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId
```

Thrown even though the code explicitly sets `entry.tenancyId = "tenant-1"` before calling
`em.persist()`. The value is visibly non-null; the error says it is null.

## Root cause

Java field access is statically resolved by the reference type at compile time. When `entry`
is declared as `CaseLedgerEntry`:

```java
entry.tenancyId = value;   // resolves to CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId (shadow field)
```

This writes to the child's own field (mapped to `case_ledger_entry.tenancy_id`). The parent's
field `LedgerEntry.tenancyId` (mapped to `ledger_entry.tenancy_id`, also `nullable=false`) is
never written. Hibernate's nullability check validates BOTH the child's property AND the parent's
property — the parent's property is null → `PropertyValueException`.

## Fix

Set both fields explicitly from any external code that touches the entity:

```java
entry.tenancyId = tenancyId;                    // CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId (case_ledger_entry)
((LedgerEntry) entry).tenancyId = tenancyId;    // LedgerEntry.tenancyId (ledger_entry)
```

The explicit cast forces the Java compiler to emit `PUTFIELD LedgerEntry.tenancyId` — a
separate bytecode instruction targeting the parent class's field declaration, distinct from
the child's shadow field.

The correct long-term fix: remove the field redeclaration from the child entity. Use a
`@SecondaryTable` or a Hibernate `@Formula` to maintain the index without the shadow field.

## Why this is non-obvious

The call site `entry.tenancyId = value` looks complete. The entity compiles and CDI-deploys
without warnings. The failure surfaces at `em.persist()` with a message naming the child entity
and property — which ARE set — not the parent entity and property — which are NOT set.

The Hibernate nullability check message `entity CaseLedgerEntry.tenancyId` refers to the
property-path in the entity class hierarchy, not the Java field that is actually null. This
leads to the investigation going in the wrong direction (inspecting the child's field assignment
rather than the parent's).

Any code that uses direct field access from outside the entity (common in JPA entities without
getters/setters) is silently broken when this pattern is in play. Only tests that actually
perform a database persist — not those that simply assign and read back — will catch it.

**See also:** [GE-20260612-1f4ed8](GE-20260612-1f4ed8.md) — JPA JOINED inheritance field shadowing + Hibernate bytecode enhancement causes NOT NULL failure

entries.title: ReactiveMessageLedgerEntryRepository.findLatestByCorrelationId queries LedgerEntry.subjectId, not MessageLedgerEntry.channelId — seeds with only channelId set return silently empty
Static entity factory creates JPA child entities without multi-tenancy fields — NOT NULL INSERT fails
entries.body:
Static entity factory creates JPA child entities without multi-tenancy fields — NOT NULL INSERT fails

### Symptom

```
org.hibernate.exception.ConstraintViolationException: column "tenancy_id" violates not-null constraint
```

Entities persisted via a static factory or utility method fail on INSERT even though the owning
parent entity has `tenancyId` set correctly.

### Context

`LedgerMerkleTree.append(digest, currentFrontier, subjectId)` is a pure static utility that
builds new `LedgerMerkleFrontier` nodes. It has no knowledge of tenancy context. The caller
in `ReactiveLedgerEntryJpaRepository.save()` sets `tenancyId` on the `LedgerEntry` being saved
but forgot to propagate it to the frontier nodes returned by `append()`. The nodes go into
`session.persist()` with `tenancyId = null`, violating the NOT NULL constraint.

### Root cause

Static factory and utility methods that create JPA entities operate outside any tenancy context.
Multi-tenancy fields (`tenancyId`, `tenantKey`, etc.) are caller responsibilities, not factory
responsibilities. The omission is invisible until the `session.persist()` flush fires — and only
on code paths where the NOT NULL column is actually written.

### Fix

Propagate multi-tenancy fields from the parent entity onto all child entities immediately after
the factory call, before any `session.persist()`:

```java
final List<LedgerMerkleFrontier> newFrontier =
    LedgerMerkleTree.append(e.digest, currentFrontier, e.subjectId);
newFrontier.forEach(node -> node.tenancyId = e.tenancyId);  // ← propagate before persist
// ... then session.persist(node) for each
```

### Why this is non-obvious

The parent entity (`LedgerEntry`) has `tenancyId` set correctly and was used for all prior
operations. The factory method looks complete — it takes all the structural parameters it needs.
The tenancy propagation step is easy to forget because it is not part of the factory's contract
and there is no type system or annotation to enforce it.

entries.title: JPA JOINED inheritance subclass with its own repository bypasses base-class save() invariants — invisible until a constraint surfaces it
JOINED inheritance silently breaks when parent @Entity becomes @MappedSuperclass
entries.body:
JOINED inheritance silently breaks when parent @Entity becomes @MappedSuperclass

## Symptom

After a library refactoring where `LedgerEntry` moved from `@Entity` (runtime module) to `@MappedSuperclass` (API module), JPQL queries using `FROM LedgerEntry` silently stop returning subclass instances. No compile error, no runtime exception — queries return empty result sets or reduced counts. Seven tests failed with symptoms like `expected: <1> but was: <0>` (attestation count) and `Expected size: 2 but was: 1` (cross-dtype query).

## Context

A library (casehub-ledger) refactored its JPA entity hierarchy:

**Before:**
```
LedgerEntry (@Entity, @Inheritance(JOINED), @Table("ledger_entry"))
  └── MessageLedgerEntry (@Entity, @DiscriminatorValue("QHORUS_MESSAGE"))
```

**After:**
```
LedgerEntry (@MappedSuperclass)  ← moved to API module
  ├── JpaLedgerEntry (@Entity, @Inheritance(JOINED), @Table("ledger_entry"))  ← new runtime class
  │     └── PlainLedgerEntry, ErasureReceiptLedgerEntry
  └── MessageLedgerEntry (@Entity, @DiscriminatorValue("QHORUS_MESSAGE"))  ← still extends LedgerEntry!
```

`MessageLedgerEntry extends LedgerEntry` compiled fine because `@MappedSuperclass` is a valid JPA supertype. But it became a standalone entity — not a JOINED subclass of `JpaLedgerEntry`.

## What was tried (didn't work)

1. Fixed import statements (`LedgerEntry` → `api.model.LedgerEntry`) — compilation fixed but tests still failed
2. Fixed `LedgerAttestation` entity creation (separate gotcha: GE-20260705-2a5555) — attestation tests still failed
3. Added debug logging to attestation path — no output because the code path wasn't reached (the entry lookup returned empty)
4. Checked tenancy consistency — correct

## Root cause

With `@MappedSuperclass`, `MessageLedgerEntry` inherits field mappings but does NOT participate in the JOINED inheritance tree rooted at `JpaLedgerEntry`. JPA treats it as a completely separate entity type.

Consequences:
- `FROM LedgerEntry` (which maps to the `JpaLedgerEntry` entity name) does NOT include `MessageLedgerEntry`
- `findEntryById(UUID)` returns `Optional.empty()` for `MessageLedgerEntry` records
- `findBySubjectId(UUID)` skips `MessageLedgerEntry` rows entirely
- Cross-dtype sequence tests fail because only `JpaLedgerEntry` subtypes are counted
- Attestation writes fail because the COMMAND entry can't be found for the causal link

## Fix

Change the parent class from `@MappedSuperclass` to the `@Entity`:

```java
// Before (broken):
import io.casehub.ledger.api.model.LedgerEntry;
public class MessageLedgerEntry extends LedgerEntry { ... }

// After (correct):
import io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model.jpa.JpaLedgerEntry;
public class MessageLedgerEntry extends JpaLedgerEntry { ... }
```

The subclass now participates in JOINED inheritance, gets `@PrePersist` (id, occurredAt), entity listeners (trace, identity), and appears in polymorphic queries.

## Why this is non-obvious

1. **No compile error** — `@MappedSuperclass` is a valid JPA supertype; `extends LedgerEntry` compiles and the `@Entity` annotation on the subclass is valid
2. **No runtime error** — JPA silently creates a standalone entity table; no warning that JOINED inheritance is broken
3. **Partial functionality** — direct queries on `MessageLedgerEntry` still work; only polymorphic queries through the parent type fail
4. **The import looks correct** — `io.casehub.ledger.api.model.LedgerEntry` is the canonical API type; using it feels right
5. **7 tests failed with misleading symptoms** — "expected 1 attestation got 0" doesn't point at an inheritance problem

### Alternatives considered

- Keep `LedgerEntry` as `@Entity` in the API module — would preserve JOINED inheritance but violates the API module's "no JPA entity, no Hibernate dependency" rule
- Add a compile-time check that subclasses of `@MappedSuperclass` are not `@DiscriminatorValue`-annotated — not available in standard JPA/Hibernate

entries.title: Ledger count assertions in @QuarkusTest must filter by LedgerEntry subclass
entries.body:
Ledger count assertions in @QuarkusTest must filter by LedgerEntry subclass

Ledger entry count assertions that rely on `findBySubjectId().size()` without filtering by subclass will fail intermittently. Multiple services can write entries to the same subject chain (e.g. safety officer notification, escalation, resolution observers), and the exact count depends on which async observers have fired by assertion time. Use `instanceof` to filter: `findBySubjectId(id, tenancyId).stream().filter(e -> e instanceof SpecificLedgerEntry).count()`. This makes the assertion correct by construction regardless of which other entries are present.

casehub-ledger plain-SQL table ledger_subject_sequence gains tenancy_id column in SNAPSHOT — import-qhorus.sql DDL must be updated manually
entries.body:
casehub-ledger plain-SQL table ledger_subject_sequence gains tenancy_id column in SNAPSHOT — import-qhorus.sql DDL must be updated manually

## Symptom

All REST endpoints that write ledger entries fail with HTTP 500. Quarkus log shows:

```
org.hibernate.exception.SQLGrammarException: Could not prepare statement
[Column "TENANCY_ID" not found; SQL statement:
  ... ledger_subject_sequence ...]
```

at `LedgerSequenceAllocator.h2NextSequenceNumber()`.

## Context

`ledger_subject_sequence` is a plain SQL table (not a JPA entity) used by
`LedgerSequenceAllocator` to allocate per-subject sequence numbers for ledger
entries. In H2 test environments, Hibernate's `drop-and-create` only creates
JPA entity tables — plain SQL tables must be created via
`quarkus.hibernate-orm."qhorus".sql-load-script` pointing to a SQL file with
`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`.

A casehub-ledger SNAPSHOT added `tenancy_id` to the table and changed the
primary key from `(subject_id)` to `(subject_id, tenancy_id)`. The consumer
project's `import-qhorus.sql` still had the old DDL with only `subject_id` as PK.
Flyway migrations in production handled the column addition automatically, but
H2 tests have no Flyway for this table — only the static `import-qhorus.sql`.

## Old DDL (breaks after SNAPSHOT)

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ledger_subject_sequence (
    subject_id UUID NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    next_seq   INT  NOT NULL DEFAULT 1
);
```

## Fix

Update `import-qhorus.sql` to match the current SNAPSHOT schema:

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ledger_subject_sequence (
    subject_id UUID         NOT NULL,
    tenancy_id VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL DEFAULT '278776f9-e1b0-46fb-9032-8bddebdcf9ce',
    next_seq   INT          NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    CONSTRAINT pk_ledger_subject_sequence PRIMARY KEY (subject_id, tenancy_id)
);
```

The default value `278776f9-e1b0-46fb-9032-8bddebdcf9ce` is `TenancyConstants.DEFAULT_TENANT_ID`
— must stay in sync with that constant.

## Why this is non-obvious

The error points at `LedgerSequenceAllocator`, not at any consumer code or migration.
Because production uses Flyway (which applies the column addition), the schema drift
only manifests in H2 tests. There is no changelog or migration note in the casehub-ledger
JAR that signals the `import-qhorus.sql` in consumer projects needs to be updated.
The only way to discover the new schema is to read the Flyway migration SQL from inside
the ledger JAR: `db/ledger/migration/V1000__ledger_base_schema.sql`.

entries.title: casehub-ledger LedgerEntry subclass: required caller-set fields for LedgerEntryRepository.save() — none documented
entries.body:
casehub-ledger LedgerEntry subclass: required caller-set fields for LedgerEntryRepository.save() — none documented

**Resolved in: casehub-ledger 0.2-SNAPSHOT (post 2026-05-11)** — `@PrePersist` was added
to `LedgerEntry` (runtime model, line 261) and now auto-assigns `id` (UUID.randomUUID()
when null) and `occurredAt` (Instant.now() when null). Writers must NOT set these fields —
the entity listener handles them. Setting them explicitly before save() is harmless but
redundant. Unit tests that mock `LedgerEntryRepository` bypass `@PrePersist` — do not
assert on `entry.id` or `entry.occurredAt` in mocked tests.

The required caller-set fields are now **5** (down from 7):

```java
AdverseEventLedgerEntry entry = new AdverseEventLedgerEntry();
// id and occurredAt: auto-set by @PrePersist — do NOT set manually
entry.subjectId = domainEntity.id;        // the aggregate being audited; scopes the sequence chain
entry.sequenceNumber = nextSeq;           // 1-based per subject; caller computes this
entry.entryType = LedgerEntryType.EVENT;  // EVENT (fact), COMMAND (intent), or ATTESTATION
entry.actorId = "system";                 // actor identity string
entry.actorType = ActorType.SYSTEM;       // HUMAN, AGENT, or SYSTEM
entry.actorRole = "MyRole";               // descriptive role, e.g. "AdverseEventReporter"
// domain-specific fields...
ledgerRepo.save(entry);
```

---

### What was undocumented (original — pre 2026-05-11)
`LedgerEntryRepository.save(entry)` required 7 base fields to be manually populated.
No builder, factory, or documentation stated which fields were required. Missing any
resulted in a DB constraint violation at runtime.

### Computing sequenceNumber
The `sequenceNumber` is the position of this entry in the per-subject chain (1-based). casehub-ledger does **not** auto-increment it. Caller pattern:

```java
int nextSeq = ledgerRepo.findLatestBySubjectId(subjectId)
    .map(e -> e.sequenceNumber + 1)
    .orElse(1);
```

### Key surprises (still current)
- `entryType`, `actorType` are enums from `io.casehub.ledger.api.model` (the API module), not `io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model`.
- `sequenceNumber` is still caller-managed — `@PrePersist` does not set it.

### Still-current surprises that were previously undocumented
- `id` was not auto-assigned at submission time — now resolved.
- `occurredAt` was not auto-set — now resolved.

### Where to find the only usage example
`casehub-ledger/runtime/src/test/java/io/casehub/ledger/privacy/LedgerPrivacyWiringIT.java` — the private `entry()` helper method at the bottom of the class.

**See also:** [GE-20260612-17c161](GE-20260612-17c161.md) — casehub-ledger LedgerProcessor build step blocks em.persist() on LedgerEntry subclasses

entries.title: casehub.ledger.identity.tokenisation.enabled=true required in tests for LedgerErasureService.erase() to do anything
entries.body:
casehub.ledger.identity.tokenisation.enabled=true required in tests for LedgerErasureService.erase() to do anything

### Symptom

`LedgerErasureService.erase(rawActorId)` always returns `ErasureResult(rawActorId, mappingFound=false, affectedEntryCount=0)` in `@QuarkusTest`, even when `LedgerEntry` records with that `actorId` have been written by the test.

### Context

Writing a `@QuarkusTest` to verify GDPR erasure — starting an investigation (which writes ledger entries with a known `actorId`), then calling `erase()` and asserting `mappingFound = true`.

### Root cause

`LedgerPrivacyProducer` produces `ActorIdentityProvider` based on a config flag:

```java
@Produces @DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped
public ActorIdentityProvider actorIdentityProvider() {
    return config.identity().tokenisation().enabled()
        ? new InternalActorIdentityProvider(em)   // creates ActorIdentity rows
        : new PassThroughActorIdentityProvider();  // no-op
}
```

The default is `false` — `PassThroughActorIdentityProvider` is a complete no-op. It never creates `ActorIdentity` rows, so `LedgerErasureService` finds nothing to erase. The `ActorIdentity` table is always empty without this flag.

### Fix

Add to `application.properties` (test):

```properties
casehub.ledger.identity.tokenisation.enabled=true
```

With this flag set, `InternalActorIdentityProvider` creates a pseudonymous `ActorIdentity` token row whenever a `LedgerEntry` is persisted with an `actorId`. `erase()` finds the token, pseudonymizes it, and returns the actual count of affected entries.

### Why this is non-obvious

The property name does not appear in casehub-ledger's documented configuration. `LedgerErasureService` is injected and callable without error — the service starts and responds normally. The return value of `mappingFound=false` looks like the actorId was never recorded in ledger entries, when in fact the issue is that the identity mapping layer was never activated.

### Caveat — do NOT enable globally if other tests assert on raw actorId strings

Enabling `casehub.ledger.identity.tokenisation.enabled=true` in a shared test `application.properties` causes `InternalActorIdentityProvider` to tokenize all actorIds at persist time — including in tests that assert on raw actorId strings (e.g., `assertThat(entry.actorId).isEqualTo("human:pi-L")`). Those tests will fail with the tokenized UUID token instead.

**Resolution:** Only enable tokenisation for tests that specifically need it. Either:
1. Keep the global test config at `false` (default). Tests asserting on `erase()` behaviour should note that `affectedEntryCount=0` is expected without tokenisation.
2. Use a `@TestProfile` with the flag set only for the specific test class that exercises erasure.

The `ConsentWithdrawalService` integration test does not need the flag — it only asserts on the HTTP response code and entity field pseudonymization, not on `ledgerEntriesAffected`.

entries.title: LedgerEntryRepository.save() triggers full Merkle chain update — concurrent writes violate UQ_MERKLE_FRONTIER_SUBJECT_LEVEL
entries.body:
LedgerEntryRepository.save() triggers full Merkle chain update — concurrent writes violate UQ_MERKLE_FRONTIER_SUBJECT_LEVEL

### Symptom

`UQ_MERKLE_FRONTIER_SUBJECT_LEVEL` unique constraint violation (`org.h2.jdbc.JdbcSQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException`) when multiple `LedgerEntry` subclasses are saved for the same `subjectId` concurrently. The exception originates inside an async CDI observer, so it is logged as:

```
ERROR DefaultAsyncObserverExceptionHandler: Failure occurred while notifying an async Observer
[method=io.casehub.ledger.service.CaseLedgerEventCapture#onCaseLifecycleEvent(...)]
Caused by: JdbcSQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException: Unique index or primary key violation:
"PUBLIC.UQ_MERKLE_FRONTIER_SUBJECT_LEVEL INDEX ON PUBLIC.LEDGER_MERKLE_FRONTIER(SUBJECT_ID, LEVEL)"
```

### Context

Two or more parallel casehub-engine workers fire for the same case simultaneously (e.g. `pattern-analysis` and `osint-screening` on the same `contextChange` tick). Each worker writes a `LedgerEntry` subclass via `LedgerEntryRepository.save()` for the same `subjectId`.

### Root cause

`LedgerEntryRepository.save()` triggers `LedgerTraceListener.prePersist()` → `LedgerEnricherPipeline.enrich()` → Merkle frontier update (`LEDGER_MERKLE_FRONTIER` table). Two concurrent saves for the same `subjectId` both try to write level 0 of the frontier in the same instant. H2's constraint fires; PostgreSQL's row-level locking serialises the writes instead.

The Merkle enrichment pipeline is not optional and not skippable through `LedgerEntryRepository` — it is wired into the JPA entity listener.

### Fix

For `LedgerEntry` subclasses that should NOT participate in the Merkle audit chain (e.g. internal attestation records not relevant to an external verifier), persist directly via `EntityManager` to bypass the enricher pipeline:

```java
// BAD for concurrent saves — triggers Merkle chain update
ledgerRepo.save(entry);

// GOOD for entities outside the Merkle chain — bypasses enricher pipeline
@PersistenceContext(unitName = "qhorus")
EntityManager em;

em.persist(entry);  // no LedgerTraceListener, no Merkle frontier update
```

If the entity MUST be in the Merkle chain, there is no clean workaround for H2 concurrent writes. The entity writes must be serialised, or the test must accept that Merkle verification (`LedgerVerificationService.verify()`) will return false in tests due to a partial frontier.

### Why this is non-obvious

`save()` sounds like a straightforward persistence operation. The Merkle chain update is a side effect buried in the JPA entity listener — not visible in the `LedgerEntryRepository` API. The constraint violation error message names the Merkle frontier table, making it look like a Merkle configuration problem rather than a concurrency issue triggered by a seemingly innocent `save()` call.

entries.title: Dedicated per-concern ledger subject isolates sequence timelines when multiple writers share a caseId
entries.body:
Dedicated per-concern ledger subject isolates sequence timelines when multiple writers share a caseId

### The technique

When multiple independent writers need to write `LedgerEntry` subclasses for the same logical entity (e.g., an investigation `caseId`) but cannot coordinate sequence number assignment, give each concern its own **dedicated, namespaced ledger subject** derived deterministically from the shared entity ID.

```java
// Instead of: entry.subjectId = caseId  (shared with all writers)
// Use a namespaced derivation:
static UUID attestationSubjectFor(UUID caseId) {
    return UUID.nameUUIDFromBytes(
        ("aml-trust-routing-attestation:" + caseId).getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
}
```

Each concern gets its own independent sequence timeline. Entries can still reference the canonical entity via a separate field:

```java
entry.subjectId = attestationSubjectFor(event.caseId());  // ledger ordering
entry.investigationCaseId = event.caseId();               // domain query field
```

Application queries use `investigationCaseId` for business lookup. Ledger chains use `subjectId` for ordering and Merkle proofs.

### Why this is non-obvious

The instinct is to use the shared entity ID (`caseId`) as the ledger subject everywhere — it creates a single unified audit chain queryable by one key. This breaks when multiple writers use independent sequence-assignment mechanisms (different repositories, different sequence tables). The constraint `IDX_LEDGER_ENTRY_SUBJECT_SEQ` enforces uniqueness globally across all subtypes for a subject, but sequence assignment is often scoped to a single repository. Using dedicated subjects eliminates the coordination requirement entirely.

The derived UUID (via `UUID.nameUUIDFromBytes`) is deterministic, stable across restarts, and collision-free for any realistic number of concerns per entity.

### When to apply

Apply when:
- Two or more CDI beans write `LedgerEntry` subtypes for the same `subjectId`
- They run in independent transactions (e.g., REQUIRES_NEW vs. outer REQUIRED)
- A single global sequence allocator (e.g., `LedgerSequenceAllocator`) is not shared between them

Do **not** apply when a single `LedgerEntryRepository.save()` is the only writer — the allocator handles ordering correctly without namespace isolation.

entries.title: Hibernate named query gains a parameter in one repo — sibling repo call site silently unbound until runtime
entries.body:
Hibernate named query gains a parameter in one repo — sibling repo call site silently unbound until runtime

### Symptom

```
org.hibernate.QueryParameterException: No argument for named parameter ':tenancyId'
  at ReactiveSqmQueryImpl.executeReactiveUpdate
```

All message dispatches fail with HTTP 500 when `casehub.ledger.hash-chain.enabled=true`.

### Context

`LedgerMerkleFrontier.deleteBySubjectAndLevel` is a `@NamedQuery` defined in `casehub-ledger`.
The ledger repo added a `:tenancyId` predicate to the query. `ReactiveLedgerEntryJpaRepository.save()`
in `casehub-qhorus` (a sibling repo) calls this named query but was never updated to bind the new parameter.
The call site compiled and deployed without error — the unbound parameter only surfaces at runtime
when the query executes.

### Root cause

JPA named queries are resolved by name at runtime, not by signature at compile time. When the
query definition in one repo gains a new parameter, every call site in every sibling repo that
uses the same named query must be manually updated. There is no compile-time or build-time
enforcement — neither the Java compiler nor the Maven build reports the mismatch.

### Fix

Bind the new parameter at every call site that uses the named query:

```java
session.createNamedQuery("LedgerMerkleFrontier.deleteBySubjectAndLevel")
    .setParameter("subjectId", e.subjectId)
    .setParameter("level", node.level)
    .setParameter("tenancyId", e.tenancyId)  // ← add when query gains this param
    .executeUpdate()
```

### Why this is non-obvious

The build succeeds. The CDI wiring is correct. The error only appears on a specific code
path (`hash-chain.enabled=true`) that may not be covered by standard CI tests. The exception
message names the parameter (`':tenancyId'`) but gives no indication of which call site is
missing the binding — a classpath-wide search is required to find the stale call site.

**See also:** [GE-20260617-54b75b](GE-20260617-54b75b.md) — Hibernate Reactive Panache repo.update() converts positional ?N params to named params — unbound at runtime

entries.title: casehub-ledger JpaLedgerEntry is abstract — use PlainLedgerEntry for test entry creation
entries.body:
casehub-ledger JpaLedgerEntry is abstract — use PlainLedgerEntry for test entry creation

### Symptom

Test code attempts to instantiate `JpaLedgerEntry` directly:

```java
var entry = new JpaLedgerEntry();  // compilation error: abstract; cannot be instantiated
```

### Context

`casehub-ledger` uses a two-tier JPA inheritance model:
- `LedgerEntry` (`@MappedSuperclass`) — defines all persistent fields
- `JpaLedgerEntry` (`@Entity`, abstract) — JOINED inheritance root
- Concrete subclasses: `PlainLedgerEntry`, `KeyRotationEntry`, `ActorIdentityBindingEntry`, `ErasureReceiptLedgerEntry`

Test code that creates generic audit entries needs the concrete `PlainLedgerEntry`, not the abstract base.

### Root cause

`JpaLedgerEntry` is the JPA inheritance root marked `abstract` — it exists to carry `@Entity`, `@Inheritance(JOINED)`, `@NamedQuery`, and `@EntityListeners` annotations. Domain-specific subclasses extend it for join-table fields. `PlainLedgerEntry` is the concrete subclass for domain-agnostic event writes (introduced with `OutcomeRecorder` in V1009).

### Fix

```java
import io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model.PlainLedgerEntry;

var entry = new PlainLedgerEntry();
entry.subjectId = UUID.randomUUID();
entry.entryType = LedgerEntryType.EVENT;
entry.actorId = "test-actor";
entry.actorType = ActorType.AGENT;
```

### Why this is non-obvious

The class hierarchy has four levels (`LedgerEntry` → `JpaLedgerEntry` → `PlainLedgerEntry`), and `JpaLedgerEntry` appears to be the "runtime" entity that tests should use. The name `PlainLedgerEntry` doesn't immediately suggest "this is what you instantiate in tests" — it sounds like a simplified variant rather than the default concrete type.
