LangChain4j 1.x UserMessage: text accessor is singleText(), not text()
entries.body:
LangChain4j 1.x UserMessage: text accessor is singleText(), not text()

## Symptom

Compile error: `cannot find symbol: method text()` when calling `.text()` on a `ChatMessage`.

## Context

Processing messages from a `ChatRequest` in a `doChat(ChatRequest)` override, trying to extract the text content to inspect or capture it in a test.

```java
// Fails — ChatMessage has no text() method
String content = request.messages().get(0).text();  // ← compile error
```

## Root Cause

`ChatMessage` is an interface with no `text()` accessor. Text content is accessible on the concrete `UserMessage` type only, via `singleText()` — not `text()`.

## Fix

Cast to `UserMessage` and call `singleText()`:

```java
// Correct
request.messages().stream()
    .filter(m -> m instanceof UserMessage)
    .map(m -> ((UserMessage) m).singleText())
    .collect(Collectors.joining());
```

## Why non-obvious

The method name change from `text()` to `singleText()` is a 1.x change. The `UserMessage` constructor accepts a plain `String`, so it reads naturally as if `.text()` should return it — but it doesn't. The method name `singleText()` signals that `UserMessage` can contain multiple `Content` objects and this returns the first text content.

entries.title: quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback

## Symptom

When the quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension is on the classpath alongside a
`@DefaultBean ChatModel` implementation, Quarkus throws at startup:

```
AmbiguousResolutionException: Ambiguous dependencies for type ChatModel and qualifiers [@Default]
  - CLASS bean [... AgentProviderChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
  - SYNTHETIC bean [... OllamaChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
```

## Context

A custom `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped ChatModel` implementation exists to serve as a
fallback (e.g. a Claude CLI bridge). The expectation is that adding the Ollama extension
places its `ChatModel` higher-priority, which should silence the `@DefaultBean`. Instead,
both are registered with `@Default` and Quarkus cannot choose between them.

## Root cause

`@DefaultBean` in Quarkus ARC means: "this bean is only active if no other `@Default`-
qualified bean of the same type is present." The mechanism works when the competing bean
is `@ApplicationScoped` with no explicit qualifier (which implicitly gets `@Default`), or
when the competing bean is annotated with `@Alternative @Priority(N)`. However, the
quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension registers its model as a **SYNTHETIC bean with an
explicit `@Default` qualifier** — not as a higher-priority alternative. ARC sees two
explicit `@Default` beans and cannot resolve.

## Fix

Veto the `@DefaultBean` explicitly when the Ollama extension is active by pairing
`@IfBuildProperty` with `-Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false` at build time:

```java
@DefaultBean
@ApplicationScoped
@IfBuildProperty(name = "casehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled",
                 stringValue = "true", enableIfMissing = true)
class AgentProviderChatModel implements ChatModel { ... }
```

```bash
# Run with Ollama — veto the DefaultBean
mvn clean test -Peval,eval-ollama \
  -Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false \
  ...
```

`mvn clean` is required to force fresh augmentation when toggling this property (see
related entry on augmentation caching).

## Why this is non-obvious

`@DefaultBean` is marketed as "the bean that loses to any other bean of the same type."
In practice it only loses to beans that don't also carry an explicit `@Default` qualifier.
Quarkus LangChain4j provider extensions register SYNTHETIC beans with explicit `@Default`
rather than `@Alternative @Priority`, making the clash non-obvious. The `@DefaultBean`
javadoc does not describe this failure mode.

**See also:** [GE-20260601-fcf0d9](GE-20260601-fcf0d9.md) — two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → AmbiguousResolutionException | [GE-20260531-1ec900](GE-20260531-1ec900.md) — Quarkus ARC registers non-CDI abstract class as @Dependent bean

entries.title: quarkus-langchain4j Ollama REST client default timeout is 10s — too short for local LLMs
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j Ollama REST client default timeout is 10s — too short for local LLMs

## What it is

The Quarkus LangChain4j Ollama extension sets a **10-second default REST client timeout**
for all chat requests. This is undocumented. For local LLMs (8B+ parameter models on CPU
or M-series Neural Engine), a single JSON-structured chat request typically takes 15–120
seconds, so the default silently causes every judge call to fail.

## Context

Appears when running eval harness tests with Ollama models as the judge. The `PromptJudge`
call fails with:

```
java.lang.IllegalStateException: Judge LLM call failed — check judge model configuration
Caused by: javax.ws.rs.ProcessingException: The timeout period of 10000ms has been exceeded
  while executing POST /api/chat for server localhost:11434
```

The timeout fires before the model finishes generating the structured JSON response.

## Fix

Pass the timeout override via system property:

```bash
"-Dquarkus.langchain4j.ollama.timeout=300s"
```

The property is not documented in the Quarkus LangChain4j extension docs or the
quarkus.io reference (as of 2026-06-14). It's discoverable only by reading the
extension's `OllamaConfig` source.

## Why this is non-obvious

The error message ("check judge model configuration") points to configuration rather
than networking/timeout, leading to checks of model name, format=json flag, and CDI
wiring — none of which are the problem. The 10-second timeout is plausible for
hosted APIs but is impractical for any local model above 3B parameters.

OpenClaw /v1/chat/completions requires model='openclaw', not the upstream provider model ID
entries.body:
OpenClaw /v1/chat/completions requires model='openclaw', not the upstream provider model ID

## OpenClaw /v1/chat/completions requires model='openclaw', not the upstream provider model ID

**ID:** GE-20260614-328420
**Stack:** OpenClaw v2026.6.x

### Symptom

Calling OpenClaw's OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint with a provider model
name returns HTTP 400:

```json
{"error":{"message":"Invalid `model`. Use `openclaw` or `openclaw/<agentId>`.",
 "type":"invalid_request_error"}}
```

### Context

When `gateway.http.endpoints.chatCompletions.enabled: true` is set in `openclaw.json`,
OpenClaw exposes `POST /v1/chat/completions`. The natural assumption is to use the
configured upstream model ID (e.g. `"mock-llm/mock-model"`, `"anthropic/claude-opus-4-6"`).

### Root cause / Undocumented behaviour

The `model` field in the request does not name the upstream LLM. It names the OpenClaw
agent. OpenClaw IS the model from the caller's perspective — it receives the request,
routes it through its agent pipeline, and calls the configured upstream provider
internally. The upstream provider model is determined by the agent's config, not the
request.

Valid model values:
- `"openclaw"` — uses the default agent
- `"openclaw/<agentId>"` — routes to a specific named agent

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:18789/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"openclaw","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"ping"}]}'
```

OpenClaw then calls its configured upstream provider (e.g. `mock-llm/mock-model` via
WireMock, or `anthropic/claude-opus-4-6`) transparently.

### Why this is non-obvious

The OpenClaw docs describe the chatCompletions endpoint as OpenAI-compatible, which
implies `model` should identify the LLM. The error message does clarify the correct
values, but the architectural reason (OpenClaw = the model, upstream = internal) is
not explained anywhere in the docs. The distinction only becomes clear after reading
the error response.

entries.title: LangChain4j EmbeddingModel does not implement TokenCountEstimator — use character-based DocumentSplitters.recursive(int, int)
entries.body:
LangChain4j EmbeddingModel does not implement TokenCountEstimator — use character-based DocumentSplitters.recursive(int, int)

`DocumentSplitters.recursive(int, int, TokenCountEstimator)` requires a `TokenCountEstimator` as the third argument for token-based segment sizing. `EmbeddingModel` does NOT implement `TokenCountEstimator` — they are separate interface hierarchies with no inheritance relationship.

### Symptom

Design spec or implementation assumes `EmbeddingModel` can be passed as the `TokenCountEstimator` argument to `DocumentSplitters.recursive()`. Compilation fails with "incompatible types."

### Context

When building a RAG chunking pipeline, the natural assumption is: "I already have an `EmbeddingModel` that handles tokenization for embeddings — it should work as a `TokenCountEstimator` for splitting too." The naming and domain proximity reinforce this assumption.

### Root cause

`EmbeddingModel` and `TokenCountEstimator` are independent interfaces in LangChain4j. `EmbeddingModel` knows how to embed text into vectors. `TokenCountEstimator` knows how to count tokens in text. Some LLM provider implementations (e.g. `OpenAiEmbeddingModel`) implement both, but the base `EmbeddingModel` interface does not extend `TokenCountEstimator`. ONNX-based models (`OnnxEmbeddingModel`) implement only `EmbeddingModel`.

### Fix

Use the character-based 2-arg overload:

```java
DocumentSplitter splitter = DocumentSplitters.recursive(1000, 200);
```

This splits by character count (paragraph → line → sentence → word fallback chain). Character counts are approximate by nature — the imprecision vs token counts is negligible for RAG chunk sizing.

### Why this is non-obvious

The `EmbeddingModel` interface handles tokenization internally (it must tokenize text before embedding it). A developer reasonably infers it exposes this capability via `TokenCountEstimator`. The class names reinforce the assumption: "Embedding" + "Model" + "Token" + "Count" — all in the same domain. The actual type hierarchy has no inheritance link between them.

### Alternatives considered

- Implementing a custom `TokenCountEstimator` that delegates to the embedding model's internal tokenizer — rejected because ONNX embedding models don't expose their tokenizer publicly
- Using HuggingFace Tokenizers JNI directly as a `TokenCountEstimator` — possible but adds JNI complexity for marginal accuracy improvement over character-based splitting

entries.title: quarkus-langchain4j-ollama added via Maven test-scope profile requires mvn clean to invalidate augmentation cache
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j-ollama added via Maven test-scope profile requires mvn clean to invalidate augmentation cache

## Symptom

After adding `quarkus-langchain4j-ollama` as a test-scope dependency inside a Maven profile
(`-Peval-ollama`), the Ollama `ChatModel` bean is not registered. Config keys are logged as
`Unrecognized configuration key "quarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.model-name"`, and the
test fails with `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` for `ChatModel`.

## Context

The module was previously built without the Ollama extension. Maven resolves the Ollama JAR
when the profile is active, but Quarkus reuses its disk-based augmentation cache from the
prior build — before the Ollama extension was on the classpath. The Ollama extension is
silently absent from augmentation: no beans registered, no config processors active.

## What was tried (didn't work)

- Running `mvn test -Peval,eval-ollama` after the JAR appeared in `~/.m2` — stale augmentation
  cache persisted, config keys still unrecognized.
- Adding `-Dquarkus.test.profile=eval` explicitly — no effect on cache.

## Root cause

Quarkus augmentation is disk-cached in `target/quarkus-app/`. When classpath changes occur
(new extension added via Maven profile), the cache invalidation heuristic does not always
detect the change, especially when the Ollama JAR was already present in `~/.m2` from a
prior `mvn dependency:resolve` call (updating file timestamps). The cache is reused, and
the Ollama extension's CDI beans are never registered.

## Fix

Run `mvn clean` before the first test run with the new profile:

```bash
JAVA_HOME=$(/usr/libexec/java_home -v 26) mvn clean test -pl eval -Peval,eval-ollama \
  -Dtest=PromptEvalTest#evaluateRealWorldScenarios \
  -Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false \
  "-Dquarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.model-name=qwen3:8b" \
  "-Dquarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.format=json" \
  "-Dquarkus.langchain4j.ollama.timeout=300s"
```

Subsequent runs without `clean` work correctly — the Ollama-aware augmentation is now cached.

## Why this is non-obvious

The "unrecognized configuration key" warning does not hint at augmentation caching — it reads
as though the extension was not added at all, not that a stale build artifact is in play.
The Ollama JAR is visible in `mvn dependency:resolve` output, making the missing registration
doubly confusing. The standard fix for missing CDI beans (`check your imports, check your
annotations`) leads nowhere.

**See also:** [GE-20260530-0178fd](GE-20260530-0178fd.md) — Quarkus @QuarkusTest augmentation requires extension deployment JARs in ~/.m2 | [GE-20260614-337397](GE-20260614-337397.md) — quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension @Default ChatModel clashes with @DefaultBean

`@DefaultBean` is marketed as "the bean that loses to any other bean of the same type."
In practice it only loses to beans that don't also carry an explicit `@Default` qualifier.
Quarkus LangChain4j provider extensions register SYNTHETIC beans with explicit `@Default`
rather than `@Alternative @Priority`, making the clash non-obvious. The `@DefaultBean`
javadoc does not describe this failure mode.

**See also:** [GE-20260601-fcf0d9](GE-20260601-fcf0d9.md) — two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → AmbiguousResolutionException | [GE-20260531-1ec900](GE-20260531-1ec900.md) — Quarkus ARC registers non-CDI abstract class as @Dependent bean

entries.title: LangChain4j Anthropic: ResponseFormat.JSON without schema throws UnsupportedFeatureException — not a degradation
entries.body:
LangChain4j Anthropic: ResponseFormat.JSON without schema throws UnsupportedFeatureException — not a degradation

## Symptom

Passing `ResponseFormat.JSON` (type only, no schema) to `ChatRequest.builder().responseFormat(...)` for an Anthropic-backed `ChatModel` throws `UnsupportedFeatureException` rather than silently degrading or prompting.

## Context

`InternalAnthropicHelper.validate(ChatRequestParameters)` is called inside `AnthropicChatModel.doChat()` before any API call is made. The validation checks:

```java
if (parameters.responseFormat() != null
        && parameters.responseFormat().type() == ResponseFormatType.JSON
        && parameters.responseFormat().jsonSchema() == null) {
    throw new UnsupportedFeatureException(...);
}
```

This means JSON mode without a schema is explicitly rejected at the LangChain4j layer — it never reaches the Anthropic API.

## Root cause

Anthropic's native API requires a JSON schema to enforce structured output. Unlike OpenAI (which supports a bare JSON mode that produces valid but unstructured JSON), Anthropic has no schema-less JSON mode. LangChain4j's Anthropic integration reflects this correctly by refusing the schemaless request rather than silently ignoring the constraint.

## Fix

Always pair `ResponseFormat.JSON` with a `JsonSchema` when using Anthropic:

```java
ResponseFormat responseFormat = ResponseFormat.builder()
    .type(ResponseFormatType.JSON)
    .jsonSchema(JsonSchema.builder()
        .name("MySchema")
        .rootElement(JsonObjectSchema.builder()
            .addStringProperty("field", "Description")
            .required("field")
            .build())
        .build())
    .build();
```

For a broad catch on provider-specific failures (including older Claude models that don't support structured output at all), wrap the `llm.chat(request)` call in `catch (Exception e)` and degrade gracefully:

```java
try {
    ChatResponse response = llm.chat(request);
    return Optional.of(parse(response.aiMessage().text()));
} catch (Exception e) {
    log.warn("Structured enrichment failed ({}), falling back to structural rendering", e.getMessage());
    return Optional.empty();
}
```

## Why this is non-obvious

The LangChain4j docs describe `ResponseFormat.JSON` as a valid type value. There is no public documentation on which providers support it with or without a schema. The `UnsupportedFeatureException` is thrown before any network call, so there is no HTTP error to debug — it looks like an in-process configuration error with no obvious connection to the Anthropic API's structured output requirements.

The `supportedCapabilities()` mechanism exists on `ChatModel` for high-level AI Services to check before using JSON schema, but `ClaudeMarkdownRenderer`-style code calling the low-level `ChatModel.chat(ChatRequest)` API bypasses that guard entirely.

### Why this fix

`ResponseFormat.JSON` with `JsonSchema` is the only valid combination for Anthropic. Adding a schema is not optional — it is the required API surface.

entries.title: LangChain4j 1.x UserMessage: text accessor is singleText(), not text()
entries.body:
LangChain4j 1.x UserMessage: text accessor is singleText(), not text()

## Symptom

Compile error: `cannot find symbol: method text()` when calling `.text()` on a `ChatMessage`.

## Context

Processing messages from a `ChatRequest` in a `doChat(ChatRequest)` override, trying to extract the text content to inspect or capture it in a test.

```java
// Fails — ChatMessage has no text() method
String content = request.messages().get(0).text();  // ← compile error
```

## Root Cause

`ChatMessage` is an interface with no `text()` accessor. Text content is accessible on the concrete `UserMessage` type only, via `singleText()` — not `text()`.

## Fix

Cast to `UserMessage` and call `singleText()`:

```java
// Correct
request.messages().stream()
    .filter(m -> m instanceof UserMessage)
    .map(m -> ((UserMessage) m).singleText())
    .collect(Collectors.joining());
```

## Why non-obvious

The method name change from `text()` to `singleText()` is a 1.x change. The `UserMessage` constructor accepts a plain `String`, so it reads naturally as if `.text()` should return it — but it doesn't. The method name `singleText()` signals that `UserMessage` can contain multiple `Content` objects and this returns the first text content.

Ollama /api/embed returns 400 when input text exceeds model context length — no truncation, no partial result
entries.body:
Ollama /api/embed returns 400 when input text exceeds model context length — no truncation, no partial result

### Symptom

`embeddingModel.embedAll()` throws `ClientWebApplicationException: Received: 'Bad Request, status code 400'` when called via the LangChain4j Quarkus Ollama integration. The 400 response body is `{"error": "the input length exceeds the context length"}` but the LangChain4j exception only surfaces the HTTP status code, not the Ollama error message.

### Context

A corpus ingestion pipeline sends document text to Ollama for embedding via `nomic-embed-text` (2048 token context window). Most documents are small (50-200 lines) and embed fine. Large reference documents (e.g. a testing principles file at ~8000 tokens) exceed the model's context window and Ollama rejects the request outright.

### Root cause

Ollama's `/api/embed` endpoint does not truncate input to the model's context length. If the tokenised input exceeds the model's `num_ctx`, the request fails with 400. There is no partial embedding, no warning, and no automatic chunking. The caller must ensure all input fits within the model's token limit.

### Fix

Split large documents before embedding. Use a recursive document splitter with a max chunk size safely below the model's context window (in characters, not tokens — a conservative 4:1 char-to-token ratio):

```properties
# For nomic-embed-text (2048 tokens ≈ 8000 chars), use 6000 for safety margin
casehub.rag.ingestion.corpora.garden.chunking=recursive
casehub.rag.ingestion.corpora.garden.chunking-max-size=6000
casehub.rag.ingestion.corpora.garden.chunking-overlap-size=500
```

### Why this is non-obvious

The error surfaces as a generic HTTP 400 in the LangChain4j REST client exception. The actual Ollama error message ("input length exceeds the context length") is not propagated — the developer sees only "Bad Request, status code 400" with no indication it's a content-length issue. In a batch ingestion of thousands of documents, the first oversized document fails and the entire batch is lost, with no indication which document caused the failure.

OpenClaw /v1/chat/completions requires model='openclaw', not the upstream provider model ID
entries.body:
OpenClaw /v1/chat/completions requires model='openclaw', not the upstream provider model ID

## OpenClaw /v1/chat/completions requires model='openclaw', not the upstream provider model ID

**ID:** GE-20260614-328420
**Stack:** OpenClaw v2026.6.x

### Symptom

Calling OpenClaw's OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint with a provider model
name returns HTTP 400:

```json
{"error":{"message":"Invalid `model`. Use `openclaw` or `openclaw/<agentId>`.",
 "type":"invalid_request_error"}}
```

### Context

When `gateway.http.endpoints.chatCompletions.enabled: true` is set in `openclaw.json`,
OpenClaw exposes `POST /v1/chat/completions`. The natural assumption is to use the
configured upstream model ID (e.g. `"mock-llm/mock-model"`, `"anthropic/claude-opus-4-6"`).

### Root cause / Undocumented behaviour

The `model` field in the request does not name the upstream LLM. It names the OpenClaw
agent. OpenClaw IS the model from the caller's perspective — it receives the request,
routes it through its agent pipeline, and calls the configured upstream provider
internally. The upstream provider model is determined by the agent's config, not the
request.

Valid model values:
- `"openclaw"` — uses the default agent
- `"openclaw/<agentId>"` — routes to a specific named agent

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:18789/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"openclaw","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"ping"}]}'
```

OpenClaw then calls its configured upstream provider (e.g. `mock-llm/mock-model` via
WireMock, or `anthropic/claude-opus-4-6`) transparently.

### Why this is non-obvious

The OpenClaw docs describe the chatCompletions endpoint as OpenAI-compatible, which
implies `model` should identify the LLM. The error message does clarify the correct
values, but the architectural reason (OpenClaw = the model, upstream = internal) is
not explained anywhere in the docs. The distinction only becomes clear after reading
the error response.

AgentProvider has two abstract methods — not a functional interface, lambdas fail at compile time
entries.body:
AgentProvider has two abstract methods — not a functional interface, lambdas fail at compile time

### Symptom
Attempting to create an `AgentProvider` test double with a lambda:
`AgentProvider provider = config -> Multi.createFrom().items(...)` fails
with a compile error — "AgentProvider is not a functional interface."

### Context
Writing tests for any class that takes `AgentProvider` (e.g. `LlmSelectedRouting`,
`SupervisorBuilder`). The interface appears single-purpose (invoke an LLM) so
lambdas seem natural.

### Root cause
`AgentProvider` has two abstract methods: `invoke(AgentSessionConfig)` returning
`Multi<AgentEvent>`, and `openSession(AgentSessionConfig)` returning a session
handle. Two abstract methods disqualifies it as a `@FunctionalInterface`.

### Fix
Use Mockito mocks instead of lambdas:
```java
var provider = Mockito.mock(AgentProvider.class);
when(provider.invoke(any())).thenReturn(
    Multi.createFrom().items(new AgentEvent.TextDelta("response text")));
```

### Why this is non-obvious
The interface name ("Provider") and its primary use (invoke an LLM) strongly
suggest a single-method functional interface. The second method (`openSession`)
is a session-management concern that most test scenarios don't need, but its
presence on the interface blocks lambda construction for all callers.

entries.title: Assert on side effects, not LLM output, when testing AI tool use
entries.body:
Assert on side effects, not LLM output, when testing AI tool use

## Assert on side effects, not LLM output, when testing AI tool use

**ID:** GE-0169
**Stack:** Any LLM with tool calling (Claude, OpenAI, etc.), any testing framework
**Labels:** `#strategy` `#testing` `#llm-testing`
**What it achieves:** Deterministic automated tests for systems where an LLM calls tools, regardless of how the LLM phrases its response.
**Context:** Testing a system where an LLM calls tools (MCP, function calling, etc.) and you want to verify the tools worked — but the LLM's text response changes between runs.

### The technique
Ignore the LLM's response text entirely. Assert exclusively on what the tools *did* to the system — database state, files created, processes started, API calls made. These are deterministic regardless of model response wording.

```java
// ❌ WRONG — fragile, breaks when model wording changes
assertThat(claudeOutput).contains("I've created a session called");

// ✅ RIGHT — deterministic, model-agnostic
var sessionExists = new ProcessBuilder("tmux", "has-session", "-t", "remotecc-e2e-test")
    .start().waitFor() == 0;
assertTrue(sessionExists, "tmux session should exist after Claude created it");
```

### Why this is non-obvious
Testing LLM systems feels like testing the LLM's output. But tool calls are the actual contract between the LLM and the system. If the tool was called with the right arguments, the effect happened — the LLM's narrative is irrelevant to correctness.

### When to use it
Any project with LLM tool use — MCP servers, OpenAI function calling, Anthropic tool_use, LangChain agents.

entries.title: Use real LLM invocations as protocol capture, replace with scripted replay for CI
entries.body:
Use real LLM invocations as protocol capture, replace with scripted replay for CI

## Use real LLM invocations as protocol capture, replace with scripted replay for CI

**ID:** GE-0170
**Stack:** Claude Code CLI, any LLM, JUnit 5 / any test framework
**Labels:** `#strategy` `#testing` `#llm-testing` `#ci-cd`
**What it achieves:** Bootstrap tests with real LLM calls to discover what the model actually does, then replace with deterministic scripted sequences for CI — fast, free, no API tokens.
**Context:** Testing MCP servers or any LLM tool-call system where you want CI that doesn't call real LLMs.

### The technique
1. Run the test once with a real LLM invocation, capturing the tool call sequence (JSON-RPC messages, MCP calls, etc.)
2. Save the sequence as a scripted replay: a test that sends the same JSON-RPC messages directly without an LLM
3. CI runs the scripted replay — deterministic, fast, no API cost
4. Re-run the real LLM test only when the MCP interface changes (new tool, renamed argument, updated description)

### Why this is non-obvious
The instinct is to either test with real LLM calls (slow, expensive, non-deterministic) or mock at the HTTP level (doesn't test the actual protocol). Protocol capture + replay gets determinism without mocking — you're testing the same message sequence the LLM actually uses.

entries.title: InMemoryWorkItemStore.scan() filters by currentPrincipal.tenancyId() — explicit tenancyId on request makes WorkItems invisible
entries.body:
InMemoryWorkItemStore.scan() filters by currentPrincipal.tenancyId() — explicit tenancyId on request makes WorkItems invisible

### Symptom
WorkItem is created successfully (handler logs confirm creation) but `workItemStore.scanAll()` returns an empty list. No error, no warning — the WorkItem silently vanishes from query results.

### Context
Occurs in `@QuarkusTest` suites using `InMemoryWorkItemStore` (the `@Alternative @Priority(1)` test implementation). The test creates a WorkItem via `WorkItemCreator.create(request)` with `tenancyId` set explicitly on the `WorkItemCreateRequest`, then queries with `workItemStore.scanAll()`.

### What was tried (didn't work)
- Verified the WorkItem was created (handler log confirmed)
- Checked CDI wiring (WorkItemSpiAdapter correctly resolved)
- Verified InMemoryWorkItemStore was the active alternative

### Root cause
`InMemoryWorkItemStore` has an asymmetry between `put()` and `scan()`:

- `put()` stamps `tenancyId` from `currentPrincipal.tenancyId()` **only when the WorkItem's tenancyId is null**
- `scan()` (and therefore `scanAll()`) filters results by `currentPrincipal.tenancyId()` **always**

When the `WorkItemCreateRequest` sets `tenancyId` explicitly (e.g. `"test-tenant"`), the value flows through `WorkItemService.create()` to the entity. `put()` sees a non-null tenancyId and does not override it. But `scan()` filters by whatever `currentPrincipal.tenancyId()` returns — which may be a different value (e.g. the platform default tenant).

Result: the WorkItem is in the store's `ConcurrentHashMap` but filtered out by every query.

### Fix
Do not set `tenancyId` on the `WorkItemCreateRequest` in test contexts. Let `InMemoryWorkItemStore.put()` stamp it from `currentPrincipal`. This ensures `put()` and `scan()` use the same tenant value.

```java
// BAD — tenancyId may not match currentPrincipal
WorkItemCreateRequest.builder()
    .title("Review")
    .tenancyId(event.tenancyId())  // explicit — bypasses put() stamp
    .build();

// GOOD — let the store stamp tenancyId from currentPrincipal
WorkItemCreateRequest.builder()
    .title("Review")
    // no .tenancyId() — put() stamps from currentPrincipal
    .build();
```

### Why this is non-obvious
The old code path (direct entity mutation + `workItem.persist()`) never hit this because `persist()` goes to JPA/Panache, not `InMemoryWorkItemStore.put()`. The tenancy filtering only matters when both creation and querying go through the in-memory store — which happens when migrating from runtime service calls to SPI calls (`WorkItemCreator`).

### Alternatives considered
- Setting `currentPrincipal.tenancyId()` to match the explicit value — possible but requires test infrastructure changes and couples tests to tenant identity
- Removing the tenancy filter from `InMemoryWorkItemStore.scan()` — would break multi-tenant test isolation

entries.title: @Alternative @Priority(1) from an external JAR does not override a non-alternative bean in Quarkus — needs exclude-types + selected-alternatives
entries.body:
@Alternative @Priority(1) from an external JAR does not override a non-alternative bean in Quarkus — needs exclude-types + selected-alternatives

## Symptom

Test assertions calling `workItemStore.scanAll()` return empty even though the handler log confirms `WorkItemService.create()` ran successfully. `planItem.getStatus()` is `RUNNING` (proving the handler completed), but the store shows nothing.

## Context

Two `WorkItemStore` beans on the test classpath:
- `JpaWorkItemStore @ApplicationScoped` — production bean from `casehub-work`
- `InMemoryWorkItemStore @Alternative @Priority(1)` — test replacement from `casehub-work-testing`

CDI 4.x spec says `@Priority` on an alternative activates it globally and it should win over non-alternatives. In Quarkus ARC 3.32.2 this does not hold when the alternative comes from an external dependency JAR.

## What was tried

- Adding `InMemoryWorkItemStore` to `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` alone → "Ambiguous dependencies" deployment failure (both beans active simultaneously)
- `quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.work.runtime.repository.jpa.JpaWorkItemStore` alone → no effect; `JpaWorkItemStore` still wins
- `@Inject InMemoryWorkItemStore workItemStore` (concrete type) in the test → bypasses CDI alternative selection; test clears the right store but `WorkItemService` still writes to JPA (H2), so `scanAll()` returns empty

## Root Cause

`@Alternative @Priority(1)` from a dependency JAR is not treated as overriding a non-alternative `@ApplicationScoped` bean by Quarkus ARC. CDI spec §2.6.2 requires `@Priority` alternatives to take precedence, but ARC's resolution appears to treat both as equally active candidates when neither is the local application class. The non-alternative wins or ambiguity is raised.

## Fix

Combine both in `src/test/resources/application.properties`:

```properties
# Remove the JPA impl from CDI discovery entirely
quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.work.runtime.repository.jpa.JpaWorkItemStore

# Explicitly select the in-memory replacement
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=\
  io.casehub.work.testing.InMemoryWorkItemStore,\
  ...other alternatives...
```

With `JpaWorkItemStore` excluded, `InMemoryWorkItemStore` is the only active `WorkItemStore` bean. Explicit `selected-alternatives` listing then activates it. Both `WorkItemService` (via `@Inject WorkItemStore`) and the test (via `@Inject InMemoryWorkItemStore`) now reference the same singleton, and `scanAll()` finds what `create()` stored.

## Why this is non-obvious

CDI 4.x spec (and Quarkus docs on alternatives) state that `@Alternative @Priority(n)` globally activates and prioritises the alternative. A developer familiar with CDI 4.x would expect `@Priority(1)` to simply work. The failure is silent — no warning is emitted, `JpaWorkItemStore` just wins quietly. The symptom (empty `scanAll()`) points toward a different root cause (session caching, test isolation) and sends debugging in the wrong direction.

**See also:** [GE-20260429-a79d0e](GE-20260429-a79d0e.md) — @Alternative @Priority auto-activates within same module | [GE-20260521-4de4f1](GE-20260521-4de4f1.md) — TestProfile.getEnabledAlternatives() replaces selected-alternatives entirely

**See also:** [GE-20260601-cee623](GE-20260601-cee623.md) — QuarkusTestProfile.getEnabledAlternatives() replaces selected-alternatives entirely

**See also:** [GE-20260601-848232](GE-20260601-848232.md) — exclude-types silently does nothing for beans from Jandex-indexed JARs

**See also:** [GE-20260604-2f0889](GE-20260604-2f0889.md) — @Alternative @Priority(N) stubs appear in @All List<T> alongside original bean

**See also:** [GE-20260616-d70e7e](GE-20260616-d70e7e.md) — selected-alternatives silently accepts non-@Alternative beans

entries.title: Panache static methods bypass CDI @Alternative stores — returns empty results silently
entries.body:
Panache static methods bypass CDI @Alternative stores — returns empty results silently

## Panache static methods bypass CDI @Alternative stores — returns empty results silently

### Symptom

Test suite activates `@Alternative @Priority(1)` InMemory stores via `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives`. Panache static queries (`Entity.<Entity>listAll()`, `Entity.find(...)`) return zero results with no error, even though data was inserted through the store.

### Root cause

Panache static methods resolve directly against JPA at the persistence layer, bypassing CDI entirely. `@Alternative` implementations intercept calls made through injected CDI interfaces, not through static Panache entry points. With InMemory stores active, the JPA entity tables are empty — Panache statics query empty tables and return zero results silently.

### Fix

In test code that activates InMemory stores, never use Panache statics to query domain entities. Always go through the injected store or service layer:

```java
// Wrong — bypasses CDI alternative, queries empty JPA table
List<Channel> channels = Channel.<Channel>listAll();

// Correct — routes through the injected alternative store
List<Channel> channels = channelStore.findAll();
// or via service/tool layer
var result = tools.listChannels();
```

### Why this is non-obvious

Panache statics look like repository methods and feel like they should respect CDI alternatives — but they don't. No error is thrown, no warning is logged; the query simply returns an empty collection. The only signal is silently wrong test data.

**See also:** [GE-20260429-a79d0e](GE-20260429-a79d0e.md) — @Alternative @Priority auto-activates without quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives

**See also:** [GE-20260519-f33c66](GE-20260519-f33c66.md) — 'Reactive' service classes may use Panache statics internally — CDI @Alternative doesn't intercept

**See also:** [GE-20260528-3d3847](GE-20260528-3d3847.md) — @Transactional on @BeforeAll static methods has no effect (same CDI proxy limitation)

**See also:** [GE-20260608-d223af](GE-20260608-d223af.md) — REST Assured GPath $.findAll returns null (not []) — Hamcrest not(empty()) silently passes on null

**See also:** [GE-20260609-49bd08](GE-20260609-49bd08.md) — static Panache entity calls bypass injected store tenant filtering

casehub-engine-persistence-memory @Alternative beans need explicit selected-alternatives for SubCaseGroupRepository and PlanItemStore
entries.body:
casehub-engine-persistence-memory @Alternative beans need explicit selected-alternatives for SubCaseGroupRepository and PlanItemStore

### Symptom

Quarkus startup fails with:

```
jakarta.enterprise.inject.spi.DeploymentException: Found 2 deployment problems:
[1] Unsatisfied dependency for type io.casehub.engine.common.spi.SubCaseGroupRepository
    - injection target: SubCaseExecutionHandler constructor
[2] Unsatisfied dependency for type io.casehub.engine.common.spi.SubCaseGroupRepository
    - injection target: SubCaseCompletionService constructor
```

### Context

When a CaseHub harness adds `casehub-engine-blackboard` (required for SubCase lifecycle and M-of-N quorum) alongside `casehub-engine-persistence-memory`, the blackboard beans (`SubCaseExecutionHandler`, `SubCaseCompletionService`) need `SubCaseGroupRepository`. The in-memory implementation (`MemorySubCaseGroupRepository`) exists in persistence-memory but is `@Alternative @ApplicationScoped` — CDI does not activate `@Alternative` beans unless explicitly selected.

The same applies to `MemoryPlanItemStore` and `MemoryReactivePlanItemStore` from the same module.

### What was tried (didn't work)

- Adding Jandex index entries for persistence-memory — beans are discovered but not activated (they're @Alternative)
- Assuming engine-testing would provide @Priority(1) overrides — engine-testing has TestCaseMetaModelRepository, TestCaseInstanceRepository, TestEventLogRepository but NOT TestSubCaseGroupRepository or TestPlanItemStore

### Root cause

`casehub-engine-persistence-memory` ships all repository implementations as `@Alternative @ApplicationScoped` — they require explicit `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` to be activated. Engine-testing provides `@Priority(1)` overrides for CaseInstanceRepository and EventLogRepository but not for SubCaseGroupRepository or PlanItemStore.

### Fix

Add to `application.properties` (test or production):

```properties
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.MemorySubCaseGroupRepository,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.MemoryPlanItemStore,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.MemoryReactivePlanItemStore
```

Append to existing `selected-alternatives` if other beans (e.g. `JpaLedgerEntryRepository`) are already listed.

### Why this is non-obvious

The error names `SubCaseGroupRepository` — but `MemorySubCaseGroupRepository` IS on the classpath and IS Jandex-indexed. The CDI error doesn't mention that the bean exists but is an unselected `@Alternative`. You have to read the source of `MemorySubCaseGroupRepository` to discover the `@Alternative` annotation, then check whether engine-testing provides an override (it doesn't for these SPIs).

## Variant — Runtime failure from implicit activation of remaining @Alternative beans

### Symptom

`@QuarkusTest` starts cleanly (no DeploymentException) because `casehub-engine-testing` provides `@Priority(1)` overrides for `CaseInstanceRepository` and `EventLogRepository`. But the first `startCase()` call in certain test classes fails with:

```
(RECIPIENT_FAILURE,8191) CaseInstance not found or wrong tenant: <uuid>
```

The error comes from `InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository.update()` (persistence-memory) — the bean is implicitly activated by Quarkus Arc as the sole `@Alternative` without a competing non-alternative, but the activation path produces intermittent initialization-order failures.

### Context

When only `SubCaseGroupRepository` and `PlanItemStore` are in `selected-alternatives`, the remaining 4 `@Alternative` beans from persistence-memory rely on Arc's implicit fallback activation:
- `InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository`
- `InMemoryCaseMetaModelRepository`
- `InMemoryEventLogRepository`
- `MemoryReactivePlanItemStore`

This implicit activation works for most test classes but fails intermittently when the test class is among the first to trigger `startCase()` in a fresh JVM — the `CaseStartedEventHandler` calls `caseInstanceRepository.update()` and the instance isn't found.

### Fix

Add all 4 remaining persistence-memory `@Alternative` beans to `selected-alternatives`:

```properties
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=\
  ...,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryCaseMetaModelRepository,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryEventLogRepository,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.MemoryReactivePlanItemStore
```

Verified in casehub-aml#58: 4 of 6 failing test classes fixed by explicit selection. 2 remaining failures (`AmlLayer7ResourceTest`, `AmlTrustRoutingAttestationTest`) may have a deeper root cause — investigation ongoing.

'Reactive' Quarkus service classes may use blocking services or Panache statics internally — CDI @Alternative in-memory stores don't intercept those paths
entries.body:
'Reactive' Quarkus service classes may use blocking services or Panache statics internally — CDI @Alternative in-memory stores don't intercept those paths

### What is undocumented

A service class annotated `@Alternative` and named with "Reactive" may internally use a `blockingService` field (injected blocking CDI service) for write operations and `Entity.find()` (a Panache static) for read operations. CDI `@Alternative @Priority(1)` in-memory stores only intercept at CDI injection points — Panache statics go directly to the underlying database regardless of what alternatives are selected.

### Context

In Quarkus Qhorus (casehubio/qhorus), `ReactiveQhorusMcpTools`:
- `sendMessage()` delegates internally to `blockingMessageService` → `MessageService.send()` → `messageStore.put()` (uses the `MessageStore` CDI alternative, i.e. `InMemoryMessageStore` in tests)
- `getChannelTimeline()` delegates to `blockingGetChannelTimeline()` → `Message.<Message>find(...)` (Panache static — queries H2 directly, bypasses `MessageStore` entirely)

Result: messages written by `sendMessage()` land in `InMemoryMessageStore` (in-memory). Messages read by `getChannelTimeline()` come from H2 (empty in tests). The two paths never share data.

### Discovery

Only visible by reading the service implementation source. The class name and method signatures suggest a uniform reactive abstraction. Not mentioned in any documentation.

### Impact on tests

Tests that call `sendMessage()` then verify the timeline via `getChannelTimeline()` always see an empty timeline in test setups using `@Alternative` in-memory stores, even though the message was "successfully" posted.

### Fix / Workaround

Identify the actual data path for each operation you need to test:
1. Check which CDI service field the MCP tool method delegates to
2. Check whether that service uses CDI store injection or Panache statics
3. For end-to-end write→read tests: use the real H2 database (don't rely on in-memory stores for both sides)

Alternatively, file an upstream issue to make the read path use the same abstraction as the write path.

**See also:** [GE-20260512-66d997](GE-20260512-66d997.md) — Panache static methods bypass CDI @Alternative stores

quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives default priority 1 creates tie with @Priority(1) subclass beans — two @ApplicationScoped instances with separate state
entries.body:
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives default priority 1 creates tie with @Priority(1) subclass beans — two @ApplicationScoped instances with separate state

### Symptom
`CaseInstance not found or wrong tenant` (or similar state-not-found error) despite the instance being saved moments earlier. The save and lookup use the same `CaseInstanceRepository` interface, but they resolve to different `@ApplicationScoped` bean instances with separate `ConcurrentHashMap` stores.

### Context
`casehub-engine-testing` provides `TestCaseInstanceRepository extends InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository` with `@Alternative @Priority(1) @ApplicationScoped`. This is the standard test harness — it auto-activates without `selected-alternatives`.

A consumer project adds `InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository` to `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` in test `application.properties`, thinking it's redundant but harmless.

### What was tried (didn't work)
- Checking event bus threading and Vert.x serialization — object identity was intact
- Verifying `currentPrincipal.tenancyId()` consistency — MockCurrentPrincipal returns a constant
- Adding more beans to `selected-alternatives` — made it worse

### Root cause
Quarkus Arc assigns a **default priority of 1** to alternatives listed in `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` that don't have `@Priority`. This creates a priority tie:

- `InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository` — priority 1 (from `selected-alternatives` default)
- `TestCaseInstanceRepository` — priority 1 (from `@Priority(1)`)

Both are `@ApplicationScoped`, so CDI creates **two separate bean instances**. Each has its own `ConcurrentHashMap<UUID, CaseInstance> store`. If CDI resolves different injection points to different beans (or resolves non-deterministically), saves go to one store and lookups to another.

### Fix
Do not add parent classes to `selected-alternatives` when the engine-testing module already provides `@Priority(1)` subclasses:

```properties
# WRONG — creates priority tie with TestCaseInstanceRepository
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=...,io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository

# RIGHT — let engine-testing's @Priority(1) beans handle it
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=...
# (omit InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository, InMemoryCaseMetaModelRepository, InMemoryEventLogRepository)
```

The engine-testing module exists specifically to provide auto-activating alternatives for test contexts. Adding the parent classes to `selected-alternatives` defeats the purpose.

### Why this is non-obvious
Adding a class to `selected-alternatives` feels like an explicit, high-confidence activation — surely it would "win" over a `@Priority(1)` subclass. But the default priority is also 1, creating an exact tie. The Quarkus docs mention the default priority but don't warn about ties with existing `@Priority(1)` alternatives on the classpath. The symptom (state not found) appears as a threading or serialization bug, not a CDI resolution issue.

quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives silently ignores %dev. profile overrides — use exclude-types instead
entries.body:
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives silently ignores %dev. profile overrides — use exclude-types instead

### Symptom
`%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` is set in `application.properties` alongside a non-profiled `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives`. In dev mode, the `@Alternative` beans listed in the `%dev.` value are never activated — ArC throws `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` for the interfaces they implement, even though the beans exist on the classpath and have Jandex indices.

### Context
Multi-profile Quarkus application needing different CDI alternatives per environment:
- Production: reactive JPA stores (`engine-persistence-hibernate`)
- Dev mode: in-memory blocking stores (`engine-persistence-memory`)
- Tests: separate `application.properties` with its own `selected-alternatives`

Both `%dev.` and non-profiled values present in the same `application.properties`.

### What was tried (didn't work)
1. `%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=MemoryPlanItemStore,...` alongside non-profiled `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=JpaPlanItemStore,...` — dev alternatives silently ignored
2. Removing the non-profiled value and using only `%dev.` and `%prod.` — still ignored
3. Verified `%dev.quarkus.arc.exclude-types` DOES work (OidcCurrentPrincipal successfully excluded in dev) — confirms profile overrides work for other ArC properties

### Root cause
`quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` is a build-time fixed property that does not honour `%profile.` prefixes. The property is resolved once during Quarkus augmentation and profile-specific values are silently discarded. This is not documented — the Quarkus configuration reference does not distinguish which ArC properties support profile overrides.

### Fix
Select ALL alternatives (both JPA and memory) in the non-profiled `selected-alternatives`. Use profile-specific `exclude-types` to control which survive in each environment:

```properties
# Non-profiled: select everything — both JPA and memory alternatives
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=\
  io.casehub.persistence.jpa.JpaPlanItemStore,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.MemoryPlanItemStore,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryCaseMetaModelRepository

# Dev: exclude reactive JPA stores → memory stores win
%dev.quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.persistence.jpa.JpaPlanItemStore,...

# Prod: exclude memory stores → JPA stores win
%prod.quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.persistence.memory.MemoryPlanItemStore,...
```

ArC processes `exclude-types` first (removing beans entirely), then resolves `selected-alternatives` among surviving beans. In each profile, only one alternative per interface survives — no ambiguity.

### Why this is non-obvious
Profile-specific overrides (`%dev.`, `%prod.`) work for most Quarkus properties, including `quarkus.arc.exclude-types`. The natural assumption is that `selected-alternatives` follows the same pattern. There is no error, warning, or log message when the profile override is ignored — the non-profiled value is silently used. The failure manifests as `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` with no hint about profile resolution.

### Why this fix
`exclude-types` is a coarser mechanism (removes the bean entirely vs just not selecting it), but it's the only ArC property that supports profile overrides. The exclude-types-first-then-resolve pattern is architecturally sound: each profile starts from the same selected set and carves out what doesn't belong.

### Alternatives considered
- **Maven profiles** — add/remove JARs per profile. Rejected: adds build complexity and doesn't work with `quarkus:dev` which uses the default Maven profile.
- **`@IfBuildProfile("dev")` wrapper beans** — create dev-only `@ApplicationScoped` beans that delegate to memory stores. Rejected: code duplication across 5+ SPIs, maintenance burden.
- **Separate `application-dev.properties`** — Quarkus doesn't support this pattern (it's a Spring Boot convention).

entries.title: Zero-duplication reactive test doubles: wrap InMemory*Store in a delegation shell returning Uni
@DefaultBean BlockingToReactiveBridge — wrap any blocking SPI as reactive, displaced by native async @Alternative
entries.body:
@DefaultBean BlockingToReactiveBridge — wrap any blocking SPI as reactive, displaced by native async @Alternative

## Context

You have a blocking SPI (`CaseMemoryStore`) in a zero-dep API module and need to expose a
reactive mirror (`ReactiveCaseMemoryStore`) so callers using Mutiny can also use the same
backends. Most blocking adapters don't need true async execution — wrapping them as
`Uni.createFrom().item(supplier)` is sufficient. But occasional adapters (e.g. a graph
database with native async traversal) do benefit from a true reactive implementation.

## What developers reach for instead

- Two independent SPIs with no connection — adapters implement both, duplicating logic
- Make the reactive SPI extend the blocking SPI — creates tight coupling and forces adapters
  to implement both interface families
- A single abstract class with default delegation — doesn't play well with CDI proxies

## The Technique

Define the blocking SPI in the zero-dep API module. Define the reactive SPI separately
(in the Quarkus module, because `Uni<>` depends on Smallrye Mutiny). Ship a
`@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` bridge class that injects the active blocking impl and
wraps each method:

```java
@DefaultBean
@ApplicationScoped
public class BlockingToReactiveBridge implements ReactiveCaseMemoryStore {

@Inject CaseMemoryStore delegate;   // whatever blocking impl is active

@Override
    public Uni<String> store(MemoryInput input) {
        return Uni.createFrom().item(() -> delegate.store(input));
    }

@Override
    public Uni<List<Memory>> query(MemoryQuery query) {
        return Uni.createFrom().item(() -> delegate.query(query));
    }

@Override
    public Uni<Void> erase(EraseRequest request) {
        return Uni.createFrom().voidItem().invoke(() -> delegate.erase(request));
    }
}
```

The CDI priority ladder then becomes:

| Tier | Class | Annotation | Active when |
|------|-------|-----------|-------------|
| 0 | `NoOpCaseMemoryStore` | `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` | No adapter |
| — | `BlockingToReactiveBridge` | `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` | Always (wraps Tier 0–2) |
| 1 | Memori adapter | `@ApplicationScoped` | Memori dep declared |
| 2 | Mem0 adapter | `@Alternative @Priority(1)` | Mem0 dep declared |
| 3 | Graphiti native-reactive | `@Alternative @Priority(2)` on `ReactiveCaseMemoryStore` | Graphiti dep declared |

When Graphiti (Tier 3) is added, it overrides the `ReactiveCaseMemoryStore` binding directly
via its higher-priority `@Alternative` — the bridge's `@DefaultBean` yields automatically.
Tier 3 does NOT need to implement the blocking SPI at all.

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

The `@DefaultBean` on the bridge is the key: it means both the bridge AND any blocking
adapter can coexist on the classpath without CDI ambiguity. The bridge always yields to a
native-reactive `@Alternative` on `ReactiveCaseMemoryStore`, and the blocking adapter
displaces the no-op on `CaseMemoryStore`. Each priority rung resolves independently.

Without `@DefaultBean`, a plain `@ApplicationScoped` bridge would collide with any real
`ReactiveCaseMemoryStore` implementation (ARC sees two beans for the same type and fails at
startup).

**Note:** Do NOT add `@Blocking` to bridge methods. `ExecutionModelAnnotationsProcessor`
rejects it on plain CDI bean methods returning `Uni` — only framework entrypoints accept it.
Thread dispatch is the entrypoint's responsibility. (See GE-20260528-74914d.)

## See Also

- `GE-20260521-d72294` — blocking and reactive store interfaces with irreconcilable signatures; this bridge avoids the problem by not having one class implement both
- `GE-20260528-74914d` — `@Blocking` rejected on CDI bean methods returning `Uni`

**See also:** [GE-20260620-9d043b](GE-20260620-9d043b.md) — CDI @Decorator double-application through blocking-to-reactive bridge — idempotency guard required (the gotcha this pattern creates)

entries.title: Quarkus ARC @DefaultBean injection points resolve before @Alternative activation in external JARs
entries.body:
Quarkus ARC @DefaultBean injection points resolve before @Alternative activation in external JARs

### Symptom

A `@DefaultBean` reactive bridge (`BlockingToReactiveCbrBridge`) that injects a blocking SPI interface (`CbrCaseMemoryStore`) silently resolves to the no-op `@DefaultBean` implementation (`NoOpCbrCaseMemoryStore`) instead of the `@Alternative @Priority(2)` in-memory implementation (`InMemoryCbrCaseMemoryStore`), even when:

- The alternative is listed in `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives`
- Both JARs are indexed via `quarkus.index-dependency`
- Direct injection of the blocking interface in a test class correctly resolves to the alternative

The retrieval returns empty with no error or warning — completely silent.

### Context

This occurs when three beans implement the same interface across two external JARs:

- **JAR A** (`casehub-neocortex-memory`): `NoOpCbrCaseMemoryStore` (`@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped`) and `BlockingToReactiveCbrBridge` (`@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped`, injects `CbrCaseMemoryStore`)
- **JAR B** (`casehub-neocortex-memory-cbr-inmem`): `InMemoryCbrCaseMemoryStore` (`@Alternative @Priority(2) @ApplicationScoped`)

The bridge in JAR A is supposed to delegate to whichever `CbrCaseMemoryStore` is active. When `InMemoryCbrCaseMemoryStore` is activated via `selected-alternatives`, direct injection works — but the bridge's own injection point does not.

### What was tried (didn't work)

1. Adding `quarkus.index-dependency` for both JARs — no effect on resolution
2. Adding `InMemoryCbrCaseMemoryStore` to `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` in the memory profile — direct injection works, bridge delegation does not
3. Adding `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` for `NoOpCbrCaseMemoryStore` — breaks CDI wiring entirely (the bridge has no delegate)

### Root cause

Quarkus ARC resolves `@DefaultBean` beans' injection points at build time. When the bridge (`@DefaultBean`) is being wired, ARC resolves its `@Inject CbrCaseMemoryStore` using the standard `@DefaultBean` resolution rules — which picks the other `@DefaultBean` (`NoOpCbrCaseMemoryStore`) in the same JAR. The `@Alternative` from the external JAR is not considered for the bridge's injection point even though it would be selected for direct injection sites.

Confirmed via `System.identityHashCode()` tracing: both the test's `@Inject CbrCaseMemoryStore` and the bridge's `@Inject CbrCaseMemoryStore delegate` resolve to the same `NoOpCbrCaseMemoryStore_ClientProxy` instance.

### Solution 1 — Bypass the reactive bridge

**Approach:** Inject the blocking interface directly and offload to a worker thread.

**Pros:** No CDI resolution ambiguity. Works with any test profile.

**Cons:** Caller must handle thread offloading explicitly.

```java
@ApplicationScoped
public class MyService {
    @Inject CbrCaseMemoryStore cbrStore; // blocking, not reactive

public Uni<List<Result>> retrieve(Query query) {
        return Uni.createFrom()
            .item(() -> cbrStore.retrieveSimilar(query, MyCase.class))
            .runSubscriptionOn(Infrastructure.getDefaultWorkerPool())
            .map(this::mapResults);
    }
}
```

### Solution 2 — Use QuarkusTestProfile.getEnabledAlternatives()

**Approach:** Override alternatives programmatically in the test profile.

**Pros:** Properly activates @Alternative beans for all injection points including bridge delegates.

**Cons:** `getEnabledAlternatives()` REPLACES (not appends to) `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` — ALL alternatives from the base profile must be re-declared. Missing one breaks other tests sharing the profile.

```java
public static class MemoryProfile implements QuarkusTestProfile {
    @Override
    public String getConfigProfile() { return "memory"; }

@Override
    public Set<Class<?>> getEnabledAlternatives() {
        return Set.of(
            InMemoryCaseMetaModelRepository.class,
            InMemoryReactiveCaseMetaModelRepository.class,
            // ... ALL other memory profile alternatives ...
            InMemoryCbrCaseMemoryStore.class);
    }
}
```

### Why this is non-obvious

The bridge pattern (`@DefaultBean` reactive wrapper delegating to `@DefaultBean` blocking implementation, replaced by `@Alternative` at test time) is a standard Quarkus CDI pattern. Nothing in Quarkus documentation warns that `@DefaultBean` injection points resolve before `@Alternative` activation. The failure is completely silent — no ambiguity error, no warning, just empty results from the no-op. Only `System.identityHashCode()` tracing reveals which implementation was actually injected.

### Why this fix

Solution 1 (bypass the bridge) is preferred because it eliminates the CDI resolution issue entirely and has no test infrastructure side effects. Solution 2 works but creates a maintenance burden — every new alternative added to the memory profile must also be added to every `getEnabledAlternatives()` override.

### Alternatives considered

- `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` for the no-op: breaks CDI wiring when the bridge needs a delegate and no alternative is available
- Using `Instance<CbrCaseMemoryStore>` with programmatic lookup: adds complexity without addressing the root cause
- Filing a Quarkus ARC bug: may be working as designed (build-time CDI optimisation)

entries.title: Panache static methods bypass CDI @Alternative stores — returns empty results silently
entries.body:
Panache static methods bypass CDI @Alternative stores — returns empty results silently

## Panache static methods bypass CDI @Alternative stores — returns empty results silently

### Symptom

Test suite activates `@Alternative @Priority(1)` InMemory stores via `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives`. Panache static queries (`Entity.<Entity>listAll()`, `Entity.find(...)`) return zero results with no error, even though data was inserted through the store.

### Root cause

Panache static methods resolve directly against JPA at the persistence layer, bypassing CDI entirely. `@Alternative` implementations intercept calls made through injected CDI interfaces, not through static Panache entry points. With InMemory stores active, the JPA entity tables are empty — Panache statics query empty tables and return zero results silently.

### Fix

In test code that activates InMemory stores, never use Panache statics to query domain entities. Always go through the injected store or service layer:

```java
// Wrong — bypasses CDI alternative, queries empty JPA table
List<Channel> channels = Channel.<Channel>listAll();

// Correct — routes through the injected alternative store
List<Channel> channels = channelStore.findAll();
// or via service/tool layer
var result = tools.listChannels();
```

### Why this is non-obvious

Panache statics look like repository methods and feel like they should respect CDI alternatives — but they don't. No error is thrown, no warning is logged; the query simply returns an empty collection. The only signal is silently wrong test data.

**See also:** [GE-20260429-a79d0e](GE-20260429-a79d0e.md) — @Alternative @Priority auto-activates without quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives

**See also:** [GE-20260519-f33c66](GE-20260519-f33c66.md) — 'Reactive' service classes may use Panache statics internally — CDI @Alternative doesn't intercept

**See also:** [GE-20260528-3d3847](GE-20260528-3d3847.md) — @Transactional on @BeforeAll static methods has no effect (same CDI proxy limitation)

**See also:** [GE-20260608-d223af](GE-20260608-d223af.md) — REST Assured GPath $.findAll returns null (not []) — Hamcrest not(empty()) silently passes on null

**See also:** [GE-20260609-49bd08](GE-20260609-49bd08.md) — static Panache entity calls bypass injected store tenant filtering

entries.title: @ApplicationScoped CDI proxy silently returns empty/null for direct field access — only method calls dispatch to the real bean
entries.body:
@ApplicationScoped CDI proxy silently returns empty/null for direct field access — only method calls dispatch to the real bean

## Symptom

A sibling CDI bean injects another `@ApplicationScoped` bean as a concrete type and accesses a package-private field on it:

```java
@Inject
InMemoryLedgerEntryRepository blocking;

// Inside a method:
blocking.entries.values().stream()...  // returns null or empty
```

The code compiles and no exception is thrown, but the field always reads as null/default, even though `blocking.save()` has populated it. Tests pass but return wrong results.

## Context

Occurred when building `InMemoryKeyRotationRepository`, which needed to read entries saved via `InMemoryLedgerEntryRepository`. The entry repo is `@ApplicationScoped`, injected into the key rotation repo via `@Inject InMemoryLedgerEntryRepository blocking`. Direct field access `blocking.entries` read the proxy's own uninitialized `entries` field, not the underlying singleton's populated map.

## Root Cause

`@ApplicationScoped` beans are wrapped in a client proxy. The proxy class extends the bean class and overrides all methods to delegate to the underlying contextual instance. However, **field reads on the proxy class access the proxy's own fields** — which are never initialized by the CDI container. Only method calls are intercepted and dispatched to the underlying singleton.

## Fix

Expose shared state via a package-private method on the owning class:

```java
// In InMemoryLedgerEntryRepository:
Collection<LedgerEntry> allEntries() {
    return entries.values();  // reads from the real singleton's field
}

// In InMemoryKeyRotationRepository:
blocking.allEntries().stream()...  // method call dispatches through proxy → real bean
```

The method call reaches the underlying singleton; `entries` is read from the real instance's field.

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

The proxy class extends the bean class, so `blocking.entries` looks syntactically valid and compiles without error. The CDI proxy pattern is commonly explained in terms of method interception — the field-access subtlety is almost never mentioned. The failure mode is also invisible: no exception, no null pointer — just an empty stream that silently produces no results, which looks like the store is empty rather than pointing at the wrong object.

### Why this fix

Exposing the field via a method is idiomatic and minimal. Alternatives like `@Produces` a `ConcurrentHashMap` or using CDI events are more complex without architectural benefit. Package-private visibility ensures the method is test-accessible within the same package while remaining an implementation detail outside it.

**See also:** [GE-20260522-99b6a0](GE-20260522-99b6a0.md) — @ApplicationScoped CDI proxy swallows field writes in test doubles

**See also:** [GE-20260608-d223af](GE-20260608-d223af.md) — REST Assured GPath $.findAll returns null — Hamcrest not(empty()) silently passes

**See also:** [GE-20260614-42f5ca](GE-20260614-42f5ca.md) — getClass().getSimpleName() on @ApplicationScoped CDI bean returns proxy class name

Hibernate dirty-check flushes PanacheEntity field writes inside Panache.withSession() — even for in-memory test stores
entries.body:
Hibernate dirty-check flushes PanacheEntity field writes inside Panache.withSession() — even for in-memory test stores

### Symptom
A JPA UPDATE fires for a field write on a `PanacheEntity` subclass, even though:
- The CDI injection test confirms the in-memory store (`InMemoryReactiveChannelStore`) is selected, not the JPA store
- The entity was created with `new Channel()` — never explicitly `persist()`ed or loaded in the current session
- `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` is correctly configured

Error:
```
org.hibernate.QueryParameterException: No argument for named parameter ':tenancyId'
```

### Context
`ReactiveMessageService.dispatch()` wraps the entire dispatch in `Panache.withSession("qhorus", () -> ...)`. Inside that session scope, the in-memory store's `updateLastActivity()` does:

```java
channel.lastActivityAt = Instant.now();
```

`Channel` is a Hibernate-enhanced `PanacheEntity`. The field write is intercepted by Hibernate's dirty tracker within the active session scope and generates a JPA UPDATE at session flush.

### Root cause
Hibernate's bytecode enhancement instruments all `PanacheEntity` subclasses with dirty tracking. Any field write on an enhanced entity within an active `Panache.withSession()` scope is detected and queued for flush — regardless of whether the entity was explicitly persisted or loaded in that session. The CDI injection test proves the right bean is injected, but it does not reveal that Hibernate's session-scoped dirty tracker is intercepting field mutations on enhanced entities.

### Fix
Make the in-memory store's `updateLastActivity()` a no-op. Do not modify enhanced entity fields in-place within a `withSession()` scope:

```java
@Override
public Uni<Void> updateLastActivity(UUID channelId, String tenancyId) {
    // No-op — modifying the Hibernate-enhanced entity in-place triggers
    // a dirty-check flush when called from within Panache.withSession().
    return Uni.createFrom().voidItem();
}
```

`lastActivityAt` is set at channel creation time via `put()`; staleness tracking is irrelevant in test contexts.

### Why this is non-obvious
The CDI direct injection test is a convincing false positive: `@Inject ReactiveChannelStore` returns `InMemoryReactiveChannelStore` ✅. This proves the right bean is injected, but it does not prove that field mutations on Hibernate-enhanced entities are safe within the dispatch session scope. The JPA UPDATE is generated by Hibernate's session-level flush mechanism, not by the in-memory store calling `repo.update()` directly.

entries.title: @Priority is NOT @Inherited — CDI proxy classes silently drop it from reflection, making bean ordering undefined
entries.body:
@Priority is NOT @Inherited — CDI proxy classes silently drop it from reflection, making bean ordering undefined

## @Priority is NOT @Inherited — CDI proxy classes silently drop it from reflection

### Symptom

Bean iteration order from `Instance<T>` is silently non-deterministic despite
`@Priority` annotations on all implementations. Sorting by
`resolver.getClass().getAnnotation(Priority.class)` returns `null` for every
bean, so all beans get `Integer.MAX_VALUE` and ordering is undefined.

### Context

When iterating CDI beans from `Instance<T>` and sorting by `@Priority` using
Java reflection. Common in composite/pipeline patterns where multiple
implementations of an SPI must execute in a defined order.

### Root cause

`@jakarta.annotation.Priority` is not meta-annotated with `@java.lang.annotation.Inherited`.
CDI proxy classes (e.g. `WebDIDResolver_ClientProxy`) are JDK subclasses of the
real bean class. `proxy.getClass().getAnnotation(Priority.class)` returns `null`
because the JDK only propagates annotations marked `@Inherited` to subclasses.

The proxy class itself carries no annotations — it is a synthetic subclass
generated by the CDI container solely for interception and scoping purposes.

### What was tried (didn't work)

```java
// Natural reflection approach — silently fails for all proxied beans
private static int priorityOf(DIDResolver resolver) {
    var priority = resolver.getClass().getAnnotation(Priority.class);
    return priority != null ? priority.value() : Integer.MAX_VALUE;
    // Always returns MAX_VALUE for proxied beans
}
```

### Fix

Use Quarkus Arc's `Instance.Handle` API to read bean metadata through the
CDI container rather than through reflection on the proxy class:

```java
@Inject
public CompositeDIDResolver(@DIDMethod Instance<DIDResolver> methodResolvers) {
    this.resolvers = methodResolvers.handles().stream()
            .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(h -> priorityOf(h)))
            .map(Instance.Handle::get)
            .collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList());
}

private static int priorityOf(Instance.Handle<?> handle) {
    var bean = handle.getBean();
    if (bean instanceof InjectableBean<?> injectable) {
        Integer p = injectable.getPriority();
        if (p != null) return p;
    }
    return Integer.MAX_VALUE;
}
```

Arc stores priority metadata at container build time (augmentation), independent
of proxy reflection. `InjectableBean.getPriority()` reads this stored value.

### Why this is non-obvious

`getClass().getAnnotation()` is the natural Java reflection approach for reading
annotations. It works for many annotations and in many contexts. The `@Inherited`
requirement is a JDK detail that only matters when the object is a subclass of
the annotated class — a situation that is universal in CDI (every injected bean
is potentially proxied) but rarely encountered in direct reflection usage.

The failure is silent: no exception, no warning. The annotation simply isn't
found, and the fallback value (typically `Integer.MAX_VALUE` or a default
priority) is used for every bean, making ordering non-deterministic.

### Alternatives considered

- **Walk superclass chain:** `resolver.getClass().getSuperclass().getAnnotation(Priority.class)`
  — works for single-level proxies but fragile if proxy depth changes or if
  the container uses a different proxy strategy.
- **`@All List<InstanceHandle<T>>`:** Quarkus-specific injection that preserves
  metadata — equivalent to `Instance.handles()` but declared at the injection site.
