entries.title: Cross-repo SPI extends creates CDI bean displacement — standalone composition required
entries.body:
Cross-repo SPI extends creates CDI bean displacement — standalone composition required

### Symptom
CDI deployment fails with ambiguous bean resolution or unexpected bean displacement when
a neural-text module's `CbrCaseMemoryStore extends CaseMemoryStore` is on the classpath
alongside platform's `CaseMemoryStore` implementations (JPA, SQLite, inmem).

### Context
`GraphCaseMemoryStore extends CaseMemoryStore` works within casehub-platform because all
implementations share the same CDI bean archive. Cross-repo, the inheritance creates three
displacement paths:

1. `QdrantCbrCaseMemoryStore` (neural-text, `@ApplicationScoped`) also satisfies
   `CaseMemoryStore` injection points — displaces `JpaMemoryStore` by priority
2. `NoOpCbrCaseMemoryStore` (neural-text, `@DefaultBean`) also becomes a
   `CaseMemoryStore @DefaultBean` — conflicts with `NoOpCaseMemoryStore` (platform)
3. Any `@Alternative` on the subtype cascades to the parent type's injection sites

### Root cause
CDI bean type resolution includes all supertypes. A bean typed as
`CbrCaseMemoryStore extends CaseMemoryStore` is injectable at both
`@Inject CbrCaseMemoryStore` and `@Inject CaseMemoryStore`. When the SPI
and its extension live in different repos (different CDI archives), the
priority/default-bean resolution rules interact across archive boundaries
in ways that don't occur within a single archive.

### Fix
Make the extended SPI a **standalone interface** — do not extend the base SPI.
Use composition via delegation:

```java
// WRONG — causes displacement
public interface CbrCaseMemoryStore extends CaseMemoryStore { ... }

// RIGHT — standalone SPI, delegates internally
public interface CbrCaseMemoryStore {
    // own methods only — no CaseMemoryStore inheritance
}

// Implementation delegates to injected CaseMemoryStore
@ApplicationScoped
public class QdrantCbrCaseMemoryStore implements CbrCaseMemoryStore {
    @Inject CaseMemoryStore delegate;  // no priority conflict
}
```

### Why this is non-obvious
The `extends` pattern works within a single repo (`GraphCaseMemoryStore extends
CaseMemoryStore` in casehub-platform) because all beans share one CDI archive.
The failure only manifests when the extending SPI lives in a different repo,
which is exactly when composition-over-inheritance is architecturally correct
but not what developers reach for first.

### Alternatives considered
- `@Typed(CbrCaseMemoryStore.class)` annotation to restrict bean types — rejected because it
  must be applied to every implementation, is easy to forget on new implementations, and
  doesn't prevent the `@DefaultBean` dual-registration problem
- Qualifier annotation to distinguish CBR from base memory beans — rejected because it
  changes the injection site contract for all existing `CaseMemoryStore` consumers

entries.title: casehub-engine-persistence-memory @Alternative beans need explicit selected-alternatives for SubCaseGroupRepository and PlanItemStore
entries.body:
casehub-engine-persistence-memory @Alternative beans need explicit selected-alternatives for SubCaseGroupRepository and PlanItemStore

### Symptom

Quarkus startup fails with:

```
jakarta.enterprise.inject.spi.DeploymentException: Found 2 deployment problems:
[1] Unsatisfied dependency for type io.casehub.engine.common.spi.SubCaseGroupRepository
    - injection target: SubCaseExecutionHandler constructor
[2] Unsatisfied dependency for type io.casehub.engine.common.spi.SubCaseGroupRepository
    - injection target: SubCaseCompletionService constructor
```

### Context

When a CaseHub harness adds `casehub-engine-blackboard` (required for SubCase lifecycle and M-of-N quorum) alongside `casehub-engine-persistence-memory`, the blackboard beans (`SubCaseExecutionHandler`, `SubCaseCompletionService`) need `SubCaseGroupRepository`. The in-memory implementation (`MemorySubCaseGroupRepository`) exists in persistence-memory but is `@Alternative @ApplicationScoped` — CDI does not activate `@Alternative` beans unless explicitly selected.

The same applies to `MemoryPlanItemStore` and `MemoryReactivePlanItemStore` from the same module.

### What was tried (didn't work)

- Adding Jandex index entries for persistence-memory — beans are discovered but not activated (they're @Alternative)
- Assuming engine-testing would provide @Priority(1) overrides — engine-testing has TestCaseMetaModelRepository, TestCaseInstanceRepository, TestEventLogRepository but NOT TestSubCaseGroupRepository or TestPlanItemStore

### Root cause

`casehub-engine-persistence-memory` ships all repository implementations as `@Alternative @ApplicationScoped` — they require explicit `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` to be activated. Engine-testing provides `@Priority(1)` overrides for CaseInstanceRepository and EventLogRepository but not for SubCaseGroupRepository or PlanItemStore.

### Fix

Add to `application.properties` (test or production):

```properties
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.MemorySubCaseGroupRepository,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.MemoryPlanItemStore,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.MemoryReactivePlanItemStore
```

Append to existing `selected-alternatives` if other beans (e.g. `JpaLedgerEntryRepository`) are already listed.

### Why this is non-obvious

The error names `SubCaseGroupRepository` — but `MemorySubCaseGroupRepository` IS on the classpath and IS Jandex-indexed. The CDI error doesn't mention that the bean exists but is an unselected `@Alternative`. You have to read the source of `MemorySubCaseGroupRepository` to discover the `@Alternative` annotation, then check whether engine-testing provides an override (it doesn't for these SPIs).

## Variant — Runtime failure from implicit activation of remaining @Alternative beans

### Symptom

`@QuarkusTest` starts cleanly (no DeploymentException) because `casehub-engine-testing` provides `@Priority(1)` overrides for `CaseInstanceRepository` and `EventLogRepository`. But the first `startCase()` call in certain test classes fails with:

```
(RECIPIENT_FAILURE,8191) CaseInstance not found or wrong tenant: <uuid>
```

The error comes from `InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository.update()` (persistence-memory) — the bean is implicitly activated by Quarkus Arc as the sole `@Alternative` without a competing non-alternative, but the activation path produces intermittent initialization-order failures.

### Context

When only `SubCaseGroupRepository` and `PlanItemStore` are in `selected-alternatives`, the remaining 4 `@Alternative` beans from persistence-memory rely on Arc's implicit fallback activation:
- `InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository`
- `InMemoryCaseMetaModelRepository`
- `InMemoryEventLogRepository`
- `MemoryReactivePlanItemStore`

This implicit activation works for most test classes but fails intermittently when the test class is among the first to trigger `startCase()` in a fresh JVM — the `CaseStartedEventHandler` calls `caseInstanceRepository.update()` and the instance isn't found.

### Fix

Add all 4 remaining persistence-memory `@Alternative` beans to `selected-alternatives`:

```properties
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=\
  ...,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryCaseMetaModelRepository,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryEventLogRepository,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.MemoryReactivePlanItemStore
```

Verified in casehub-aml#58: 4 of 6 failing test classes fixed by explicit selection. 2 remaining failures (`AmlLayer7ResourceTest`, `AmlTrustRoutingAttestationTest`) may have a deeper root cause — investigation ongoing.

entries.title: @DefaultBean BlockingToReactiveBridge — wrap any blocking SPI as reactive, displaced by native async @Alternative
entries.body:
@DefaultBean BlockingToReactiveBridge — wrap any blocking SPI as reactive, displaced by native async @Alternative

## Context

You have a blocking SPI (`CaseMemoryStore`) in a zero-dep API module and need to expose a
reactive mirror (`ReactiveCaseMemoryStore`) so callers using Mutiny can also use the same
backends. Most blocking adapters don't need true async execution — wrapping them as
`Uni.createFrom().item(supplier)` is sufficient. But occasional adapters (e.g. a graph
database with native async traversal) do benefit from a true reactive implementation.

## What developers reach for instead

- Two independent SPIs with no connection — adapters implement both, duplicating logic
- Make the reactive SPI extend the blocking SPI — creates tight coupling and forces adapters
  to implement both interface families
- A single abstract class with default delegation — doesn't play well with CDI proxies

## The Technique

Define the blocking SPI in the zero-dep API module. Define the reactive SPI separately
(in the Quarkus module, because `Uni<>` depends on Smallrye Mutiny). Ship a
`@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` bridge class that injects the active blocking impl and
wraps each method:

```java
@DefaultBean
@ApplicationScoped
public class BlockingToReactiveBridge implements ReactiveCaseMemoryStore {

@Inject CaseMemoryStore delegate;   // whatever blocking impl is active

@Override
    public Uni<String> store(MemoryInput input) {
        return Uni.createFrom().item(() -> delegate.store(input));
    }

@Override
    public Uni<List<Memory>> query(MemoryQuery query) {
        return Uni.createFrom().item(() -> delegate.query(query));
    }

@Override
    public Uni<Void> erase(EraseRequest request) {
        return Uni.createFrom().voidItem().invoke(() -> delegate.erase(request));
    }
}
```

The CDI priority ladder then becomes:

| Tier | Class | Annotation | Active when |
|------|-------|-----------|-------------|
| 0 | `NoOpCaseMemoryStore` | `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` | No adapter |
| — | `BlockingToReactiveBridge` | `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` | Always (wraps Tier 0–2) |
| 1 | Memori adapter | `@ApplicationScoped` | Memori dep declared |
| 2 | Mem0 adapter | `@Alternative @Priority(1)` | Mem0 dep declared |
| 3 | Graphiti native-reactive | `@Alternative @Priority(2)` on `ReactiveCaseMemoryStore` | Graphiti dep declared |

When Graphiti (Tier 3) is added, it overrides the `ReactiveCaseMemoryStore` binding directly
via its higher-priority `@Alternative` — the bridge's `@DefaultBean` yields automatically.
Tier 3 does NOT need to implement the blocking SPI at all.

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

The `@DefaultBean` on the bridge is the key: it means both the bridge AND any blocking
adapter can coexist on the classpath without CDI ambiguity. The bridge always yields to a
native-reactive `@Alternative` on `ReactiveCaseMemoryStore`, and the blocking adapter
displaces the no-op on `CaseMemoryStore`. Each priority rung resolves independently.

Without `@DefaultBean`, a plain `@ApplicationScoped` bridge would collide with any real
`ReactiveCaseMemoryStore` implementation (ARC sees two beans for the same type and fails at
startup).

**Note:** Do NOT add `@Blocking` to bridge methods. `ExecutionModelAnnotationsProcessor`
rejects it on plain CDI bean methods returning `Uni` — only framework entrypoints accept it.
Thread dispatch is the entrypoint's responsibility. (See GE-20260528-74914d.)

## See Also

- `GE-20260521-d72294` — blocking and reactive store interfaces with irreconcilable signatures; this bridge avoids the problem by not having one class implement both
- `GE-20260528-74914d` — `@Blocking` rejected on CDI bean methods returning `Uni`

**See also:** [GE-20260620-9d043b](GE-20260620-9d043b.md) — CDI @Decorator double-application through blocking-to-reactive bridge — idempotency guard required (the gotcha this pattern creates)

`ChannelBackend` has multiple coexisting implementations selected by name (`backendId()`), yet it is a gateway because it bridges external messaging infrastructure.

## Domain types and non-interface packages

Records, enums, and value objects are not a category — they are the vocabulary the four categories operate on.

Three placement patterns:

1. **Colocated with a service facade** — domain types live alongside the facade in `api/<domain>/`. Examples: `Channel` in `api/channel/` with `ChannelManager`.
2. **Standalone domain package** — domain types whose sub-domain is significant but which have no facade or SPI of their own. Examples: `api/data/`, `api/instance/`. Their associated stores live in `api/store/`.
3. **Domain-scoped sub-package with its own SPI** — a sub-domain package that combines domain types AND an SPI interface tightly coupled to those types. Example: `api/watchdog/` contains the `Watchdog` record, alert context types, AND `WatchdogAlertRouter` (an SPI). Domain-scoped SPIs colocate with their domain package when the SPI's method signatures are tightly coupled to the domain types; cross-cutting SPIs go in `api/spi/`.

CDI qualifiers and framework annotations (e.g. `@CrossTenant` in `api/qualifier/`) are infrastructure, not domain types or interface categories. They may exist in `api/` as needed.

entries.title: CDI @Alternative reactive wrapper with private new Impl() delegate is a separate instance from the CDI bean — @AfterEach clear() silently targets the wrong object
@Priority is NOT @Inherited — CDI proxy classes silently drop it from reflection, making bean ordering undefined
entries.body:
@Priority is NOT @Inherited — CDI proxy classes silently drop it from reflection, making bean ordering undefined

## @Priority is NOT @Inherited — CDI proxy classes silently drop it from reflection

### Symptom

Bean iteration order from `Instance<T>` is silently non-deterministic despite
`@Priority` annotations on all implementations. Sorting by
`resolver.getClass().getAnnotation(Priority.class)` returns `null` for every
bean, so all beans get `Integer.MAX_VALUE` and ordering is undefined.

### Context

When iterating CDI beans from `Instance<T>` and sorting by `@Priority` using
Java reflection. Common in composite/pipeline patterns where multiple
implementations of an SPI must execute in a defined order.

### Root cause

`@jakarta.annotation.Priority` is not meta-annotated with `@java.lang.annotation.Inherited`.
CDI proxy classes (e.g. `WebDIDResolver_ClientProxy`) are JDK subclasses of the
real bean class. `proxy.getClass().getAnnotation(Priority.class)` returns `null`
because the JDK only propagates annotations marked `@Inherited` to subclasses.

The proxy class itself carries no annotations — it is a synthetic subclass
generated by the CDI container solely for interception and scoping purposes.

### What was tried (didn't work)

```java
// Natural reflection approach — silently fails for all proxied beans
private static int priorityOf(DIDResolver resolver) {
    var priority = resolver.getClass().getAnnotation(Priority.class);
    return priority != null ? priority.value() : Integer.MAX_VALUE;
    // Always returns MAX_VALUE for proxied beans
}
```

### Fix

Use Quarkus Arc's `Instance.Handle` API to read bean metadata through the
CDI container rather than through reflection on the proxy class:

```java
@Inject
public CompositeDIDResolver(@DIDMethod Instance<DIDResolver> methodResolvers) {
    this.resolvers = methodResolvers.handles().stream()
            .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(h -> priorityOf(h)))
            .map(Instance.Handle::get)
            .collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList());
}

private static int priorityOf(Instance.Handle<?> handle) {
    var bean = handle.getBean();
    if (bean instanceof InjectableBean<?> injectable) {
        Integer p = injectable.getPriority();
        if (p != null) return p;
    }
    return Integer.MAX_VALUE;
}
```

Arc stores priority metadata at container build time (augmentation), independent
of proxy reflection. `InjectableBean.getPriority()` reads this stored value.

### Why this is non-obvious

`getClass().getAnnotation()` is the natural Java reflection approach for reading
annotations. It works for many annotations and in many contexts. The `@Inherited`
requirement is a JDK detail that only matters when the object is a subclass of
the annotated class — a situation that is universal in CDI (every injected bean
is potentially proxied) but rarely encountered in direct reflection usage.

The failure is silent: no exception, no warning. The annotation simply isn't
found, and the fallback value (typically `Integer.MAX_VALUE` or a default
priority) is used for every bean, making ordering non-deterministic.

### Alternatives considered

- **Walk superclass chain:** `resolver.getClass().getSuperclass().getAnnotation(Priority.class)`
  — works for single-level proxies but fragile if proxy depth changes or if
  the container uses a different proxy strategy.
- **`@All List<InstanceHandle<T>>`:** Quarkus-specific injection that preserves
  metadata — equivalent to `Instance.handles()` but declared at the injection site.

entries.title: Quarkus augmentation demands datasource for extension-registered JPA entities even when in-memory CDI alternatives handle persistence
entries.body:
Quarkus augmentation demands datasource for extension-registered JPA entities even when in-memory CDI alternatives handle persistence

### Symptom

Test module depends on a Quarkus extension (e.g. `casehub-ledger`) whose runtime JAR contains `@Entity` classes. The test classpath includes an in-memory persistence module with `@Alternative @Priority(1)` implementations that bypass JPA entirely. Despite this, Quarkus startup fails:

```
ConfigurationException: Persistence unit '<default>' defines entities
[io.casehub.ledger.runtime.model.ActorIdentity, ...] but its datasource
'<default>' cannot be found: Datasource '<default>' is not configured.
```

### Context

The test module's `pom.xml` depends on the Quarkus extension runtime and an in-memory persistence module. No datasource is configured because the in-memory implementations handle all reads/writes via `ConcurrentHashMap` — JPA is never used at runtime.

### What was tried (didn't work)

Running tests with only the in-memory persistence module on the classpath and no datasource configuration. Expected the `@Alternative @Priority(1)` in-memory implementations to eliminate the need for any JPA/datasource setup.

### Root cause

Quarkus augmentation discovers `@Entity` classes via Jandex index scanning of extension runtime JARs. `HibernateOrmProcessor#configurationDescriptorBuilding` validates that every persistence unit with discovered entities has a configured datasource. This validation runs at **build time** — before CDI bean resolution. `@Alternative @Priority(1)` annotations are CDI concepts resolved at **runtime**. Augmentation has no visibility into which CDI alternatives will replace which beans.

The mental model "in-memory alternatives replace JPA" is correct at runtime but wrong at augmentation time.

### Fix

Add `quarkus-jdbc-h2` as a test dependency and configure a minimal H2 datasource in `application.properties`:

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.quarkus</groupId>
  <artifactId>quarkus-jdbc-h2</artifactId>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
```

```properties
quarkus.datasource.db-kind=h2
quarkus.datasource.jdbc.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb;MODE=PostgreSQL;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1
quarkus.datasource.username=sa
quarkus.datasource.password=

quarkus.hibernate-orm.database.generation=none
quarkus.flyway.migrate-at-start=true
quarkus.flyway.locations=classpath:db/ledger/migration
```

The datasource satisfies augmentation validation. The in-memory `@Alternative @Priority(1)` implementations still handle all actual persistence at runtime — H2 is never queried.

### Why this is non-obvious

The `@Alternative @Priority(1)` pattern is specifically designed to replace default implementations. A developer correctly reasons: "I'm replacing all JPA repositories with in-memory alternatives, so I don't need a datasource." This reasoning is valid at the CDI layer but fails because Quarkus augmentation validates the JPA layer independently, before CDI alternatives are resolved.

### Why this fix

The H2 datasource is a no-op cost — it exists only to satisfy augmentation. The alternative (`quarkus.hibernate-orm.enabled=false`) would disable the entire Hibernate subsystem, which may break other extension features that rely on entity metadata even when in-memory persistence handles the actual data.

### Alternatives considered

- `quarkus.hibernate-orm.enabled=false` — disables Hibernate entirely; rejected because extension deployment processors may rely on entity metadata for build-time validation or code generation
- Excluding entity classes from Jandex — not feasible; the entities are in the extension JAR which is already indexed

entries.title: qhorus persistence-memory module creates three-way CDI ambiguity — reactive wrappers must also be excluded
entries.body:
qhorus persistence-memory module creates three-way CDI ambiguity — reactive wrappers must also be excluded

### Symptom

29 CDI `DeploymentException` errors at Quarkus augmentation time — `Ambiguous dependencies` for every qhorus store type (`InstanceStore`, `ChannelStore`, `MessageStore`, `CommitmentStore`, `DataStore`, `DeliveryCursorStore`, `WatchdogStore`, `ChannelBindingStore`) plus their `@CrossTenant` variants.

### Context

Consumer app (casehub-aml) has three qhorus modules on the classpath:
- `qhorus-runtime` — JPA stores (`io.casehub.qhorus.runtime.store.jpa.*`)
- `qhorus-testing` — in-memory test stores (`io.casehub.qhorus.testing.*`)
- `qhorus-persistence-memory` — standalone in-memory stores (`io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.*`)

All three provide implementations at `@ApplicationScoped @Default` with no `@Alternative` or `@Priority` disambiguation.

### What was tried (didn't work)

1. Rebuilding qhorus locally (`mvn install -DskipTests`) — same result; the ambiguity is in the source, not a bad build artifact.
2. Excluding only the 12 blocking `InMemory*Store` classes from `persistence-memory` — resolves the ambiguity but creates 2 new `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` errors.

### Root cause

The new `qhorus-persistence-memory` module added `InMemory*Store` beans in `io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.*` at `@ApplicationScoped @Default` — same qualifiers as both the JPA stores and the testing module stores. No priority hierarchy was established.

The reactive wrappers (`InMemoryReactiveMessageStore`, `InMemoryReactiveChannelStore`) inject the blocking stores **by concrete type**, not by interface:

```java
// InMemoryReactiveMessageStore
@Inject InMemoryMessageStore blocking;  // concrete type, not MessageStore interface
```

This means excluding the blocking stores without also excluding the reactive wrappers creates `UnsatisfiedResolutionException`.

### Solution 1 — per-class exclude-types

**Approach:** Exclude all persistence-memory stores individually via `quarkus.arc.exclude-types`
**Pros:** No Maven dependency changes; works when persistence-memory is a transitive dep you can't control
**Cons:** Must list every class (14+); must include reactive wrappers too (they inject blocking stores by concrete type); breaks if qhorus-testing also injects persistence-memory classes by concrete type

```properties
quarkus.arc.exclude-types=\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryChannelBindingStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryChannelStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryCommitmentStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryCrossTenantChannelStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryCrossTenantCommitmentStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryCrossTenantMessageStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryCrossTenantWatchdogStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryDataStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryDeliveryCursorStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryInstanceStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryMessageStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryWatchdogStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryReactiveMessageStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryReactiveChannelStore
```

### Solution 2 — Maven dependency exclusion (recommended)

**Approach:** Exclude `casehub-qhorus-persistence-memory` from the `casehub-qhorus-testing` dependency in the consumer `pom.xml`
**Pros:** One exclusion rule; no `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` needed; eliminates the ambiguity at the dependency level before CDI even sees the beans
**Cons:** Only works when `qhorus-testing` is a direct dependency (not transitive)

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.casehub</groupId>
  <artifactId>casehub-qhorus-testing</artifactId>
  <scope>test</scope>
  <exclusions>
    <exclusion>
      <groupId>io.casehub</groupId>
      <artifactId>casehub-qhorus-persistence-memory</artifactId>
    </exclusion>
  </exclusions>
</dependency>
```

Verified in casehub-life: the testing jar's stores are self-contained — they do not delegate to persistence-memory stores internally. With the exclusion, only the testing jar's `@Alternative @Priority(1)` stores are discovered, and they win over the JPA stores cleanly.

### Why this is non-obvious

The initial symptom (29 ambiguous dependencies) points at the blocking stores. Excluding them seems like the complete fix. But the reactive wrappers have a direct dependency on the concrete blocking store class — not the interface — so excluding the blocking stores creates a new unsatisfied dependency that only surfaces on the next build. Two rounds of "fix one CDI error, get a different one" before reaching the real solution.

### Alternatives considered

- **Rebuilding qhorus** — tried first, doesn't help; the ambiguity is intentional in the source
- **Adding `@Alternative @Priority` to qhorus source** — correct long-term fix but requires a qhorus PR
- **Excluding by package prefix** — Quarkus `exclude-types` doesn't support wildcards; must list each class

entries.title: @Alternative @Priority(1) from an external JAR does not override a non-alternative bean in Quarkus — needs exclude-types + selected-alternatives
entries.body:
@Alternative @Priority(1) from an external JAR does not override a non-alternative bean in Quarkus — needs exclude-types + selected-alternatives

## Symptom

Test assertions calling `workItemStore.scanAll()` return empty even though the handler log confirms `WorkItemService.create()` ran successfully. `planItem.getStatus()` is `RUNNING` (proving the handler completed), but the store shows nothing.

## Context

Two `WorkItemStore` beans on the test classpath:
- `JpaWorkItemStore @ApplicationScoped` — production bean from `casehub-work`
- `InMemoryWorkItemStore @Alternative @Priority(1)` — test replacement from `casehub-work-testing`

CDI 4.x spec says `@Priority` on an alternative activates it globally and it should win over non-alternatives. In Quarkus ARC 3.32.2 this does not hold when the alternative comes from an external dependency JAR.

## What was tried

- Adding `InMemoryWorkItemStore` to `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` alone → "Ambiguous dependencies" deployment failure (both beans active simultaneously)
- `quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.work.runtime.repository.jpa.JpaWorkItemStore` alone → no effect; `JpaWorkItemStore` still wins
- `@Inject InMemoryWorkItemStore workItemStore` (concrete type) in the test → bypasses CDI alternative selection; test clears the right store but `WorkItemService` still writes to JPA (H2), so `scanAll()` returns empty

## Root Cause

`@Alternative @Priority(1)` from a dependency JAR is not treated as overriding a non-alternative `@ApplicationScoped` bean by Quarkus ARC. CDI spec §2.6.2 requires `@Priority` alternatives to take precedence, but ARC's resolution appears to treat both as equally active candidates when neither is the local application class. The non-alternative wins or ambiguity is raised.

## Fix

Combine both in `src/test/resources/application.properties`:

```properties
# Remove the JPA impl from CDI discovery entirely
quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.work.runtime.repository.jpa.JpaWorkItemStore

# Explicitly select the in-memory replacement
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=\
  io.casehub.work.testing.InMemoryWorkItemStore,\
  ...other alternatives...
```

With `JpaWorkItemStore` excluded, `InMemoryWorkItemStore` is the only active `WorkItemStore` bean. Explicit `selected-alternatives` listing then activates it. Both `WorkItemService` (via `@Inject WorkItemStore`) and the test (via `@Inject InMemoryWorkItemStore`) now reference the same singleton, and `scanAll()` finds what `create()` stored.

## Why this is non-obvious

CDI 4.x spec (and Quarkus docs on alternatives) state that `@Alternative @Priority(n)` globally activates and prioritises the alternative. A developer familiar with CDI 4.x would expect `@Priority(1)` to simply work. The failure is silent — no warning is emitted, `JpaWorkItemStore` just wins quietly. The symptom (empty `scanAll()`) points toward a different root cause (session caching, test isolation) and sends debugging in the wrong direction.

**See also:** [GE-20260429-a79d0e](GE-20260429-a79d0e.md) — @Alternative @Priority auto-activates within same module | [GE-20260521-4de4f1](GE-20260521-4de4f1.md) — TestProfile.getEnabledAlternatives() replaces selected-alternatives entirely

**See also:** [GE-20260601-cee623](GE-20260601-cee623.md) — QuarkusTestProfile.getEnabledAlternatives() replaces selected-alternatives entirely

**See also:** [GE-20260601-848232](GE-20260601-848232.md) — exclude-types silently does nothing for beans from Jandex-indexed JARs

**See also:** [GE-20260604-2f0889](GE-20260604-2f0889.md) — @Alternative @Priority(N) stubs appear in @All List<T> alongside original bean

**See also:** [GE-20260616-d70e7e](GE-20260616-d70e7e.md) — selected-alternatives silently accepts non-@Alternative beans

quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives silently ignores %dev. profile overrides — use exclude-types instead
entries.body:
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives silently ignores %dev. profile overrides — use exclude-types instead

### Symptom
`%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` is set in `application.properties` alongside a non-profiled `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives`. In dev mode, the `@Alternative` beans listed in the `%dev.` value are never activated — ArC throws `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` for the interfaces they implement, even though the beans exist on the classpath and have Jandex indices.

### Context
Multi-profile Quarkus application needing different CDI alternatives per environment:
- Production: reactive JPA stores (`engine-persistence-hibernate`)
- Dev mode: in-memory blocking stores (`engine-persistence-memory`)
- Tests: separate `application.properties` with its own `selected-alternatives`

Both `%dev.` and non-profiled values present in the same `application.properties`.

### What was tried (didn't work)
1. `%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=MemoryPlanItemStore,...` alongside non-profiled `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=JpaPlanItemStore,...` — dev alternatives silently ignored
2. Removing the non-profiled value and using only `%dev.` and `%prod.` — still ignored
3. Verified `%dev.quarkus.arc.exclude-types` DOES work (OidcCurrentPrincipal successfully excluded in dev) — confirms profile overrides work for other ArC properties

### Root cause
`quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` is a build-time fixed property that does not honour `%profile.` prefixes. The property is resolved once during Quarkus augmentation and profile-specific values are silently discarded. This is not documented — the Quarkus configuration reference does not distinguish which ArC properties support profile overrides.

### Fix
Select ALL alternatives (both JPA and memory) in the non-profiled `selected-alternatives`. Use profile-specific `exclude-types` to control which survive in each environment:

```properties
# Non-profiled: select everything — both JPA and memory alternatives
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=\
  io.casehub.persistence.jpa.JpaPlanItemStore,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.MemoryPlanItemStore,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryCaseMetaModelRepository

# Dev: exclude reactive JPA stores → memory stores win
%dev.quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.persistence.jpa.JpaPlanItemStore,...

# Prod: exclude memory stores → JPA stores win
%prod.quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.persistence.memory.MemoryPlanItemStore,...
```

ArC processes `exclude-types` first (removing beans entirely), then resolves `selected-alternatives` among surviving beans. In each profile, only one alternative per interface survives — no ambiguity.

### Why this is non-obvious
Profile-specific overrides (`%dev.`, `%prod.`) work for most Quarkus properties, including `quarkus.arc.exclude-types`. The natural assumption is that `selected-alternatives` follows the same pattern. There is no error, warning, or log message when the profile override is ignored — the non-profiled value is silently used. The failure manifests as `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` with no hint about profile resolution.

### Why this fix
`exclude-types` is a coarser mechanism (removes the bean entirely vs just not selecting it), but it's the only ArC property that supports profile overrides. The exclude-types-first-then-resolve pattern is architecturally sound: each profile starts from the same selected set and carves out what doesn't belong.

### Alternatives considered
- **Maven profiles** — add/remove JARs per profile. Rejected: adds build complexity and doesn't work with `quarkus:dev` which uses the default Maven profile.
- **`@IfBuildProfile("dev")` wrapper beans** — create dev-only `@ApplicationScoped` beans that delegate to memory stores. Rejected: code duplication across 5+ SPIs, maintenance burden.
- **Separate `application-dev.properties`** — Quarkus doesn't support this pattern (it's a Spring Boot convention).

entries.title: CDI @Qualifier + AnnotationLiteral producer for configurable named resource in Quarkus extensions
@Alternative @Qualifier on the bean class restricts CDI injection to qualifier-scoped points — prevents ambiguity with plain interface injection

entries.body:
# Module Tier Structure

Three-tier rule for modular library design. Applies to any Quarkus extension or multi-module library.

## The Three Tiers

| Tier | Contents | Dependencies allowed |
|------|----------|---------------------|
| **Tier 1 — Pure-Java SPI** (`api/`) | Interfaces, records, enums, value types | Zero framework deps. CDI annotation JARs (`jakarta.inject-api`, `jakarta.enterprise.cdi-api`) and Mutiny (`io.smallrye.reactive:mutiny` as `provided`) are acceptable — both are inert without a container/runtime and every Quarkus consumer already has them. JPA and Quarkus runtime types remain excluded. |
| **Tier 2 — Core library** (`core/`) | Shared logic, routing strategies, utilities | Tier 1 deps + lightweight libraries. No JPA, no datasource requirements. |
| **Tier 3 — Full extension** (`runtime/`) | CDI beans, JPA entities, Flyway migrations, REST resources | Everything — Quarkus runtime, JPA, datasource config. |

## Rules

**SPI method signatures must not expose heavy external SDK types.** Consumers implement Tier 1 interfaces — their compile classpath should not force vendor SDKs.

**JPA entities must not co-locate with domain SPIs.** Placing entities in the SPI module forces all consumers to configure a datasource. Entities belong in Tier 3 or a dedicated `persistence-*` module.

**Persistence module split.** When a library needs both a domain SPI and a JPA implementation, split them: SPI in Tier 1, JPA impl in a separate `persistence-hibernate/` or `persistence-jpa/` module. Consumers that don't need persistence depend on Tier 1 only.

## SPI Default Patterns

Three patterns for SPI defaults, each with a different rationale:

| Pattern | When to use | Default impl location |
|---------|-------------|----------------------|
| **No-op default** | Operational SPIs where skipping the operation leaves the system functional (`WorkerProvisioner`, `CaseChannelProvider`) | Same pure-Java module as the SPI |
| **Populated default** | Vocabulary/registry SPIs where an empty implementation breaks routing immediately (`CapabilityRegistry`) | Same pure-Java module as the SPI |
| **No-op `@DefaultBean`** | Store SPIs that maintain persistent state (`CaseMemoryStore`, `WorkItemStore`) | Mock module (Tier 3) |

**Anti-pattern:** labelling an `InMemoryXxx` as `@DefaultBean`. `@DefaultBean` means no-op, not in-memory. The in-memory working implementation is `@Alternative @Priority(N)` in a separate `persistence-memory/` module, activated by classpath presence.

## References

- [`persistence-backend-cdi-priority`](persistence-backend-cdi-priority.md) — CDI priority ladder for persistence backends
- [`maven-submodule-folder-naming`](../casehub/maven-submodule-folder-naming.md) — folder naming convention

entries.title: @IfBuildProfile + @Alternative + @Priority resolves CDI without selected-alternatives in indexed JARs
entries.body:
@IfBuildProfile + @Alternative + @Priority resolves CDI without selected-alternatives in indexed JARs

### Symptom

Adding a dev-profile-only CDI bean (e.g., a `CurrentPrincipal` for dev mode) via `%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=com.example.DevBean` causes startup failures — all beans from the non-profiled `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` list disappear.

### Context

Quarkus profile-specific properties (`%dev.`, `%test.`, `%prod.`) completely **replace** their non-profiled counterparts. If the base `application.properties` has:

```properties
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=\
  com.example.JpaRepo,\
  com.example.JpaPlanItemStore,\
  com.example.JpaSubCaseGroupRepo
```

Adding `%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=com.example.DevBean` drops all three JPA alternatives in dev mode — CDI startup fails with unsatisfied dependency errors for every bean that was in the original list.

### Root cause

Profile-specific properties in Quarkus are full replacements, not merges. This is by design (SmallRye Config behaviour), but the failure mode is silent — no warning that the non-profiled value was dropped.

### Fix

Use bean-level annotations instead of `selected-alternatives`:

```java
@ApplicationScoped
@Alternative
@Priority(150)  // beats OidcCurrentPrincipal @Priority(100)
@IfBuildProfile("dev")
public class DemoCurrentPrincipal implements CurrentPrincipal {
    @Override public String tenancyId() { return "demo-tenant"; }
    @Override public String actorId()   { return "demo-user"; }
}
```

**Requirements:**
1. The bean must live in a **Jandex-indexed JAR** (e.g., the application's own `runtime/` module). ArC discovers it automatically — no `selected-alternatives` entry needed.
2. `@IfBuildProfile("dev")` excludes the bean entirely from non-dev builds — no ambiguity in production.
3. `@Priority(150)` resolves over competing `@Alternative` beans (e.g., `OidcCurrentPrincipal @Priority(100)`) via standard ArC priority resolution.

This is the same mechanism by which `OidcCurrentPrincipal @Alternative @Priority(100)` beats `MockCurrentPrincipal @DefaultBean` in production — without being listed in `selected-alternatives`.

### Why this is non-obvious

The natural instinct is `%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=MyDevBean` — it looks like the standard profile-override pattern. The replacement behaviour is documented for SmallRye Config but not prominently flagged in the Quarkus CDI guide. The failure (dropped JPA alternatives) manifests as unrelated `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` errors that don't mention `selected-alternatives` at all.

### Why this fix

`@IfBuildProfile + @Priority` solves the problem at the bean level — no configuration property needed. The alternative (duplicating the full `selected-alternatives` list in every profile override) is fragile and drifts as new alternatives are added.

### Alternatives considered

- **Duplicate the full list in `%dev.`** — works but fragile; every new `@Alternative` bean must be added to every profile-specific override. Drifts silently.
- **Use `@UnlessBuildProfile("prod")` instead of `@IfBuildProfile("dev")`** — activates in both dev and test profiles, which may not be desired. Test profile has its own `FixedCurrentPrincipal @Priority(200)`.

entries.body:
Hibernate `@OneToMany` collections must be initialized with `ArrayList`, not `CopyOnWriteArrayList`

## Hibernate `@OneToMany` collections must be initialized with `ArrayList`, not `CopyOnWriteArrayList`

**ID:** GE-0142
**Stack:** Hibernate ORM 6.x, Quarkus 3.17.5 (likely all Hibernate 6.x versions)
**Symptom:** Unit tests pass. Integration tests that load the entity from the database fail — the `@OneToMany` collection either throws an unexpected exception or behaves as if empty when accessed outside the entity's loading context.

### Root cause
Hibernate replaces field-initialized collections with its own `PersistentBag` (or `PersistentList`) proxy at load time. This works reliably for `java.util.ArrayList` initializers. When the field is initialized with `CopyOnWriteArrayList`, Hibernate may not reliably recognize it as a replaceable collection — the proxy wrapping can silently fail or behave incorrectly. Unit tests never expose this because Hibernate does not load the entity from the database; it only affects database round-trips.

### Fix
Always initialize `@OneToMany` and `@ManyToMany` fields with `new ArrayList<>()`:

```java
// Wrong — passes unit tests, fails integration tests
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "parentTask", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
private List<HibernateTask> childTasks = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

// Correct
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "parentTask", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
private List<HibernateTask> childTasks = new ArrayList<>();
```

If thread-safety is needed at the application layer, wrap on access: `Collections.synchronizedList(entity.getChildTasks())` — but do not use `CopyOnWriteArrayList` as the field initializer.

### Why non-obvious
`CopyOnWriteArrayList` implements `List` and is a perfectly valid Java collection. Nothing in Hibernate ORM documentation, Quarkus documentation, or the `@OneToMany` Javadoc warns against using non-standard `List` implementations as field initializers. The failure is invisible in unit tests and only surfaces when entities are persisted and fetched from a real database.

*Score: 12/15 · Included because: silent failure, unit tests mask the bug, nothing in any documentation warns about this constraint · Reservation: specific to teams using CopyOnWriteArrayList for thread safety in entities*

ConcurrentHashMap.put() happens-before only covers future get() calls — not code that obtained the value reference before the put()
entries.body:
ConcurrentHashMap.put() happens-before only covers future get() calls — not code that obtained the value reference before the put()

## Symptom

Code uses `ConcurrentHashMap` as a thread-safe cache. One thread does `cache.put(id, obj)` then later mutates `obj.field`. A second thread calls `cache.get(id)` — which is defined to happen-after the `put()` — then reads `obj.field` and sees a stale value. Less obviously: a third thread that obtained the reference via an earlier `cache.get()` (or via any other path before the `put()`) also sees a stale `obj.field` even though the `put()` semantically "published" the object.

In this session: `CaseInstance.state` changes were invisible to threads that had obtained a reference to the `CaseInstance` before the state update was published via `cache.put()`.

## Root Cause

The JMM happens-before guarantee from `ConcurrentHashMap.put(k, v)` is: "the state seen by the mapping function or the put() call is visible to any thread that subsequently calls `get(k)` and observes the new value." This guarantee is established at the moment `get()` returns the post-put value.

It covers:
- The value `v` itself (reference visibility)
- Fields written to `v` **before** the `put()` call (publication via the put's write barrier)

It does NOT cover:
- Fields written to `v` **after** the `put()` call
- Any code path that obtained the reference to `v` before this particular `put()` — those threads have no synchronisation barrier between their earlier `get()` and the subsequent field mutation

If a thread modifies `obj.field` after `cache.put()`, that write is only guaranteed visible to threads that call `cache.get()` in a future operation. Threads that already hold a reference — whether from before the put, or from the put itself — see whatever their CPU cache contains.

## Fix

**Option A — Publish immutable state:** Use an immutable value type. Replace `obj.field = newValue` with `cache.put(id, new Obj(newValue))`. Every reader calls `get()` to see current state, establishing the happens-before at each read.

**Option B — `volatile` field:** Declare `volatile State field` on the mutable object. `volatile` writes are visible to all subsequent reads regardless of how the reference was obtained.

**Option C — Use the cache as the memory barrier:** Force all readers to call `cache.get()` for every field read — never hold the reference across mutations. Practical only if the cache is small and reads are infrequent.

In the session: `CaseInstance.state` was made `volatile` so changes published via the engine's own state machine were visible to the `CaseInstanceCache.get()` completion check without requiring a re-put.

## Why this is non-obvious

"ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe" is true but misleadingly coarse. The thread-safety guarantee is for the map structure (no corruption, consistent iteration). The happens-before guarantee is specifically for `get()` observing a `put()` — it does not extend to field-level visibility on the value object after it has been placed in the map. Developers who know that `volatile` is needed for shared fields often miss that a ConcurrentHashMap lookup alone does not establish a barrier for code holding a pre-obtained reference.

**See also:** [GE-20260616-57201e](GE-20260616-57201e.md) — ConcurrentHashMap.put() happens-before get() in the same map

entries.title: ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet().add() provides atomic idempotent registration without explicit locks
entries.body:
ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet().add() provides atomic idempotent registration without explicit locks

### Context

You need to register a resource (e.g. a backend in a registry, a channel in a gateway, a listener on a topic) exactly once per key, even under concurrent access from multiple threads. You want to avoid explicit locks, `synchronized` blocks, and the awkward semantics of `computeIfAbsent` when the computation has side effects.

### Technique

```java
private final Set<UUID> registeredKeys = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();

public void ensureRegistered(UUID key) {
    if (registeredKeys.add(key)) {   // atomic: exactly one thread returns true
        doRegistration(key);          // called exactly once per key
    }
}

public void deregister(UUID key) {
    registeredKeys.remove(key);      // subsequent ensureRegistered() will re-register
}
```

`ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()` returns a `Set<K>` backed by a ConcurrentHashMap. `Set.add()` returns `true` if the element was actually added (was absent) and `false` if it was already present. Under concurrent access, exactly one thread gets `true` — all others get `false` and skip the side effect. No explicit locking required.

### Why this is non-obvious

Most developers reach for `synchronized(this)` or `computeIfAbsent`. The `newKeySet().add()` pattern:
- Is 2 lines vs 5-10 for a `synchronized` block
- Returns the boolean signal the caller needs directly from `add()`
- Has guaranteed CAS semantics from the ConcurrentHashMap backing
- Clearly expresses intent: "register this key once, skip if already registered"

`computeIfAbsent` also works but its Javadoc warns that the computation must not modify the map — using it to trigger side effects (registration) is semantically awkward and potentially unsafe if the side effect is not pure. The `Set.add()` pattern has no such restriction.

### Constraints

The side effect in `doRegistration()` must be safe to call after `add()` returns but before other threads observe the registration in the set. If `doRegistration()` itself must be atomic with the `add()` (e.g. the registration step reads back the key), this pattern is insufficient — use a dedicated lock or a more explicit state machine.

ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent blocks all same-bucket keys while mapping function runs — unusable for network calls
entries.body:
ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent blocks all same-bucket keys while mapping function runs — unusable for network calls

## Symptom

Using `computeIfAbsent` to cache external provider contexts (e.g. fetching a public key from Vault Transit on first use) causes unexpected latency spikes. Under concurrent load, a thread loading one actor's context can block threads loading a different actor's context — even though the keys are completely unrelated.

In extreme cases with synchronised re-entry (the mapping function internally calls back into the map for a different key that hashes to the same bucket), the JVM may deadlock.

## Context

Per-actorId context cache in an `AgentSigner` implementation. First `sign()` call per actor triggers `loadContext(actorId)` which makes an HTTP call to Vault. Subsequent calls should be instant (cache hit).

```java
// WRONG — computeIfAbsent holds the bucket lock during the HTTP call
Optional<C> cached = contextCache.computeIfAbsent(actorId, id -> {
    return loadContext(id);  // HTTP call — may take hundreds of ms
});
```

## Root cause

`ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent` acquires an internal per-bucket lock (striped lock on the bin node) for the duration of the mapping function. While one thread is inside a slow mapping function:
- **All other threads needing any key in the same hash bucket are blocked** — not just the same key
- A second thread calling `computeIfAbsent` for a different key that happens to share the same hash bucket will block until the first completes
- If the mapping function itself calls back into the same map (re-entrant), the JDK **throws `IllegalStateException: Recursive update`** in Java 9+

The Javadoc says "the computation should be short and simple" but gives no hint that slow computations block an entire hash bucket.

## Fix

Use `get()` / `putIfAbsent()` instead. Accept duplicate loads on cold start (two threads for the same key both call `loadContext` — idempotent results are safe):

```java
// CORRECT — no bucket lock held during the network call
Optional<C> cached = contextCache.get(actorId);
if (cached == null) {
    Optional<C> loaded = loadContext(actorId);  // HTTP call, no lock held
    Optional<C> racing = contextCache.putIfAbsent(actorId, loaded);
    cached = racing != null ? racing : loaded;
}
```

`putIfAbsent` is atomic but only holds the lock for the map update itself (microseconds), not for the compute function. The trade-off: on cold start, two threads may both call `loadContext` for the same key. The second's result is discarded (the first writer wins). For idempotent loads (same Vault key → same result), this is safe.

## Why this is non-obvious

The name `computeIfAbsent` implies "compute and store if the key is missing" — developers naturally assume the lock scope is narrow (just the map update). The Javadoc recommends "short and simple" but doesn't say "or you block the entire hash bucket." The symptom (unrelated keys blocking each other) is completely surprising. Developers discovering the issue often suspect their HTTP client or Vault server, not the cache implementation.

`computeIfAbsent` is the correct and safe choice when the mapping function is fast and in-memory. The problem is specifically with slow or blocking mapping functions.

### Why this fix

`putIfAbsent` releases the lock before the network call even starts. The duplicate-load race is the accepted trade-off: two threads load the same key concurrently, one result is discarded. For caches where loading is idempotent and deterministic (fetching a public key from a KMS), this is always safe and preferable to blocking the bucket.

entries.title: H2 Merkle frontier constraint violation cascades @QuarkusTest suite — CaseDefinition not found
entries.body:
H2 Merkle frontier constraint violation cascades @QuarkusTest suite — CaseDefinition not found

## Symptom

Tests fail non-deterministically with:

```
(RECIPIENT_FAILURE,8191) CaseDefinition not found for case: <UUID>
at SchedulerService.registerScheduledTriggers()
```

The failing test has no relationship to the case definition loader. The case definition IS registered at startup (verified: "Registering case: aml-investigation" appears in logs).

## Context

`@QuarkusTest` suite where multiple tests start casehub-engine investigations in sequence. H2 in-memory database with casehub-ledger entities on the qhorus persistence unit (`casehub.ledger.datasource=qhorus`). Multiple Quartz worker threads (default thread pool size).

## What was tried (didn't work)

- Adding `MemorySubCaseGroupRepository` and `MemoryPlanItemStore` to `selected-alternatives` (fixed CDI startup but not the cascade)
- Checking `DefaultCaseDefinitionRegistry` registration logic — confirmed synchronous via `.await().atMost(30s)`
- Checking `TestCaseMetaModelRepository` thread safety — `ConcurrentHashMap`, should be safe

## Root cause

Multiple Quartz worker jobs for the same investigation case run concurrently. Each job writes a `WorkerDecisionEntry` which triggers a Merkle Mountain Range frontier update (`INSERT INTO ledger_merkle_frontier`). H2 lacks PostgreSQL row-level locking — two concurrent writes violate `UQ_MERKLE_FRONTIER_SUBJECT_LEVEL (subject_id, level)`. The second write fails with `ConstraintViolationException`. The JTA transaction rolls back, leaving the **qhorus `EntityManager` in a poisoned state**. The next investigation's `startCase()` fires a Vert.x event bus message; the poisoned EntityManager causes processing to fail; Vert.x returns `RECIPIENT_FAILURE,8191 CaseDefinition not found`. All subsequent tests cascade-fail the same way.

The symptom is three hops from the cause: concurrent Quartz writes → Merkle race → poisoned EntityManager → `CaseDefinition not found`.

## Fix

Set `casehub.ledger.hash-chain.enabled=false` in test `application.properties`:

```properties
casehub.ledger.hash-chain.enabled=false
```

This disables Merkle leaf hash computation and frontier updates entirely — `LedgerEntry.digest = null`, no `INSERT INTO ledger_merkle_frontier`. The hash chain is owned by casehub-ledger and tested in its own suite; consumer apps test that entries are written with the correct structure, not that the cryptographic chain is intact. See also casehub garden protocol PP-20260604-f45c95.

## Why this is non-obvious

The symptom (`CaseDefinition not found`) is reported from the *next* investigation's case startup, not from the investigation that caused the Merkle violation. The failing test has nothing to do with case definitions. The `DefaultCaseDefinitionRegistry` is proven populated at startup. The poisoned EntityManager is an invisible intermediate state. H2 vs PostgreSQL locking semantics is the root cause.

### Why this fix

The hash chain is a compliance/cryptography concern belonging to casehub-ledger. Consumer app tests verify entry presence and causal chain structure — not cryptographic integrity. Disabling it in tests is architecturally correct, not a workaround.

### Alternatives considered

- Single-threaded Quartz (`quarkus.quartz.thread-count=1`): makes investigations sequential but drains time out for complex suites
- Investigation drain pattern (GE-20260605-c91317): necessary but not sufficient without the hash-chain flag — H2 is still vulnerable to concurrent workers in the same investigation

H2 2.x MVStore MERGE INTO is not concurrent-safe for first-inserts
entries.body:
H2 2.x MVStore MERGE INTO is not concurrent-safe for first-inserts

### Context

`MERGE INTO table USING (...) WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT` is used as an
atomic upsert — e.g. for sequence allocation tables that need "insert if absent,
update if present."

### Symptom

Under concurrent writes from multiple threads targeting the same new primary key,
one or more transactions throw:

```
Unique index or primary key violation: "PUBLIC.PK_<table> INDEX ..."
SQL statement: MERGE INTO <table> AS t USING ... WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT ...
```

The failure only occurs on first-insert for a new key. Subsequent writes (where
the row already exists) hit `WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE` and succeed. Serial tests
pass; concurrent tests fail.

### Root Cause

H2 2.0 (July 2021) switched the default storage engine from **page-store**
(table-level locking) to **MVStore** (MVCC / row-level). Under MVStore, `MERGE INTO`
evaluates `WHEN NOT MATCHED` non-atomically:

1. Transaction A reads — row absent → plans INSERT
2. Transaction B reads — row absent → plans INSERT
3. Transaction A inserts → succeeds
4. Transaction B inserts → unique constraint violation (row now exists)

The conflict is not suppressed — it propagates as a `ConstraintViolationException`,
poisoning Transaction B's `EntityManager` and requiring a full transaction rollback.

Documentation and Javadoc written for H2 1.x stated "H2 uses table-level locking."
This was true for page-store. It is false for MVStore.

### Fix

Replace the single-statement `MERGE INTO` with two statements:

```java
// INSERT ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING — concurrent first-inserts are safe.
// H2 2.2+ in MODE=PostgreSQL supports the no-column-target form only:
// ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (not ON CONFLICT (col1, col2) DO NOTHING).
em.createNativeQuery(
    "INSERT INTO sequence_table (subject_id, tenancy_id, next_seq) " +
    "VALUES (CAST(?1 AS UUID), ?2, 1) " +
    "ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING")
    .setParameter(1, subjectId).setParameter(2, tenancyId).executeUpdate();

em.createNativeQuery(
    "UPDATE sequence_table SET next_seq = next_seq + 1 " +
    "WHERE subject_id = CAST(?1 AS UUID) AND tenancy_id = ?2")
    .setParameter(1, subjectId).setParameter(2, tenancyId).executeUpdate();
```

Both PostgreSQL and H2 2.2+ (in `MODE=PostgreSQL`) accept this SQL. The `UPDATE`
acquires a row lock held for the transaction duration, serialising concurrent writes.

### Why this is non-obvious

H2 2.0 silently changed the default storage engine — existing `MERGE INTO` code
that worked correctly for years under H2 1.x breaks only under concurrent load.
Serial unit tests always pass. The failure surfaces only in integration test suites
that exercise concurrent writes (e.g. Quartz workers, concurrent HTTP handlers).

The Javadoc claiming "H2 uses table-level locking" remained in the codebase long
after H2 2.x shipped, reinforcing the incorrect assumption.

### Why this fix

`MERGE INTO` evaluated in a single statement appears atomic but is not under MVCC.
The two-statement approach makes the sequence explicit: one statement that safely
handles concurrent first-inserts (DO NOTHING on conflict), and one that serialises
via row lock. This is identical to PostgreSQL's `INSERT ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING +
UPDATE` pattern and can be unified across both dialects with the same SQL.

### Alternatives considered

- **`LOCK_MODE=1` on H2 URL** — does not restore table-level locking for MVStore tables;
  the flag only affects the discontinued page-store engine.
- **`REQUIRES_NEW` inner transaction for first-insert** — adds a class and transaction
  boundary just for the initial-insert edge case; rejected as unnecessary complexity.
- **`SELECT FOR UPDATE` / pessimistic lock** — cannot lock a row that doesn't exist yet;
  fails silently on first-insert (same race condition).

**See also:** [GE-20260605-b734b3](GE-20260605-b734b3.md) — SQL-standard MERGE INTO USING WHEN MATCHED/NOT MATCHED for portable H2 + PostgreSQL atomic upsert (the technique that addresses this H2 limitation)

**See also:** [GE-20260618-0ed34c](GE-20260618-0ed34c.md) — H2 LOCK_MODE=1 has no effect with MVStore (failed workaround for this problem) | [GE-20260618-73a023](GE-20260618-73a023.md) — H2 JDBC getMetaData().getURL() drops connection properties

Hibernate `@OneToMany` collections must be initialized with `ArrayList`, not `CopyOnWriteArrayList`

## Hibernate `@OneToMany` collections must be initialized with `ArrayList`, not `CopyOnWriteArrayList`

**ID:** GE-0142
**Stack:** Hibernate ORM 6.x, Quarkus 3.17.5 (likely all Hibernate 6.x versions)
**Symptom:** Unit tests pass. Integration tests that load the entity from the database fail — the `@OneToMany` collection either throws an unexpected exception or behaves as if empty when accessed outside the entity's loading context.

### Root cause
Hibernate replaces field-initialized collections with its own `PersistentBag` (or `PersistentList`) proxy at load time. This works reliably for `java.util.ArrayList` initializers. When the field is initialized with `CopyOnWriteArrayList`, Hibernate may not reliably recognize it as a replaceable collection — the proxy wrapping can silently fail or behave incorrectly. Unit tests never expose this because Hibernate does not load the entity from the database; it only affects database round-trips.

### Fix
Always initialize `@OneToMany` and `@ManyToMany` fields with `new ArrayList<>()`:

```java
// Wrong — passes unit tests, fails integration tests
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "parentTask", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
private List<HibernateTask> childTasks = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

// Correct
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "parentTask", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
private List<HibernateTask> childTasks = new ArrayList<>();
```

If thread-safety is needed at the application layer, wrap on access: `Collections.synchronizedList(entity.getChildTasks())` — but do not use `CopyOnWriteArrayList` as the field initializer.

### Why non-obvious
`CopyOnWriteArrayList` implements `List` and is a perfectly valid Java collection. Nothing in Hibernate ORM documentation, Quarkus documentation, or the `@OneToMany` Javadoc warns against using non-standard `List` implementations as field initializers. The failure is invisible in unit tests and only surfaces when entities are persisted and fetched from a real database.

*Score: 12/15 · Included because: silent failure, unit tests mask the bug, nothing in any documentation warns about this constraint · Reservation: specific to teams using CopyOnWriteArrayList for thread safety in entities*

entries.title: ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent blocks all same-bucket keys while mapping function runs — unusable for network calls
entries.body:
ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent blocks all same-bucket keys while mapping function runs — unusable for network calls

## Symptom

Using `computeIfAbsent` to cache external provider contexts (e.g. fetching a public key from Vault Transit on first use) causes unexpected latency spikes. Under concurrent load, a thread loading one actor's context can block threads loading a different actor's context — even though the keys are completely unrelated.

In extreme cases with synchronised re-entry (the mapping function internally calls back into the map for a different key that hashes to the same bucket), the JVM may deadlock.

## Context

Per-actorId context cache in an `AgentSigner` implementation. First `sign()` call per actor triggers `loadContext(actorId)` which makes an HTTP call to Vault. Subsequent calls should be instant (cache hit).

```java
// WRONG — computeIfAbsent holds the bucket lock during the HTTP call
Optional<C> cached = contextCache.computeIfAbsent(actorId, id -> {
    return loadContext(id);  // HTTP call — may take hundreds of ms
});
```

## Root cause

`ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent` acquires an internal per-bucket lock (striped lock on the bin node) for the duration of the mapping function. While one thread is inside a slow mapping function:
- **All other threads needing any key in the same hash bucket are blocked** — not just the same key
- A second thread calling `computeIfAbsent` for a different key that happens to share the same hash bucket will block until the first completes
- If the mapping function itself calls back into the same map (re-entrant), the JDK **throws `IllegalStateException: Recursive update`** in Java 9+

The Javadoc says "the computation should be short and simple" but gives no hint that slow computations block an entire hash bucket.

## Fix

Use `get()` / `putIfAbsent()` instead. Accept duplicate loads on cold start (two threads for the same key both call `loadContext` — idempotent results are safe):

```java
// CORRECT — no bucket lock held during the network call
Optional<C> cached = contextCache.get(actorId);
if (cached == null) {
    Optional<C> loaded = loadContext(actorId);  // HTTP call, no lock held
    Optional<C> racing = contextCache.putIfAbsent(actorId, loaded);
    cached = racing != null ? racing : loaded;
}
```

`putIfAbsent` is atomic but only holds the lock for the map update itself (microseconds), not for the compute function. The trade-off: on cold start, two threads may both call `loadContext` for the same key. The second's result is discarded (the first writer wins). For idempotent loads (same Vault key → same result), this is safe.

## Why this is non-obvious

The name `computeIfAbsent` implies "compute and store if the key is missing" — developers naturally assume the lock scope is narrow (just the map update). The Javadoc recommends "short and simple" but doesn't say "or you block the entire hash bucket." The symptom (unrelated keys blocking each other) is completely surprising. Developers discovering the issue often suspect their HTTP client or Vault server, not the cache implementation.

`computeIfAbsent` is the correct and safe choice when the mapping function is fast and in-memory. The problem is specifically with slow or blocking mapping functions.

### Why this fix

`putIfAbsent` releases the lock before the network call even starts. The duplicate-load race is the accepted trade-off: two threads load the same key concurrently, one result is discarded. For caches where loading is idempotent and deterministic (fetching a public key from a KMS), this is always safe and preferable to blocking the bucket.

entries.title: COLLECT and EPHEMERAL channel semantics: SELECT-then-DELETE is not atomic under READ_COMMITTED isolation
entries.body:
COLLECT and EPHEMERAL channel semantics: SELECT-then-DELETE is not atomic under READ_COMMITTED isolation

## COLLECT and EPHEMERAL channel semantics: SELECT-then-DELETE is not atomic under READ_COMMITTED isolation

**ID:** GE-20260414-62a6df
**Stack:** Quarkus 3.32.2, Hibernate ORM 6.x, Panache, H2 2.4.x / PostgreSQL
**Symptom:** Under concurrent load, two consumers calling `check_messages` on a COLLECT or EPHEMERAL channel simultaneously both receive the same messages — double delivery. The `@Transactional` method does not prevent this.
**Context:** Any implementation of "deliver-and-clear" semantics using a SELECT followed by a DELETE in the same `@Transactional` method, under the default `READ_COMMITTED` isolation level.

### What was tried (didn't work)

- Wrapping SELECT and DELETE in a single `@Transactional` method — insufficient under READ_COMMITTED
- Using Panache's `.list()` followed by `.delete()` — same isolation problem

### Root cause

Under `READ_COMMITTED` isolation (the default for H2 and PostgreSQL), two transactions that both start before either commits can both execute the SELECT and see the same rows. Both then execute the DELETE. The first DELETE commits; the second DELETE either deletes zero rows (the rows are already gone) or succeeds on its own snapshot. But both transactions have already returned the rows to their callers — double delivery has occurred.

`@Transactional` in Quarkus defaults to `READ_COMMITTED`. This isolation level provides per-statement consistency, not per-transaction snapshot consistency.

```java
// This pattern is NOT safe for exactly-once under concurrent reads:
@Transactional
public List<Message> collectAndClear(UUID channelId) {
    List<Message> messages = Message.find("channelId = ?1", channelId).list();  // snapshot A
    Message.delete("channelId = ?1", channelId);                                // deletes snapshot A's rows
    return messages;  // but another transaction already saw the same rows
}
```

### Sequential delivery (the common case)

If only one reader calls `check_messages` at a time, the deliver-and-clear pattern is correct and safe. The issue only surfaces under true concurrent reads from multiple threads/processes simultaneously.

### Fix — two options

**Option 1: `SELECT FOR UPDATE` (locks rows before reading)**

```java
@Transactional
public List<Message> collectAndClear(UUID channelId) {
    // Lock rows first — other transactions must wait
    List<Message> messages = Message.getEntityManager()
        .createNativeQuery("SELECT * FROM message WHERE channel_id = ? FOR UPDATE", Message.class)
        .setParameter(1, channelId)
        .getResultList();
    Message.delete("channelId = ?1", channelId);
    return messages;
}
```

**Option 2: Higher isolation (`REPEATABLE_READ` or `SERIALIZABLE`)**

In Quarkus, configure the datasource isolation level:
```properties
quarkus.datasource.jdbc.transaction-isolation-level=repeatable-read
```

Or per-transaction via the JTA API. `REPEATABLE_READ` ensures both the SELECT and DELETE see the same consistent snapshot. Suitable for PostgreSQL; H2 supports it.

### Mitigation for most production cases

In practice, multi-agent systems rarely have two agents calling `check_messages` on the same COLLECT/EPHEMERAL channel simultaneously. The sequential-delivery guarantee is correct for the realistic case. The concurrent double-delivery is worth documenting but typically requires explicit concurrent architecture to trigger.

### Why non-obvious

`@Transactional` sounds like it should guarantee atomicity across all operations within the method. It does guarantee atomicity (the DELETE will roll back if anything fails) and isolation from other transactions that MODIFY rows. But `READ_COMMITTED` does NOT prevent another read-only transaction from seeing the same rows before the DELETE commits. The gap between "transactional" and "exactly-once" under concurrent reads is subtle.
