entries.title: Removing @Alternative from one bean in a multi-implementation CDI chain silently changes resolution — no AmbiguousResolutionException
entries.body:
Removing @Alternative from one bean in a multi-implementation CDI chain silently changes resolution — no AmbiguousResolutionException

### Symptom

After removing `@Alternative @Priority(2)` from one CDI bean, a different bean
silently becomes the active implementation. No `AmbiguousResolutionException`, no
warning, no log. Tests that depend on the removed bean's behaviour fail with
unrelated-looking assertion errors.

### Context

Three implementations of the same port interface coexist in the build:

| Bean | Annotations | Role |
|------|------------|------|
| `PrReviewService` | `@ApplicationScoped @DefaultBean` | Layer 1 naive baseline |
| `QhorusPrReviewService` | `@ApplicationScoped @Alternative @Priority(1)` | Layer 3 qhorus messaging |
| `PrReviewCaseService` | `@ApplicationScoped @Alternative @Priority(2)` | Layer 5 engine (active) |

This is the CDI displacement pattern for progressive layer integration — each layer
adds an implementation; CDI priority determines which is active at runtime.

### What was tried (didn't work)

Removed `@Alternative @Priority(2)` from `PrReviewCaseService` to fix an anti-pattern
documented in ARC42STORIES §8 ("CDI priority gymnastics"). Expected: the plain
`@ApplicationScoped` bean would still displace the `@DefaultBean` baseline via
Quarkus's `@DefaultBean` semantics.

### Root cause

CDI resolution rules interact in a non-obvious way:

1. `@DefaultBean` beans are suppressed when any non-`@DefaultBean` bean exists ✅
2. Activated `@Alternative` beans (with `@Priority`) take precedence over regular beans ⚠️
3. After removing `@Alternative` from `PrReviewCaseService`, it becomes a regular bean
4. `QhorusPrReviewService` (`@Alternative @Priority(1)`) is still an activated alternative
5. **Rule 2 applies**: the activated alternative wins over the regular bean
6. `QhorusPrReviewService` becomes the active implementation — silently

The mental model "I'm just removing unnecessary annotations" is wrong. The annotations
are load-bearing: they participate in a priority chain where every bean's annotation
set matters.

### Fix

All implementations in the `@Alternative` chain must be addressed together, not one at
a time. To properly fix the anti-pattern:

- Either make ALL non-baseline implementations use `@DefaultBean` displacement
  (remove `@Alternative @Priority` from all of them and ensure only one non-`@DefaultBean` exists)
- Or keep the `@Alternative @Priority` chain intact and accept it as the mechanism
  for layer coexistence

Do not remove `@Alternative` from one bean without checking what other `@Alternative`
implementations exist for the same interface.

### Why this is non-obvious

Most developers reason about CDI alternatives in pairs: "my bean vs the default."
The three-way interaction (DefaultBean + Alternative(1) + Alternative(2)) is rarely
encountered, and the silent resolution change (no exception, wrong bean) gives no
diagnostic signal. The symptom (test assertion failure on unrelated data) is
completely disconnected from the cause (CDI annotation change).

### Why this fix

The obvious approach — "just remove the anti-pattern annotation" — is wrong because
it treats the annotations as decoration rather than as a load-bearing priority chain.
The fix requires understanding the full set of implementations and their annotation
interactions before changing any single one.

### Alternatives considered

- Remove `@Alternative @Priority(2)` from only the active bean → silently breaks resolution (this gotcha)
- Remove `@Alternative` from ALL implementations and use `@DefaultBean` displacement → requires ensuring exactly one non-`@DefaultBean` impl, and retiring or `@DefaultBean`-ing the intermediate layers
- Keep `@Alternative @Priority` chain as-is → accepted as the working mechanism until a coordinated cleanup addresses all implementations together

**See also:** GE-20260626-c21b02 — @DefaultBean suppression by any Instance<T> peer, a different silent failure in the same CDI displacement space.

entries.title: Two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → Quarkus AmbiguousResolutionException, not Unsatisfied
entries.body:
Two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → Quarkus AmbiguousResolutionException, not Unsatisfied

## What happened

Two `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` implementations of the same SPI type appeared on the CDI
classpath simultaneously (one from a platform mock library, one from a persistence testing module).
Quarkus reported **"Ambiguous dependencies"** and refused to start — even though both beans
explicitly said "I am a default, defer to anyone else".

## Why this is non-obvious

`@DefaultBean` is documented as "yield to any other bean of the same type". With two
`@DefaultBean` beans and no non-default implementation, neither bean yields — the contract
("yield to someone else") cannot resolve because there IS no "someone else" with higher
precedence. The error message is **Ambiguous** (same as two regular `@ApplicationScoped`
beans conflicting), not **Unsatisfied** (what you'd expect if both were supposedly yielding).
Developers often assume two `@DefaultBean` beans resolve cleanly because they both "opt in"
to being overridden.

## Root cause

CDI/ARC `@DefaultBean` semantics: a default bean is only eligible when no other bean at
the same or higher priority is eligible. With two `@DefaultBean` beans and no higher-priority
bean, the tie-break is undefined — ARC treats this as an ambiguous injection point.

## Fix

Exclude the unwanted `@DefaultBean` implementation via `application.properties`:
```properties
quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.platform.mock.MockCurrentPrincipal,\
  io.casehub.platform.mock.MockGroupMembershipProvider,\
  io.casehub.platform.mock.MockPreferenceProvider
```

This removes the conflicting bean from CDI discovery entirely, leaving the desired
`@DefaultBean` as the sole implementation. Prefer excluding the one that returns null or
uninitialized values rather than the one with correct sentinel behaviour.

### Why this fix

`@Alternative @Priority(N)` would also work, but requires activating it via
`selected-alternatives` — that is a heavier configuration change and makes the
intent less clear. `exclude-types` is surgical: "this specific class should not
participate in CDI at all in this context."

### Alternative — use `Instance<T>` with `isUnsatisfied()` to avoid the conflict entirely

Rather than excluding a conflicting bean after the fact, don't provide a competing `@DefaultBean` in the extension at all. Inject `Instance<T>` and check `isUnsatisfied()` at call time:

```java
@Inject Instance<PreferenceProvider> preferenceProviderInstance;

int threshold;
if (preferenceProviderInstance.isUnsatisfied()) {
    threshold = DEFAULT_VALUE;  // no provider on classpath
} else {
    threshold = preferenceProviderInstance.get().resolve(...).getOrDefault(KEY).value();
}
```

`Instance<T>` always satisfies its own injection point (the container injects the `Instance` holder, not `T` directly). When zero beans of type `T` exist, `isUnsatisfied()` returns `true`; when one is active, `.get()` returns it. No `@DefaultBean` is added to the extension, so no conflict can arise.

**Best for:** library/extension authors who control their own code and want to make a platform SPI optional without contributing a competing `@DefaultBean`.

**Limitation:** requires call-site guards (`isUnsatisfied()` before `.get()`); callers that inject `T` directly still get an ambiguous point if two `@DefaultBean` beans exist from other sources.

## Constraints

Applies when both `@DefaultBean` implementations reach the CDI container's scanning phase
(i.e. both are indexed via `quarkus.index-dependency` or are in the app's own sources).
In two-repo / multi-module projects, platform library JARs can silently contribute
`@DefaultBean` mocks that conflict with internal no-ops.

## Alternatives considered

- Mark one bean `@Alternative @Priority(1)` instead of `@DefaultBean` — works but changes
  the semantics of the "winning" bean and requires `selected-alternatives` configuration.
- Remove one of the `@DefaultBean` implementations from the classpath entirely — clean, but
  may not be possible if it comes from a third-party dependency.

## Invalidation triggers

Would change if Quarkus ARC adds a deterministic tie-break for two `@DefaultBean` beans
(e.g. favour the one in the current module's sources). Track Quarkus changelog for ARC
`@DefaultBean` resolution changes.

**See also:** [GE-20260515-fd3156](GE-20260515-fd3156.md) — @DefaultBean must be on @Produces method not on the class | [GE-20260529-ab148d](GE-20260529-ab148d.md) — multiple CDI constructors without @Inject → UnsatisfiedResolutionException | [GE-20260601-848232](GE-20260601-848232.md) — exclude-types silently does nothing for Jandex-indexed JARs

**See also:** [GE-20260604-2f0889](GE-20260604-2f0889.md) — @Alternative @Priority(N) stubs appear in @All List<T> alongside original bean

**See also:** [GE-20260609-26ffa5](GE-20260609-26ffa5.md) — @ApplicationScoped POJO + @Produces for same type causes CDI ambiguous bean resolution

**See also:** [GE-20260515-99cf39](GE-20260515-99cf39.md) — config-driven @Produces @DefaultBean for engine-internal strategy selection

**See also:** [GE-20260614-337397](GE-20260614-337397.md) — quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel, clashing with @DefaultBean fallback | [GE-20260604-b3d2ef](GE-20260604-b3d2ef.md) — quarkus-flow CDI extension already registers WorkflowApplication — adding @Produces causes ambiguity

**See also:** [GE-20260615-6c4767](../casehub-engine/GE-20260615-6c4767.md) — adding custom CDI qualifier to @ApplicationScoped removes @Default

**See also:** GE-20260627-51e402 — @Alternative totally suppresses @DefaultBean (not just deprioritized, gone from container)

entries.title: @Alternative @Priority(n) in CDI 4.0/Quarkus globally activates the alternative — causes AmbiguousResolutionException
entries.body:
@Alternative @Priority(n) in CDI 4.0/Quarkus globally activates the alternative — causes AmbiguousResolutionException

## @Alternative @Priority(n) in CDI 4.0/Quarkus globally activates the alternative — causes AmbiguousResolutionException

### Stack
Quarkus 3.31.1, CDI 4.0

### Symptom
Multiple beans implement the same SPI interface. Each alternative is annotated with
`@Alternative @Priority(10)` as well as `@ApplicationScoped`. On Quarkus startup, the
application fails with `AmbiguousResolutionException` — all implementations are active
simultaneously.

```
AmbiguousResolutionException: Ambiguous dependencies for type ContextDiffStrategy
and qualifiers [@Default]: [TopLevelContextDiffStrategy, JsonPatchContextDiffStrategy, 
NoOpContextDiffStrategy]
```

### Context
SPI pattern where one default bean and two `@Alternative` beans implement an interface.
The intent was to activate one alternative at a time via
`quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` in `application.properties`.

### What was tried
Adding `@Priority(10)` alongside `@Alternative` — expected this to be a ranking hint
that would help CDI resolve ambiguity. Instead, `@Priority` on an `@Alternative` is what
globally activates the bean in CDI 4.0, making all three implementations simultaneously
active and causing the ambiguous resolution error.

### Root cause
In CDI 4.0 (Jakarta EE 10), `@Alternative @Priority(n)` is a shorthand for globally
activating an alternative across the entire application — no `beans.xml` or
`selected-alternatives` config needed. When ALL alternatives carry this annotation,
they are ALL active, which breaks injection points expecting a single bean.

### Solution 1 — Remove @Priority, use selected-alternatives config
**Approach:** Strip `@Priority` from all alternatives; activate one via config.
**Pros:** Per-profile/per-module control without code changes; the intended Quarkus mechanism for SPI switching.
**Cons:** Requires a config entry per activation; all alternatives default to inactive.

Remove `@Priority` from all `@Alternative` beans. Activate a specific alternative only
via `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` in `application.properties`:

```java
// WRONG — @Priority globally activates the alternative in CDI 4.0
@Alternative
@Priority(10)
@ApplicationScoped
public class MyAlternativeImpl implements MyInterface { ... }

// CORRECT — @Alternative only; activation controlled by config
@Alternative
@ApplicationScoped
public class MyAlternativeImpl implements MyInterface { ... }
```

```properties
# application.properties — activate the desired alternative
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=com.example.MyAlternativeImpl
```

### Solution 2 — Use different @Priority values to establish precedence
**Approach:** Keep `@Alternative @Priority` but assign distinct priority values; CDI resolves to the highest.
**Pros:** No config entry needed; the default (lowest priority) is always active, the override (highest priority) wins when present on the classpath. Works naturally for optional-module patterns where a higher-capability implementation should auto-replace the baseline.
**Cons:** All alternatives are always globally active (the core CDI 4.0 behaviour). The "default" must have the lowest priority; adding a third implementation requires careful priority assignment.

```java
// Default — always active; lowest priority loses when a higher one is present
@Alternative
@Priority(0)
@ApplicationScoped
public class ClaimFirstStrategy implements WorkerSelectionStrategy { ... }

// Override — higher priority wins; active only when on the classpath
@Alternative
@Priority(1)
@ApplicationScoped
public class SemanticWorkerSelectionStrategy implements WorkerSelectionStrategy { ... }
```

CDI injects the `@Priority(1)` bean when both are present; falls back to `@Priority(0)` when only
the default module is on the classpath. No `beans.xml` or `selected-alternatives` required.

**When to choose Solution 2 over Solution 1:** When the override is an optional module (not always
on the classpath) and the default must always be present. Config-based activation (Solution 1)
requires an explicit entry even for the default case; priority-based resolution (Solution 2) makes
the default zero-configuration.

### Why this is non-obvious
The `@Priority` annotation is commonly used alongside `@Alternative` in CDI tutorials
and examples from the CDI 2.x era, where `@Priority` on an alternative was a *ranking*
hint. In CDI 4.0 the semantics changed — `@Priority` on an `@Alternative` is now an
*activation* mechanism (equivalent to listing it in `beans.xml` with a priority). The
Quarkus docs for `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` don't warn about this interaction.

### Why this fix
`quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` gives per-profile/per-module control via config,
which is the intended Quarkus mechanism for SPI switching (same as how `PanningStrategyLoopControl`
and other engine SPIs are activated). It doesn't require code changes to switch backends.

**See also:** GE-20260422-ebb91d — AmbiguousResolutionException from multiple unqualified @ApplicationScoped beans

**See also:** GE-20260427-97650e "CDI ambiguity when adding second implementation of a quarkus-ledger repository interface"
**See also:** GE-20260427-62d3ab — use @Alternative @Priority(1) inner beans in @QuarkusTest to spy on SPI call sites
**See also:** [GE-20260427-c2b84f — @Alternative @Priority(1) beans in a test-helper jar are invisible to downstream @QuarkusTest — no Jandex index](GE-20260427-c2b84f.md)

### Update — Test-refactoring trap: two classes declaring the same @Alternative

During a test refactoring, if two `@QuarkusTest` classes *simultaneously* declare an
`@Alternative @Priority(2)` inner class implementing the same type, Quarkus boot fails
with `AmbiguousResolutionException` even though `mvn test-compile` passes cleanly. The
compile succeeds because both classes are syntactically valid; the CDI conflict only
surfaces at application startup.

entries.title: @Alternative without @Priority silently disables @IfBuildProperty-gated beans — dependencies activate, service does not
@DefaultBean lives in io.quarkus.arc, not jakarta.enterprise.inject
entries.body:
@DefaultBean lives in io.quarkus.arc, not jakarta.enterprise.inject

## Symptom

```
error: cannot find symbol
  symbol: class DefaultBean
  location: package jakarta.enterprise.inject
```

The error gives no hint that the annotation exists — just that it doesn't exist
in the package you reached for.

## Context

When writing a `@DefaultBean` CDI bean in a Quarkus extension or application.
`@DefaultBean` marks a bean as the fallback when no higher-priority bean is
present — the Quarkus Arc equivalent of Spring's `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`.

## Root cause

`@DefaultBean` is a Quarkus Arc-specific annotation. It is not part of the
Jakarta CDI spec, so it doesn't live in `jakarta.enterprise.inject`. It lives
in `io.quarkus.arc`.

## Fix

```java
// Wrong — jakarta CDI doesn't have this
import jakarta.enterprise.inject.DefaultBean;

// Right — Quarkus Arc annotation
import io.quarkus.arc.DefaultBean;
```

## Why this is non-obvious

If you know CDI, `jakarta.enterprise.inject` is the natural package to reach for.
The compile error only says the class doesn't exist there — not that it exists
somewhere else. Easy to waste time searching for a CDI spec addition that never
happened.

**See also:** GE-20260427-543663 — @Produces @DefaultBean for library-level overridable CDI defaults (correct usage)

**See also:** [GE-20260515-fd3156](GE-20260515-fd3156.md) — @DefaultBean on @Produces method makes the produced bean default (related annotation gotcha)

**See also:** [GE-20260601-fcf0d9](GE-20260601-fcf0d9.md) — two @DefaultBean beans for same type → AmbiguousResolutionException

**See also:** [GE-20260604-81a6a6](GE-20260604-81a6a6.md) — @DefaultBean @Unremovable required when injection point is in a different Maven module

**See also:** [GE-20260609-18a0b1](GE-20260609-18a0b1.md) — quarkus.index-dependency for a JAR with jandex.idx double-scans it

@IfBuildProfile + @Alternative + @Priority resolves CDI without selected-alternatives in indexed JARs
entries.body:
@IfBuildProfile + @Alternative + @Priority resolves CDI without selected-alternatives in indexed JARs

### Symptom

Adding a dev-profile-only CDI bean (e.g., a `CurrentPrincipal` for dev mode) via `%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=com.example.DevBean` causes startup failures — all beans from the non-profiled `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` list disappear.

### Context

Quarkus profile-specific properties (`%dev.`, `%test.`, `%prod.`) completely **replace** their non-profiled counterparts. If the base `application.properties` has:

```properties
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=\
  com.example.JpaRepo,\
  com.example.JpaPlanItemStore,\
  com.example.JpaSubCaseGroupRepo
```

Adding `%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=com.example.DevBean` drops all three JPA alternatives in dev mode — CDI startup fails with unsatisfied dependency errors for every bean that was in the original list.

### Root cause

Profile-specific properties in Quarkus are full replacements, not merges. This is by design (SmallRye Config behaviour), but the failure mode is silent — no warning that the non-profiled value was dropped.

### Fix

Use bean-level annotations instead of `selected-alternatives`:

```java
@ApplicationScoped
@Alternative
@Priority(150)  // beats OidcCurrentPrincipal @Priority(100)
@IfBuildProfile("dev")
public class DemoCurrentPrincipal implements CurrentPrincipal {
    @Override public String tenancyId() { return "demo-tenant"; }
    @Override public String actorId()   { return "demo-user"; }
}
```

**Requirements:**
1. The bean must live in a **Jandex-indexed JAR** (e.g., the application's own `runtime/` module). ArC discovers it automatically — no `selected-alternatives` entry needed.
2. `@IfBuildProfile("dev")` excludes the bean entirely from non-dev builds — no ambiguity in production.
3. `@Priority(150)` resolves over competing `@Alternative` beans (e.g., `OidcCurrentPrincipal @Priority(100)`) via standard ArC priority resolution.

This is the same mechanism by which `OidcCurrentPrincipal @Alternative @Priority(100)` beats `MockCurrentPrincipal @DefaultBean` in production — without being listed in `selected-alternatives`.

### Why this is non-obvious

The natural instinct is `%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=MyDevBean` — it looks like the standard profile-override pattern. The replacement behaviour is documented for SmallRye Config but not prominently flagged in the Quarkus CDI guide. The failure (dropped JPA alternatives) manifests as unrelated `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` errors that don't mention `selected-alternatives` at all.

### Why this fix

`@IfBuildProfile + @Priority` solves the problem at the bean level — no configuration property needed. The alternative (duplicating the full `selected-alternatives` list in every profile override) is fragile and drifts as new alternatives are added.

### Alternatives considered

- **Duplicate the full list in `%dev.`** — works but fragile; every new `@Alternative` bean must be added to every profile-specific override. Drifts silently.
- **Use `@UnlessBuildProfile("prod")` instead of `@IfBuildProfile("dev")`** — activates in both dev and test profiles, which may not be desired. Test profile has its own `FixedCurrentPrincipal @Priority(200)`.

entries.body:
CDI @Alternative bypass for quarkus:build: non-@Alternative subclass in app module

## CDI @Alternative bypass for quarkus:build: non-@Alternative subclass in app module

### What

When `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` fails to activate `@Alternative` beans during `quarkus:build` (see GE-20260524-2b587e), create a non-`@Alternative @ApplicationScoped` subclass of each needed `@Alternative` bean directly in the application module's own source.

### Why it works

CDI does NOT inherit `@Alternative` from superclasses. A subclass without `@Alternative` is treated as a regular `@Default @ApplicationScoped` bean, satisfying injection points without any `selected-alternatives` configuration. Quarkus always indexes the application module's own source, so the subclass is always discovered — no `quarkus.index-dependency` required.

### Code

For each `@Alternative @ApplicationScoped` SPI implementation in a dependency jar:

```java
// In the application module (src/main/java):
package com.example.app.spi;

import com.lib.InMemoryEventLogRepository;
import jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped;

@ApplicationScoped  // no @Alternative — this is @Default
public class AppEventLogRepository extends InMemoryEventLogRepository {}
```

Repeat for each SPI. Inject CDI fields from the parent class are satisfied normally — CDI handles injection into inherited fields when creating the child bean.

### When to use this

- `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` isn't activating alternatives during `quarkus:build`
- In-memory/dev implementations needed in production build without real backend (tutorial projects, early-stage dev)
- Want zero `selected-alternatives` configuration while keeping implementation reuse

### Why this is non-obvious

Developers reach for `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` (the documented mechanism). When that fails silently, the natural next attempt is compile-scope + index-dependency — which also fails. The subclass approach requires knowing that `@Alternative` is not inherited by subclasses, which is a CDI spec detail most developers haven't needed to rely on.

**See also:** [GE-20260524-2b587e](GE-20260524-2b587e.md) — quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives does not activate @Alternative beans during quarkus:build (the problem this technique solves)

**See also:** [GE-20260427-543663](../quarkus/GE-20260427-543663.md) — @Produces @DefaultBean for library-level overridable CDI defaults

entries.title: Resolve CDI ambiguity between two competing @DefaultBean implementations by introducing a concrete non-default bean
entries.body:
Resolve CDI ambiguity between two competing @DefaultBean implementations by introducing a concrete non-default bean

## Context

Two `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` beans from different JARs both implement the same interface. CDI can't resolve which to use and throws `AmbiguousResolutionException`. Standard approaches don't help:

- `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` is silently ignored for beans from Jandex-indexed JARs (see GE-20260601-848232)
- Marking one as `@Alternative` requires changes to a JAR you don't own
- `@Priority` on `@Alternative` has CDI 2.0 global-scope problems

## Technique

Add a concrete `@ApplicationScoped` bean to your project (production or test sources as appropriate) that implements the conflicting interface:

```java
@ApplicationScoped
public class ProjectGroupMembershipProvider implements GroupMembershipProvider {
    @Override
    public Set<GroupMember> membersOf(String groupName) {
        return Set.of(); // or delegate to preferred implementation
    }
}
```

CDI selects the most-specific non-default bean. Since your bean is NOT `@DefaultBean`, it wins over both competing `@DefaultBean` implementations and the `AmbiguousResolutionException` is resolved. No changes to any JAR required.

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

Most developers reach for `exclude-types` first (fails silently for Jandex-indexed JARs), then try `@Priority` on one of the `@DefaultBean` beans (requires modifying third-party JARs), then consider `@Alternative` + `selected-alternatives` (same problem). The CDI suppression rule — "a non-default bean beats all @DefaultBean candidates for the same type" — is the correct lever, and a thin adapter class is the minimal mechanism that activates it without touching any dependency.

**See also:** [GE-20260601-848232](GE-20260601-848232.md) — exclude-types silently does nothing for Jandex JARs | [GE-20260601-3dbc80](GE-20260601-3dbc80.md) — exclude-types as technique for @DefaultBean ambiguity

**See also:** [GE-20260601-7a3b38](GE-20260601-7a3b38.md) — @DefaultBean invisible when supertype JAR has no Jandex index

**See also:** [GE-20260616-d70e7e](GE-20260616-d70e7e.md) — selected-alternatives silently accepts non-@Alternative beans

entries.title: CDI AmbiguousResolutionException when multiple @ApplicationScoped beans implement the same SPI interface
entries.body:
CDI AmbiguousResolutionException when multiple @ApplicationScoped beans implement the same SPI interface

## Symptom

`@QuarkusTest` fails at boot with `AmbiguousResolutionException: Ambiguous dependencies for type X`. The production code compiles and the beans look correct.

## Context

Defining multiple `@ApplicationScoped` implementations of the same SPI interface (e.g. three `SkillProfileProvider` implementations) so users can choose which to activate. All three are unqualified, so CDI cannot resolve which one to inject at a single injection point.

## What was tried

Adding all three as `@ApplicationScoped` beans, assuming CDI would pick the first one or throw a clear build-time error.

## Root cause

CDI requires exactly one unambiguous bean per injection type when no qualifier is used. Multiple unqualified `@ApplicationScoped` beans implementing the same interface all compete — CDI cannot resolve the injection point and throws at container startup, not at compile time.

## Fix

Designate exactly one implementation as the default (leave it unqualified `@ApplicationScoped`). Mark all others with `@Alternative`:

```java
// Default — CDI injects this when no override is present
@ApplicationScoped
public class WorkerProfileSkillProfileProvider implements SkillProfileProvider { ... }

// Not active by default — user activates via @Alternative @Priority(1)
@ApplicationScoped
@Alternative
public class CapabilitiesSkillProfileProvider implements SkillProfileProvider { ... }

@ApplicationScoped
@Alternative
public class ResolutionHistorySkillProfileProvider implements SkillProfileProvider { ... }
```

Users override the default at their own application level:

```java
@ApplicationScoped
@Alternative
@Priority(1)
public class MyCustomProvider implements SkillProfileProvider { ... }
```

## Why this is non-obvious

The error only appears at `@QuarkusTest` boot — compile succeeds silently. The fix (marking non-default implementations `@Alternative`) is easy once known, but the CDI resolution rules around `@Alternative` vs unqualified beans are non-obvious. The natural instinct is to let the user pick via config, not via CDI qualifiers.

**See also:** GE-20260415-884e48 — @Alternative @Priority(n) globally activates the alternative in CDI 4.0 | GE-20260417-c59817 — quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives activates @Alternative beans in application.properties | GE-20260421-1cfae6 — @Produces @DefaultBean provides consumer-replaceable CDI defaults without @Alternative

**See also:** [GE-20260428-9311f8](GE-20260428-9311f8.md) — casehub-engine @ApplicationScoped no-op SPI beans collide with consumer implementations when engine is indexed | [GE-20260427-97650e](GE-20260427-97650e.md) — CDI ambiguity when adding second implementation of a quarkus-ledger repository interface

**See also:** GE-20260427-62d3ab "Use @Alternative @Priority(1) inner beans in @QuarkusTest to spy on SPI call sites without Mockito"
**See also:** GE-20260427-c2b84f — @Alternative @Priority(1) beans in test-helper jar are invisible without Jandex index

## Update — Variant: two @DefaultBean impls for the same type

`@DefaultBean` in Quarkus Arc means "use this if no non-default bean for this type exists."
When **two** `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` beans implement the same interface, Arc cannot
resolve the injection point — both are default, neither wins — and throws
`AmbiguousResolutionException` as soon as any production bean injects that type. The symptom
only surfaces once an `@Inject` for the interface is added; before that the ambiguity exists
silently in the CDI container.

**Scenario:** Two library modules each provide a `@DefaultBean CurrentPrincipal` for
"uncontested" environments (`MockCurrentPrincipal` from casehub-platform, `QhorusInboundCurrentPrincipal`
from casehub-qhorus). Adding `@Inject CurrentPrincipal` to any production bean in the app
module triggers the error — the injection point forces CDI to resolve and it finds two equals.

**Fix — exclude one at application level:**

```properties
# application.properties — exclude the stub; the runtime principal wins
quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.platform.mock.MockCurrentPrincipal
```

**Test fix — use quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives to force a third, definitive impl:**

```properties
# src/test/resources/application.properties
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=io.casehub.platform.testing.FixedCurrentPrincipal
```

**Why @DefaultBean differs from @Alternative:** `@DefaultBean` is not in the CDI spec — it is
a Quarkus Arc extension that says "this bean loses to any explicit non-default bean." But when
two `@DefaultBean` beans compete, there is no winner — Arc throws rather than picking arbitrarily.
The `@Alternative` pattern (one winner, rest marked alternative) is the correct SPI design for
exactly-one-at-a-time. `@DefaultBean` is for extension-provided stubs that yield to consumer
overrides, not for multiple peers. Two `@DefaultBean` peers should be refactored so that only one
module provides the default; the other moves to `@Alternative`.

entries.title: quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives in application.properties activates @Alternative beans in @QuarkusTest — beans.xml is ignored
entries.body:
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives in application.properties activates @Alternative beans in @QuarkusTest — beans.xml is ignored

## What it is

`quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` in `application.properties` (or test `application.properties`) is the correct way to activate `@Alternative` CDI beans in a Quarkus application — including in `@QuarkusTest` contexts.

```properties
# In src/test/resources/application.properties or src/main/resources/application.properties
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=com.example.MyAlternativeRepository
```

Multiple alternatives can be comma-separated.

## Why it's undocumented / non-obvious

The standard CDI mechanism for activating alternatives is `beans.xml`:
```xml
<beans>
  <alternatives>
    <class>com.example.MyAlternativeRepository</class>
  </alternatives>
</beans>
```

In Quarkus with Arc (the CDI implementation), **`beans.xml` alternative activation is silently ignored at build time**. Arc processes CDI at build time and does not honour the `beans.xml` `<alternatives>` section. There is no warning, no error — the `@Alternative` bean is simply not activated, and the original bean (or no bean) is used instead. This causes `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` at startup if nothing else provides the bean.

The `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` property is the Quarkus-specific replacement but is not prominently documented alongside the `@Alternative` annotation documentation.

## Context

Common scenario: a Quarkus extension provides an `@Alternative @ApplicationScoped` repository bean (e.g. `JpaLedgerEntryRepository`) that yields to consumer-provided implementations in production. In `@QuarkusTest` integration tests, you want to activate the base implementation since no consumer repo exists in the test module.

## Fix

Add to `src/test/resources/application.properties`:

```properties
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=io.example.JpaLedgerEntryRepository
```

Do NOT add `<alternatives>` to `beans.xml` — it will have no effect in Quarkus Arc.

## Why this is non-obvious

The CDI spec says `beans.xml` alternatives work. Quarkus Arc silently diverges from this for build-time optimization reasons. The property name `selected-alternatives` is not listed in the CDI or Arc extension documentation alongside `@Alternative` — it requires reading the Arc configuration reference which is separate from the CDI programming model docs.

## Update — test-local classes in src/test/java need no quarkus.index-dependency

When the `@Alternative` class lives in a **external jar** (a separate Maven module), you must tell Quarkus to index it:

```properties
quarkus.index-dependency.mymodule.group-id=io.example
quarkus.index-dependency.mymodule.artifact-id=my-alternatives-module
```

However, if the `@Alternative` class lives directly in `src/test/java/` of the same module, **no `quarkus.index-dependency` is needed**. Quarkus automatically indexes the test source root for `@QuarkusTest`. Only classes in external jars require the explicit index-dependency config.

```properties
# This is sufficient when @Alternative classes are in src/test/java/:
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=io.example.InMemoryRepository

# quarkus.index-dependency is NOT needed — test sources are auto-indexed
```

This is useful when avoiding Maven module cycles: copy the alternative implementations into the module's own `src/test/java/` and the `selected-alternatives` property works without any additional indexing configuration.

## Update — @Alternative @IfBuildProperty beans also need selected-alternatives (not just @QuarkusTest)

When `@Alternative` is combined with `@IfBuildProperty`, the bean is registered at build time when the property matches, but **registration alone does not make it the active CDI alternative**. The `@Alternative` selection still requires `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives`, even in production `application.properties`.

This surfaces when activating a Quarkus extension's reactive stack via a build property. For example, Qhorus's reactive services are `@Alternative @IfBuildProperty(name = "quarkus.datasource.qhorus.reactive", stringValue = "true") @ApplicationScoped`. Setting the property in `application.properties` registers the beans at augmentation but they still do not win CDI resolution without explicit selection:

```properties
# application.properties — both properties are required to activate reactive Qhorus beans
quarkus.datasource.qhorus.reactive=true
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=\
  io.casehub.qhorus.runtime.channel.ReactiveChannelService,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.runtime.message.ReactiveMessageService,\
  ...
```

**The @Priority workaround:** If the bean is annotated `@Alternative @Priority(N)`, Arc selects it automatically without `selected-alternatives`. The `@Priority` annotation is the preferred mechanism for extension-provided alternatives that should activate without consumer configuration. For consumer-configured beans, `selected-alternatives` remains the explicit control point.

## Update — selected-alternatives is build-time: %test. profile prefix has no effect

`quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` is evaluated during Quarkus augmentation (build time), not at runtime. Profile prefixes like `%test.` are resolved at runtime and therefore **have no effect** on this property.

This means you must write:
```properties
# CORRECT — no profile prefix; the property applies globally at augmentation
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=io.casehub.persistence.memory.MemorySubCaseGroupRepository
```

Not:
```properties
# WRONG — %test. is silently ignored for build-time properties; the alternative is not activated
%test.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=io.casehub.persistence.memory.MemorySubCaseGroupRepository
```

quarkus.arc.exclude-types resolves @DefaultBean ambiguity between two Jandex-indexed framework JARs
entries.body:
quarkus.arc.exclude-types resolves @DefaultBean ambiguity between two Jandex-indexed framework JARs

## Context

Two Jandex-indexed framework JARs both provide `@DefaultBean` implementations for the same SPI type. Both are on the test classpath. Quarkus CDI augmentation reports ambiguous dependencies:

```
Ambiguous dependencies for type io.example.SomeProvider and qualifiers [@Default]
  - CLASS bean [...DefaultImpl...] (jar-a)
  - CLASS bean [...MockImpl...] (jar-b)
```

Changing scope or modifying either JAR is not an option. The less-capable no-op implementation should lose.

## Technique

Add the less-capable bean to `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` in the test `application.properties`. Quarkus removes it from CDI scanning entirely, leaving the more-capable implementation as the sole `@DefaultBean`:

```properties
# src/test/resources/application.properties
quarkus.arc.exclude-types=\
  io.example.NoOpSomeProvider,\
  io.example.AnotherNoOpBean
```

Multiple types are comma-separated with backslash continuation. Each entry is a fully-qualified class name. Excluded types are invisible to CDI — the remaining `@DefaultBean` wins without ambiguity.

## Why this is non-obvious

The natural responses to a CDI ambiguity are: change scope, add `@Priority`, or use `beans.xml` alternatives. `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` is a Quarkus-specific property that completely removes a class from CDI scanning — it doesn't just lower priority, it makes the class invisible. Most developers don't reach for it because the Quarkus docs present it as a workaround for scheduler-incompatible beans (a different use case), not as a general CDI conflict resolver.

**See also:** [GE-20260601-848232](GE-20260601-848232.md) — quarkus.arc.exclude-types silently does nothing for beans from Jandex-indexed JARs (contradicts this entry — verify your scenario) | [GE-20260601-81be07](GE-20260601-81be07.md) — resolve ambiguity by introducing a concrete non-default bean

entries.body:
langchain4j-agentic DeclarativeUtil has a single CDI resolver hook for @ChatModelSupplier only — no equivalent for other supplier types

### What it is
`DeclarativeUtil` in `langchain4j-agentic` exposes a single static list `chatSupplierParameterResolvers` with one registration method `addChatSupplierParameterResolver(ChatSupplierParameterResolver)`. This resolver hook fires only during `@ChatModelSupplier` and `@StreamingChatModelSupplier` processing. All other supplier annotations (`@ToolsSupplier`, `@ChatMemorySupplier`, `@ChatMemoryProviderSupplier`, `@ContentRetrieverSupplier`, `@RetrievalAugmentorSupplier`, `@AgentListenerSupplier`, `@ToolProviderSupplier`) call `checkArguments(method)` which enforces **zero parameters** before invoking the static method directly — no resolver hook exists for these paths.

### Why this matters for framework integrators
Any DI framework (Quarkus, Spring, Guice) wanting to inject CDI/Spring beans into supplier methods is blocked for all supplier types except chat model suppliers. The `@CdiBean` workaround in `quarkus-langchain4j` only works for `@ChatModelSupplier` as a result. Users who need a CDI-managed `ContentRetriever` or `ChatMemory` must use `Arc.container()` or `ApplicationContext.getBean()` inside the static method body — bypassing injection, scope management, and testability.

### How to discover this
Only by decompiling `langchain4j-agentic-1.15.1-beta25.jar` and reading `DeclarativeUtil.class`. The library has no published Javadoc for internal classes and no documentation of the SPI surface area.

```bash
# Locate the JAR
find ~/.m2/repository/dev/langchain4j/langchain4j-agentic -name "*.jar" | grep -v sources | head -1

# The class structure reveals: addChatSupplierParameterResolver() is the only hook
# All other configureAgent() branches call checkArguments() then invokeStatic()
```

### Workaround
For Quarkus: use `SyntheticCreationalContext.getInjectedReference()` in the synthetic bean creator (`AgenticRecorder`) to inject CDI beans at agent construction time, bypassing the static supplier method entirely. This requires detecting at build time that no static supplier method exists for a given type, then adding a CDI injection point for that type.

### Upstream path
An upstream PR to `langchain4j-agentic` should propose a general `SupplierParameterResolver` SPI (not chat-model-specific) and add resolver hooks to all supplier type branches in `configureAgent()`. Frame as a DI-framework-agnostic improvement — Spring users would benefit from the same hook.

### Why this is non-obvious
The library name suggests platform independence (`langchain4j` not `langchain4j-spring`), so the assumption is that all supplier types are equally extensible. The asymmetry between `@ChatModelSupplier` (has a resolver hook) and all other supplier annotations (do not) is not mentioned in any README, Javadoc, or issue tracker. The class is package-private in the library with no stable API guarantee.

entries.title: nomic-embed-text treats Java class names and CDI annotations as generic tokens — keyword embedding search is catastrophically worse than substring matching
entries.body:
nomic-embed-text treats Java class names and CDI annotations as generic tokens — keyword embedding search is catastrophically worse than substring matching

## Symptom

Embedding-based search (Qdrant + nomic-embed-text) returns plausible-looking but
semantically wrong results when queried with Java class names, CDI annotations,
or framework-specific identifiers. No error — the results just aren't relevant.

Examples from a 14-scenario benchmark:
- `@DefaultBean` → matched WireMock and Arabic Letter Mark entries
- `ChatModel` → matched HTTP caching and Maven caching entries
- `shadowing` → matched Shadow DOM entries instead of JPA field shadowing
- `stream` → matched Java streams, SSE, PostgreSQL notifications instead of CloudEvents

## Context

A garden corpus (~1,960 entries) indexed with nomic-embed-text 768-dim dense
embeddings in Qdrant. Three search methods compared across 14 real-world scenarios
(6 GitHub issues + 8 spec domains):

1. `git grep` with keywords (substring matching)
2. gardenSearch with same keywords (embedding similarity)
3. gardenSearch with natural language description (embedding similarity)

## What was tried (didn't work)

Keyword-based embedding search — passing the same keyword strings used for grep
to the vector search engine. Expected: at least comparable results since the
embedding should understand the terms. Actual: catastrophic failure in 12/14
scenarios. Average precision 32% vs grep's 65%.

## Root cause

General-purpose embedding models like nomic-embed-text are trained on natural
language corpora. Java identifiers (`ChatModel`, `ConcurrentHashMap`), CDI
annotations (`@DefaultBean`, `@Alternative`), and framework config properties
(`quarkus.datasource.active`) have no pre-trained semantic weight. The model
treats them as generic English tokens:

- `ChatModel` → "chat" + "model" → matches anything about conversations or models
- `@DefaultBean` → "default" + "bean" → matches anything with "default" in it
- `shadowing` → matches the English word, not the JPA concept

This is silent — relevance scores (0.53–0.70) look normal. The results are
well-ordered noise.

## Fix

Use natural language descriptions instead of keywords when querying embedding-based
search. The same engine with NL queries ("CDI ambiguous dependency resolution when
@Default bean conflicts with @DefaultBean in multi-module Quarkus application")
recovered to 62% average precision — competitive with grep's 65%.

The keyword catastrophe is a query formulation problem, not a retrieval problem.
NL queries give the embedding model enough semantic context to locate relevant
entries even when those entries use different vocabulary.

### Why this fix

Keywords work for substring matching because they match character sequences. They
fail for embedding search because the embedding model needs semantic context to
produce meaningful vectors. A keyword like `@DefaultBean` is a pointer to a
concept — substring matching follows the pointer; embedding search needs the
concept spelled out.

## Why this is non-obvious

Embedding models are marketed as understanding meaning, not just matching strings.
The expectation is that they should handle domain vocabulary at least as well as
grep. The failure is counterintuitive: a more sophisticated retrieval mechanism
produces dramatically worse results than a simple substring match — but only for
domain-specific identifiers, not for natural language descriptions of the same
concepts.

### Alternatives considered

- **Domain-tuned embedding model:** would likely fix the vocabulary gap but
  requires significant investment in fine-tuning data and training pipeline.
- **SPLADE hybrid search:** adds learned sparse token matching alongside dense
  embeddings — may recover keyword precision without domain tuning. Testing
  planned (Hortora/engine#28).
- **BM25/full-text index:** classic keyword retrieval that scales. Would handle
  exact identifiers but adds infrastructure complexity.

LangChain4j Anthropic: ResponseFormat.JSON without schema throws UnsupportedFeatureException — not a degradation
entries.body:
LangChain4j Anthropic: ResponseFormat.JSON without schema throws UnsupportedFeatureException — not a degradation

## Symptom

Passing `ResponseFormat.JSON` (type only, no schema) to `ChatRequest.builder().responseFormat(...)` for an Anthropic-backed `ChatModel` throws `UnsupportedFeatureException` rather than silently degrading or prompting.

## Context

`InternalAnthropicHelper.validate(ChatRequestParameters)` is called inside `AnthropicChatModel.doChat()` before any API call is made. The validation checks:

```java
if (parameters.responseFormat() != null
        && parameters.responseFormat().type() == ResponseFormatType.JSON
        && parameters.responseFormat().jsonSchema() == null) {
    throw new UnsupportedFeatureException(...);
}
```

This means JSON mode without a schema is explicitly rejected at the LangChain4j layer — it never reaches the Anthropic API.

## Root cause

Anthropic's native API requires a JSON schema to enforce structured output. Unlike OpenAI (which supports a bare JSON mode that produces valid but unstructured JSON), Anthropic has no schema-less JSON mode. LangChain4j's Anthropic integration reflects this correctly by refusing the schemaless request rather than silently ignoring the constraint.

## Fix

Always pair `ResponseFormat.JSON` with a `JsonSchema` when using Anthropic:

```java
ResponseFormat responseFormat = ResponseFormat.builder()
    .type(ResponseFormatType.JSON)
    .jsonSchema(JsonSchema.builder()
        .name("MySchema")
        .rootElement(JsonObjectSchema.builder()
            .addStringProperty("field", "Description")
            .required("field")
            .build())
        .build())
    .build();
```

For a broad catch on provider-specific failures (including older Claude models that don't support structured output at all), wrap the `llm.chat(request)` call in `catch (Exception e)` and degrade gracefully:

```java
try {
    ChatResponse response = llm.chat(request);
    return Optional.of(parse(response.aiMessage().text()));
} catch (Exception e) {
    log.warn("Structured enrichment failed ({}), falling back to structural rendering", e.getMessage());
    return Optional.empty();
}
```

## Why this is non-obvious

The LangChain4j docs describe `ResponseFormat.JSON` as a valid type value. There is no public documentation on which providers support it with or without a schema. The `UnsupportedFeatureException` is thrown before any network call, so there is no HTTP error to debug — it looks like an in-process configuration error with no obvious connection to the Anthropic API's structured output requirements.

The `supportedCapabilities()` mechanism exists on `ChatModel` for high-level AI Services to check before using JSON schema, but `ClaudeMarkdownRenderer`-style code calling the low-level `ChatModel.chat(ChatRequest)` API bypasses that guard entirely.

### Why this fix

`ResponseFormat.JSON` with `JsonSchema` is the only valid combination for Anthropic. Adding a schema is not optional — it is the required API surface.

entries.title: BM25 corpus isolation tests fail when test documents share common tokens with the query across corpuses
entries.body:
BM25 corpus isolation tests fail when test documents share common tokens with the query across corpuses

### Symptom

A corpus isolation test asserts that searching corpus2 for `ChatModel` returns empty results, even though only corpus1 contains that term. The test fails: corpus2 returns a result.

### Context

Two test corpuses:
- corpus1: `"ChatModel in Quarkus"` (should match)
- corpus2: `"Python ML model"` (should NOT match)

The BM25 tokenizer produces `[chatmodel, chat, model]` for the query `ChatModel`. The token `model` appears in corpus2's document `"Python ML model"`. BM25 correctly finds it — the corpus isolation is working (separate indexes), but the test data shares a common token.

### Root cause

Test data design — not a code bug. The query `ChatModel` decomposes to `[chatmodel, chat, model]`. Any document containing `model` in any corpus will match on that token. The test falsely assumes no token overlap between the query and corpus2's content.

### Fix

Use test documents with zero token overlap with the query:

```java
// Bad — "model" overlaps with ChatModel → [chatmodel, chat, model]
registry.addChunk(corpus2, "doc2", "Python ML model", Map.of(), Map.of());

// Good — no tokens in common with ChatModel
registry.addChunk(corpus2, "doc2",
    "Hibernate lazy loading fails outside transaction", Map.of(), Map.of());
```

### Why this is non-obvious

With standard word tokenizers, `ChatModel` is a single token — no overlap with `model`. With CamelCase-aware tokenizers that split compounds into components, the token set expands and overlaps become common. Test data that looks obviously different (`ChatModel` vs `Python ML model`) shares a token through CamelCase decomposition. The failure only surfaces when the tokenizer is CamelCase-aware — it works with standard tokenizers.

entries.title: OpenClaw /v1/chat/completions requires model='openclaw', not the upstream provider model ID
entries.body:
OpenClaw /v1/chat/completions requires model='openclaw', not the upstream provider model ID

## OpenClaw /v1/chat/completions requires model='openclaw', not the upstream provider model ID

**ID:** GE-20260614-328420
**Stack:** OpenClaw v2026.6.x

### Symptom

Calling OpenClaw's OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint with a provider model
name returns HTTP 400:

```json
{"error":{"message":"Invalid `model`. Use `openclaw` or `openclaw/<agentId>`.",
 "type":"invalid_request_error"}}
```

### Context

When `gateway.http.endpoints.chatCompletions.enabled: true` is set in `openclaw.json`,
OpenClaw exposes `POST /v1/chat/completions`. The natural assumption is to use the
configured upstream model ID (e.g. `"mock-llm/mock-model"`, `"anthropic/claude-opus-4-6"`).

### Root cause / Undocumented behaviour

The `model` field in the request does not name the upstream LLM. It names the OpenClaw
agent. OpenClaw IS the model from the caller's perspective — it receives the request,
routes it through its agent pipeline, and calls the configured upstream provider
internally. The upstream provider model is determined by the agent's config, not the
request.

Valid model values:
- `"openclaw"` — uses the default agent
- `"openclaw/<agentId>"` — routes to a specific named agent

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:18789/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"openclaw","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"ping"}]}'
```

OpenClaw then calls its configured upstream provider (e.g. `mock-llm/mock-model` via
WireMock, or `anthropic/claude-opus-4-6`) transparently.

### Why this is non-obvious

The OpenClaw docs describe the chatCompletions endpoint as OpenAI-compatible, which
implies `model` should identify the LLM. The error message does clarify the correct
values, but the architectural reason (OpenClaw = the model, upstream = internal) is
not explained anywhere in the docs. The distinction only becomes clear after reading
the error response.

LangChain4j 1.x UserMessage: text accessor is singleText(), not text()
entries.body:
LangChain4j 1.x UserMessage: text accessor is singleText(), not text()

## Symptom

Compile error: `cannot find symbol: method text()` when calling `.text()` on a `ChatMessage`.

## Context

Processing messages from a `ChatRequest` in a `doChat(ChatRequest)` override, trying to extract the text content to inspect or capture it in a test.

```java
// Fails — ChatMessage has no text() method
String content = request.messages().get(0).text();  // ← compile error
```

## Root Cause

`ChatMessage` is an interface with no `text()` accessor. Text content is accessible on the concrete `UserMessage` type only, via `singleText()` — not `text()`.

## Fix

Cast to `UserMessage` and call `singleText()`:

```java
// Correct
request.messages().stream()
    .filter(m -> m instanceof UserMessage)
    .map(m -> ((UserMessage) m).singleText())
    .collect(Collectors.joining());
```

## Why non-obvious

The method name change from `text()` to `singleText()` is a 1.x change. The `UserMessage` constructor accepts a plain `String`, so it reads naturally as if `.text()` should return it — but it doesn't. The method name `singleText()` signals that `UserMessage` can contain multiple `Content` objects and this returns the first text content.

entries.title: quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback

## Symptom

When the quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension is on the classpath alongside a
`@DefaultBean ChatModel` implementation, Quarkus throws at startup:

```
AmbiguousResolutionException: Ambiguous dependencies for type ChatModel and qualifiers [@Default]
  - CLASS bean [... AgentProviderChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
  - SYNTHETIC bean [... OllamaChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
```

## Context

A custom `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped ChatModel` implementation exists to serve as a
fallback (e.g. a Claude CLI bridge). The expectation is that adding the Ollama extension
places its `ChatModel` higher-priority, which should silence the `@DefaultBean`. Instead,
both are registered with `@Default` and Quarkus cannot choose between them.

## Root cause

`@DefaultBean` in Quarkus ARC means: "this bean is only active if no other `@Default`-
qualified bean of the same type is present." The mechanism works when the competing bean
is `@ApplicationScoped` with no explicit qualifier (which implicitly gets `@Default`), or
when the competing bean is annotated with `@Alternative @Priority(N)`. However, the
quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension registers its model as a **SYNTHETIC bean with an
explicit `@Default` qualifier** — not as a higher-priority alternative. ARC sees two
explicit `@Default` beans and cannot resolve.

## Fix

Veto the `@DefaultBean` explicitly when the Ollama extension is active by pairing
`@IfBuildProperty` with `-Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false` at build time:

```java
@DefaultBean
@ApplicationScoped
@IfBuildProperty(name = "casehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled",
                 stringValue = "true", enableIfMissing = true)
class AgentProviderChatModel implements ChatModel { ... }
```

```bash
# Run with Ollama — veto the DefaultBean
mvn clean test -Peval,eval-ollama \
  -Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false \
  ...
```

`mvn clean` is required to force fresh augmentation when toggling this property (see
related entry on augmentation caching).

## Why this is non-obvious

`@DefaultBean` is marketed as "the bean that loses to any other bean of the same type."
In practice it only loses to beans that don't also carry an explicit `@Default` qualifier.
Quarkus LangChain4j provider extensions register SYNTHETIC beans with explicit `@Default`
rather than `@Alternative @Priority`, making the clash non-obvious. The `@DefaultBean`
javadoc does not describe this failure mode.

**See also:** [GE-20260601-fcf0d9](GE-20260601-fcf0d9.md) — two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → AmbiguousResolutionException | [GE-20260531-1ec900](GE-20260531-1ec900.md) — Quarkus ARC registers non-CDI abstract class as @Dependent bean

entries.title: Quarkus Arc @Alternative does not suppress injection point validation of displaced beans
entries.body:
Quarkus Arc @Alternative does not suppress injection point validation of displaced beans

### Symptom
Consumer `@QuarkusTest` fails with `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` for a dependency
(`ChatModel`) that only the production bean needs — even though an `@Alternative @Priority(1)`
test stub exists for the same SPI and would be selected.

### Context
`LlmQueryExpander` is `@ApplicationScoped` with `@IfBuildProperty(enableIfMissing=true)` — registered by default.
Its constructor requires `ChatModel`. `InMemoryQueryExpander` is `@Alternative @Priority(1)` implementing
the same `QueryExpander` SPI. In a `@QuarkusTest` without a `ChatModel` bean, the expectation is that
`InMemoryQueryExpander` replaces `LlmQueryExpander` and no `ChatModel` is needed.

### What was tried (didn't work)
Adding `InMemoryQueryExpander` as `@Alternative @Priority(1)` to the test classpath. The alternative
is correctly selected for `QueryExpander` injection points, but `LlmQueryExpander` is still a
registered bean and its `ChatModel` constructor parameter is still validated.

### Root cause
Quarkus Arc validates injection points of ALL registered beans at build time — not just the
selected bean for a given type. `@Alternative` controls which bean is injected at consumer
injection points, but does NOT suppress validation of other registered beans' own injection
points. A registered bean with an unsatisfied dependency causes a build failure regardless
of whether it would ever be instantiated.

### Fix
Two complementary approaches:

1. **Remove `enableIfMissing = true`** from `@IfBuildProperty` — require explicit mode
   selection so the heavy bean is only registered when the consumer explicitly opts in.

2. **Add a `@DefaultBean` no-op** that implements the SPI with zero dependencies.
   `@DefaultBean` is displaced by any `@ApplicationScoped` bean (when mode is set)
   or `@Alternative` (in tests). The no-op ensures a bean always exists without
   dragging in heavy transitive dependencies.

### Why this is non-obvious
The mental model of `@Alternative` suggests it "replaces" the original bean. In standard
CDI (Weld), this is closer to true — alternatives affect typesafe resolution. But Quarkus
Arc performs aggressive build-time validation of ALL registered beans' injection points,
including beans that will never be instantiated because a higher-priority alternative exists.
The distinction between "not selected" and "not registered" is invisible until it breaks.

```java
ResponseFormat responseFormat = ResponseFormat.builder()
    .type(ResponseFormatType.JSON)
    .jsonSchema(JsonSchema.builder()
        .name("MySchema")
        .rootElement(JsonObjectSchema.builder()
            .addStringProperty("field", "Description")
            .required("field")
            .build())
        .build())
    .build();
```

For a broad catch on provider-specific failures (including older Claude models that don't support structured output at all), wrap the `llm.chat(request)` call in `catch (Exception e)` and degrade gracefully:

```java
try {
    ChatResponse response = llm.chat(request);
    return Optional.of(parse(response.aiMessage().text()));
} catch (Exception e) {
    log.warn("Structured enrichment failed ({}), falling back to structural rendering", e.getMessage());
    return Optional.empty();
}
```

## Why this is non-obvious

The LangChain4j docs describe `ResponseFormat.JSON` as a valid type value. There is no public documentation on which providers support it with or without a schema. The `UnsupportedFeatureException` is thrown before any network call, so there is no HTTP error to debug — it looks like an in-process configuration error with no obvious connection to the Anthropic API's structured output requirements.

The `supportedCapabilities()` mechanism exists on `ChatModel` for high-level AI Services to check before using JSON schema, but `ClaudeMarkdownRenderer`-style code calling the low-level `ChatModel.chat(ChatRequest)` API bypasses that guard entirely.

### Why this fix

`ResponseFormat.JSON` with `JsonSchema` is the only valid combination for Anthropic. Adding a schema is not optional — it is the required API surface.

quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback

## Symptom

When the quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension is on the classpath alongside a
`@DefaultBean ChatModel` implementation, Quarkus throws at startup:

```
AmbiguousResolutionException: Ambiguous dependencies for type ChatModel and qualifiers [@Default]
  - CLASS bean [... AgentProviderChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
  - SYNTHETIC bean [... OllamaChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
```

## Context

A custom `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped ChatModel` implementation exists to serve as a
fallback (e.g. a Claude CLI bridge). The expectation is that adding the Ollama extension
places its `ChatModel` higher-priority, which should silence the `@DefaultBean`. Instead,
both are registered with `@Default` and Quarkus cannot choose between them.

## Root cause

`@DefaultBean` in Quarkus ARC means: "this bean is only active if no other `@Default`-
qualified bean of the same type is present." The mechanism works when the competing bean
is `@ApplicationScoped` with no explicit qualifier (which implicitly gets `@Default`), or
when the competing bean is annotated with `@Alternative @Priority(N)`. However, the
quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension registers its model as a **SYNTHETIC bean with an
explicit `@Default` qualifier** — not as a higher-priority alternative. ARC sees two
explicit `@Default` beans and cannot resolve.

## Fix

Veto the `@DefaultBean` explicitly when the Ollama extension is active by pairing
`@IfBuildProperty` with `-Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false` at build time:

```java
@DefaultBean
@ApplicationScoped
@IfBuildProperty(name = "casehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled",
                 stringValue = "true", enableIfMissing = true)
class AgentProviderChatModel implements ChatModel { ... }
```

```bash
# Run with Ollama — veto the DefaultBean
mvn clean test -Peval,eval-ollama \
  -Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false \
  ...
```

`mvn clean` is required to force fresh augmentation when toggling this property (see
related entry on augmentation caching).

## Why this is non-obvious

`@DefaultBean` is marketed as "the bean that loses to any other bean of the same type."
In practice it only loses to beans that don't also carry an explicit `@Default` qualifier.
Quarkus LangChain4j provider extensions register SYNTHETIC beans with explicit `@Default`
rather than `@Alternative @Priority`, making the clash non-obvious. The `@DefaultBean`
javadoc does not describe this failure mode.

**See also:** [GE-20260601-fcf0d9](GE-20260601-fcf0d9.md) — two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → AmbiguousResolutionException | [GE-20260531-1ec900](GE-20260531-1ec900.md) — Quarkus ARC registers non-CDI abstract class as @Dependent bean

entries.title: OpenClaw /v1/chat/completions requires model='openclaw', not the upstream provider model ID
entries.body:
OpenClaw /v1/chat/completions requires model='openclaw', not the upstream provider model ID

## OpenClaw /v1/chat/completions requires model='openclaw', not the upstream provider model ID

**ID:** GE-20260614-328420
**Stack:** OpenClaw v2026.6.x

### Symptom

Calling OpenClaw's OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint with a provider model
name returns HTTP 400:

```json
{"error":{"message":"Invalid `model`. Use `openclaw` or `openclaw/<agentId>`.",
 "type":"invalid_request_error"}}
```

### Context

When `gateway.http.endpoints.chatCompletions.enabled: true` is set in `openclaw.json`,
OpenClaw exposes `POST /v1/chat/completions`. The natural assumption is to use the
configured upstream model ID (e.g. `"mock-llm/mock-model"`, `"anthropic/claude-opus-4-6"`).

### Root cause / Undocumented behaviour

The `model` field in the request does not name the upstream LLM. It names the OpenClaw
agent. OpenClaw IS the model from the caller's perspective — it receives the request,
routes it through its agent pipeline, and calls the configured upstream provider
internally. The upstream provider model is determined by the agent's config, not the
request.

Valid model values:
- `"openclaw"` — uses the default agent
- `"openclaw/<agentId>"` — routes to a specific named agent

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:18789/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"openclaw","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"ping"}]}'
```

OpenClaw then calls its configured upstream provider (e.g. `mock-llm/mock-model` via
WireMock, or `anthropic/claude-opus-4-6`) transparently.

### Why this is non-obvious

The OpenClaw docs describe the chatCompletions endpoint as OpenAI-compatible, which
implies `model` should identify the LLM. The error message does clarify the correct
values, but the architectural reason (OpenClaw = the model, upstream = internal) is
not explained anywhere in the docs. The distinction only becomes clear after reading
the error response.

entries.title: LangChain4j 1.x UserMessage: text accessor is singleText(), not text()
entries.body:
LangChain4j 1.x UserMessage: text accessor is singleText(), not text()

## Symptom

Compile error: `cannot find symbol: method text()` when calling `.text()` on a `ChatMessage`.

## Context

Processing messages from a `ChatRequest` in a `doChat(ChatRequest)` override, trying to extract the text content to inspect or capture it in a test.

```java
// Fails — ChatMessage has no text() method
String content = request.messages().get(0).text();  // ← compile error
```

## Root Cause

`ChatMessage` is an interface with no `text()` accessor. Text content is accessible on the concrete `UserMessage` type only, via `singleText()` — not `text()`.

## Fix

Cast to `UserMessage` and call `singleText()`:

```java
// Correct
request.messages().stream()
    .filter(m -> m instanceof UserMessage)
    .map(m -> ((UserMessage) m).singleText())
    .collect(Collectors.joining());
```

## Why non-obvious

The method name change from `text()` to `singleText()` is a 1.x change. The `UserMessage` constructor accepts a plain `String`, so it reads naturally as if `.text()` should return it — but it doesn't. The method name `singleText()` signals that `UserMessage` can contain multiple `Content` objects and this returns the first text content.

LangChain4j EmbeddingModel does not implement TokenCountEstimator — use character-based DocumentSplitters.recursive(int, int)
entries.body:
LangChain4j EmbeddingModel does not implement TokenCountEstimator — use character-based DocumentSplitters.recursive(int, int)

`DocumentSplitters.recursive(int, int, TokenCountEstimator)` requires a `TokenCountEstimator` as the third argument for token-based segment sizing. `EmbeddingModel` does NOT implement `TokenCountEstimator` — they are separate interface hierarchies with no inheritance relationship.

### Symptom

Design spec or implementation assumes `EmbeddingModel` can be passed as the `TokenCountEstimator` argument to `DocumentSplitters.recursive()`. Compilation fails with "incompatible types."

### Context

When building a RAG chunking pipeline, the natural assumption is: "I already have an `EmbeddingModel` that handles tokenization for embeddings — it should work as a `TokenCountEstimator` for splitting too." The naming and domain proximity reinforce this assumption.

### Root cause

`EmbeddingModel` and `TokenCountEstimator` are independent interfaces in LangChain4j. `EmbeddingModel` knows how to embed text into vectors. `TokenCountEstimator` knows how to count tokens in text. Some LLM provider implementations (e.g. `OpenAiEmbeddingModel`) implement both, but the base `EmbeddingModel` interface does not extend `TokenCountEstimator`. ONNX-based models (`OnnxEmbeddingModel`) implement only `EmbeddingModel`.

### Fix

Use the character-based 2-arg overload:

```java
DocumentSplitter splitter = DocumentSplitters.recursive(1000, 200);
```

This splits by character count (paragraph → line → sentence → word fallback chain). Character counts are approximate by nature — the imprecision vs token counts is negligible for RAG chunk sizing.

### Why this is non-obvious

The `EmbeddingModel` interface handles tokenization internally (it must tokenize text before embedding it). A developer reasonably infers it exposes this capability via `TokenCountEstimator`. The class names reinforce the assumption: "Embedding" + "Model" + "Token" + "Count" — all in the same domain. The actual type hierarchy has no inheritance link between them.

### Alternatives considered

- Implementing a custom `TokenCountEstimator` that delegates to the embedding model's internal tokenizer — rejected because ONNX embedding models don't expose their tokenizer publicly
- Using HuggingFace Tokenizers JNI directly as a `TokenCountEstimator` — possible but adds JNI complexity for marginal accuracy improvement over character-based splitting

Spawn a research agent with targeted academic + standards queries to drive architecture decisions
entries.body:
Spawn a research agent with targeted academic + standards queries to drive architecture decisions

### Context
Facing an architecture decision (e.g. LLM agent identity model for an audit ledger) with
multiple viable options but no clear winner from first principles. Standard web search
returns surface-level results; ChatGPT-style prompting produces plausible-sounding but
unverified recommendations.

### Technique
Spawn a dedicated research subagent with a precise multi-query brief covering:
- Specific academic sources (arxiv, Google Scholar)
- Standards bodies (W3C, NIST, ISO, EU regulatory text)
- Industry framework implementations (LangChain, AutoGen, CrewAI docs)
- Named papers and RFCs where known

Structure the brief as explicit numbered search targets, not open-ended questions:
```
1. Web search: "LLM agent identity accountability audit"
2. Web search: "W3C PROV agent identity"
3. arxiv search: "agent identity accountability provenance" academic papers
4. Search: "NIST AI agent identity", "ISO AI traceability agent"
5. Search: "LangChain agent identity", "AutoGen agent accountability"
```

Return format: findings per source, consensus view, gaps/open questions.

### Why this is non-obvious
The instinct is to ask the model directly ("what's the best approach to X?") or do
ad-hoc web searches. Spawning an agent with a structured multi-source brief produces
a qualitatively different result: actual citations, contradictions between sources
surfaced, and awareness of what is vs isn't standardised. The synthesised output
directly informs design decisions with academic backing rather than model priors.

In this pattern, the design work stays in the main context; the research subagent
handles the retrieval. The human synthesises from the agent's report — delegation
of search, not delegation of understanding.

entries.title: LangChain4j EmbeddingSearchRequest.filter() pushes domain/metadata filters into Qdrant pre-scoring
entries.body:
LangChain4j EmbeddingSearchRequest.filter() pushes domain/metadata filters into Qdrant pre-scoring

## LangChain4j EmbeddingSearchRequest.filter() pushes domain/metadata filters into Qdrant pre-scoring

**Stack:** LangChain4j 1.x, Qdrant

Pass a `Filter` to `EmbeddingSearchRequest.builder().filter()` to apply a metadata
payload filter in Qdrant *before* vector similarity scoring. `QdrantFilterConverter`
translates it to a gRPC `FieldCondition`. Only entries matching the filter participate
in the similarity computation, so the `maxResults` limit is respected correctly.

### Context

A post-retrieval Java stream filter on `embeddingStore.search(request).matches()` is
incorrect at scale. With `maxResults=8` and a corpus of 100 domain=tools entries plus
5 domain=jvm entries, a search with domain=jvm may return 8 tools entries (all more
similar to the query), the Java filter removes them all, and the caller receives 0
results — silently.

### The technique

```java
import dev.langchain4j.store.embedding.filter.Filter;
import dev.langchain4j.store.embedding.filter.comparison.IsEqualTo;

Filter domainFilter = (domain != null && !domain.isBlank())
        ? new IsEqualTo("domain", domain)
        : null;

var request = EmbeddingSearchRequest.builder()
        .queryEmbedding(queryEmbedding)
        .maxResults(maxResults)
        .filter(domainFilter)   // null = no filter
        .build();

List<SearchResult> results = embeddingStore.search(request).matches().stream()
        .map(...)               // no post-retrieval filter needed
        .toList();
```

### Filter chain (verified from bytecode)

`IsEqualTo("domain", value)` → `EmbeddingSearchRequest.filter()` → `QdrantEmbeddingStore.search()` → `QdrantFilterConverter.buildEqCondition()` → Qdrant gRPC `FieldCondition` (server-side payload filter).

Available filter types (all in `dev.langchain4j.store.embedding.filter.comparison`):
`IsEqualTo`, `IsNotEqualTo`, `IsIn`, `IsNotIn`, `IsGreaterThan`, `IsLessThan`,
`ContainsString`. Logical combinators: `And`, `Or`, `Not` (in `...filter.logical`).

`InMemoryEmbeddingStore` (used in `@QuarkusTest` mocks) also honours the filter —
tests behave correctly without a real Qdrant instance.

### Why this is non-obvious

A developer adding domain filtering naturally reaches for Java stream `.filter()` on
the returned matches. The `EmbeddingSearchRequest.filter()` API exists but is not
prominently documented for the Qdrant integration. The correctness issue (limit
truncation at scale) only becomes visible with a corpus large enough that
same-domain entries don't dominate the top-N by similarity.
