@LookupIfProperty for conditional CDI bean activation via Instance<> — cleaner than inert-bean pattern
entries.body:
@LookupIfProperty for conditional CDI bean activation via Instance<> — cleaner than inert-bean pattern

### Context
A Quarkus application ships multiple provider implementations of an SPI (e.g. `DeviceProvider`) in one Docker image. Each provider should be independently enableable via config (`provider.enabled=true/false`). Disabled providers must be invisible to `Instance<DeviceProvider>` iteration — not just "present but returning empty results."

### What a skilled developer would normally do
Guard in `@PostConstruct`: check `enabled`, skip initialization if false. Make every method return a no-op result (`discover()` → empty list, `dispatch()` → FAILED, `status()` → DISCONNECTED). This is the "inert-bean" pattern — the bean exists but does nothing.

Problems with inert beans:
- The bean IS discovered by `Instance<DeviceProvider>` — callers see a broken provider
- `@PostConstruct` still runs (and may fail if config properties are missing)
- Every method needs guard logic
- SmallRye Config still validates all `@ConfigMapping` properties at startup (see GE-20260626-e0ecaf)

### Technique
Use `@LookupIfProperty` from Quarkus ARC:

```java
@ApplicationScoped
@LookupIfProperty(name = "casehub.iot.homeassistant.enabled", stringValue = "true")
public class HomeAssistantProvider implements DeviceProvider { ... }
```

When `enabled` is absent or `false`:
- The bean is never instantiated
- `@PostConstruct` never runs
- `Instance<DeviceProvider>` iteration skips it entirely
- No guard logic needed in any method

Combined with `Optional<String>` on all `@ConfigMapping` properties (GE-20260626-e0ecaf), this allows disabled providers to exist on the classpath without causing config validation failures or appearing in the provider registry.

### Why this is non-obvious
`@LookupIfProperty` is less well-known than `@IfBuildProperty` (which is build-time only and prevents runtime reconfiguration). The naming — "lookup if" vs "if build" — doesn't clearly convey the difference. Many developers reach for `@IfBuildProperty` first, discover it prevents runtime toggling in Docker images, and then fall back to the inert-bean pattern instead of finding `@LookupIfProperty`.

entries.title: Quarkus Arc @Alternative does not suppress injection point validation of displaced beans
entries.body:
Quarkus Arc @Alternative does not suppress injection point validation of displaced beans

### Symptom
Consumer `@QuarkusTest` fails with `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` for a dependency
(`ChatModel`) that only the production bean needs — even though an `@Alternative @Priority(1)`
test stub exists for the same SPI and would be selected.

### Context
`LlmQueryExpander` is `@ApplicationScoped` with `@IfBuildProperty(enableIfMissing=true)` — registered by default.
Its constructor requires `ChatModel`. `InMemoryQueryExpander` is `@Alternative @Priority(1)` implementing
the same `QueryExpander` SPI. In a `@QuarkusTest` without a `ChatModel` bean, the expectation is that
`InMemoryQueryExpander` replaces `LlmQueryExpander` and no `ChatModel` is needed.

### What was tried (didn't work)
Adding `InMemoryQueryExpander` as `@Alternative @Priority(1)` to the test classpath. The alternative
is correctly selected for `QueryExpander` injection points, but `LlmQueryExpander` is still a
registered bean and its `ChatModel` constructor parameter is still validated.

### Root cause
Quarkus Arc validates injection points of ALL registered beans at build time — not just the
selected bean for a given type. `@Alternative` controls which bean is injected at consumer
injection points, but does NOT suppress validation of other registered beans' own injection
points. A registered bean with an unsatisfied dependency causes a build failure regardless
of whether it would ever be instantiated.

### Fix
Two complementary approaches:

1. **Remove `enableIfMissing = true`** from `@IfBuildProperty` — require explicit mode
   selection so the heavy bean is only registered when the consumer explicitly opts in.

2. **Add a `@DefaultBean` no-op** that implements the SPI with zero dependencies.
   `@DefaultBean` is displaced by any `@ApplicationScoped` bean (when mode is set)
   or `@Alternative` (in tests). The no-op ensures a bean always exists without
   dragging in heavy transitive dependencies.

### Why this is non-obvious
The mental model of `@Alternative` suggests it "replaces" the original bean. In standard
CDI (Weld), this is closer to true — alternatives affect typesafe resolution. But Quarkus
Arc performs aggressive build-time validation of ALL registered beans' injection points,
including beans that will never be instantiated because a higher-priority alternative exists.
The distinction between "not selected" and "not registered" is invisible until it breaks.

langchain4j-agentic DeclarativeUtil has a single CDI resolver hook for @ChatModelSupplier only — no equivalent for other supplier types
entries.body:
langchain4j-agentic DeclarativeUtil has a single CDI resolver hook for @ChatModelSupplier only — no equivalent for other supplier types

### What it is
`DeclarativeUtil` in `langchain4j-agentic` exposes a single static list `chatSupplierParameterResolvers` with one registration method `addChatSupplierParameterResolver(ChatSupplierParameterResolver)`. This resolver hook fires only during `@ChatModelSupplier` and `@StreamingChatModelSupplier` processing. All other supplier annotations (`@ToolsSupplier`, `@ChatMemorySupplier`, `@ChatMemoryProviderSupplier`, `@ContentRetrieverSupplier`, `@RetrievalAugmentorSupplier`, `@AgentListenerSupplier`, `@ToolProviderSupplier`) call `checkArguments(method)` which enforces **zero parameters** before invoking the static method directly — no resolver hook exists for these paths.

### Why this matters for framework integrators
Any DI framework (Quarkus, Spring, Guice) wanting to inject CDI/Spring beans into supplier methods is blocked for all supplier types except chat model suppliers. The `@CdiBean` workaround in `quarkus-langchain4j` only works for `@ChatModelSupplier` as a result. Users who need a CDI-managed `ContentRetriever` or `ChatMemory` must use `Arc.container()` or `ApplicationContext.getBean()` inside the static method body — bypassing injection, scope management, and testability.

### How to discover this
Only by decompiling `langchain4j-agentic-1.15.1-beta25.jar` and reading `DeclarativeUtil.class`. The library has no published Javadoc for internal classes and no documentation of the SPI surface area.

```bash
# Locate the JAR
find ~/.m2/repository/dev/langchain4j/langchain4j-agentic -name "*.jar" | grep -v sources | head -1

# The class structure reveals: addChatSupplierParameterResolver() is the only hook
# All other configureAgent() branches call checkArguments() then invokeStatic()
```

### Workaround
For Quarkus: use `SyntheticCreationalContext.getInjectedReference()` in the synthetic bean creator (`AgenticRecorder`) to inject CDI beans at agent construction time, bypassing the static supplier method entirely. This requires detecting at build time that no static supplier method exists for a given type, then adding a CDI injection point for that type.

### Upstream path
An upstream PR to `langchain4j-agentic` should propose a general `SupplierParameterResolver` SPI (not chat-model-specific) and add resolver hooks to all supplier type branches in `configureAgent()`. Frame as a DI-framework-agnostic improvement — Spring users would benefit from the same hook.

### Why this is non-obvious
The library name suggests platform independence (`langchain4j` not `langchain4j-spring`), so the assumption is that all supplier types are equally extensible. The asymmetry between `@ChatModelSupplier` (has a resolver hook) and all other supplier annotations (do not) is not mentioned in any README, Javadoc, or issue tracker. The class is package-private in the library with no stable API guarantee.

PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY @QuarkusTest: subscribe to unfiltered stream to confirm channel active before asserting on filtered results
entries.body:
PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY @QuarkusTest: subscribe to unfiltered stream to confirm channel active before asserting on filtered results

## Symptom

A `@QuarkusTest` integration test for a PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY broadcaster
fails intermittently with `ConditionTimeoutException` — the awaitility condition
times out even though the test logic is correct and passing in most CI runs. The
same commit SHA shows both pass and fail on successive runs.

## Context

`PostgresWorkItemEventBroadcaster.startListening()` is annotated `@PostConstruct`.
It issues a `LISTEN <channel>` command via the Vert.x reactive PG client — an async
call that returns immediately; the LISTEN is established on the Vert.x event loop
after control returns to the caller. Quarkus marks the application ready after all
`@PostConstruct` calls return, but does not wait for their async work to complete.

Tests that subscribe to a filtered stream and immediately fire events may do so
before the LISTEN is registered with PostgreSQL. Events published via `pg_notify`
reach the subscriber connection only after LISTEN is active — events fired before
that are silently dropped.

## What was tried (didn't work)

Increasing the awaitility timeout from 5 seconds to 10 seconds: reduced flake
frequency but did not eliminate it (the root cause is the LISTEN not being active,
not the notify→receive path being slow).

## Fix — Warm-up probe

Before subscribing to the filtered stream, subscribe to the **unfiltered** stream and
wait for a known event to arrive. This confirms the LISTEN channel is established and
the full async path (pg_notify → subscriber connection → BroadcastProcessor) is working:

```java
// 1. Subscribe to unfiltered stream BEFORE creating any items
final List<WorkItemLifecycleEvent> warmup = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
broadcaster.stream(null, null).subscribe().with(warmup::add);

// 2. Create the target item and wait for its CREATED event to arrive
final WorkItem target = createWorkItem("Target item");
Awaitility.await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
        .until(() -> warmup.stream().anyMatch(e -> target.id.equals(e.workItemId())));

// 3. LISTEN channel confirmed active — now subscribe to the filtered stream
final List<WorkItemLifecycleEvent> received = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
broadcaster.stream(target.id, null).subscribe().with(received::add);

// 4. Proceed with the test (noise items, claims, assertions)
```

The `BroadcastProcessor` is a hot stream — events emitted before subscription are
lost. Subscribing before creating any items ensures the warm-up probe captures the
CREATED event and the subsequent filtered subscription captures all later events.

## Why this is non-obvious

The application appears fully ready (HTTP is serving, CDI is wired) when the tests
start. The `@PostConstruct` has returned. There is no visible gap — but the LISTEN
command is in flight on the Vert.x event loop and may not have been acknowledged by
PostgreSQL yet. The failure only appears when the first `pg_notify` fires before that
acknowledgement arrives, which depends on container startup speed and event loop
scheduling in CI.

Bumping the awaitility timeout is the instinctive fix but addresses the wrong problem.
The test doesn't need more time to wait for the result — it needs to confirm the
infrastructure is ready before generating the result.

LangChain4j Anthropic: ResponseFormat.JSON without schema throws UnsupportedFeatureException — not a degradation
entries.body:
LangChain4j Anthropic: ResponseFormat.JSON without schema throws UnsupportedFeatureException — not a degradation

## Symptom

Passing `ResponseFormat.JSON` (type only, no schema) to `ChatRequest.builder().responseFormat(...)` for an Anthropic-backed `ChatModel` throws `UnsupportedFeatureException` rather than silently degrading or prompting.

## Context

`InternalAnthropicHelper.validate(ChatRequestParameters)` is called inside `AnthropicChatModel.doChat()` before any API call is made. The validation checks:

```java
if (parameters.responseFormat() != null
        && parameters.responseFormat().type() == ResponseFormatType.JSON
        && parameters.responseFormat().jsonSchema() == null) {
    throw new UnsupportedFeatureException(...);
}
```

This means JSON mode without a schema is explicitly rejected at the LangChain4j layer — it never reaches the Anthropic API.

## Root cause

Anthropic's native API requires a JSON schema to enforce structured output. Unlike OpenAI (which supports a bare JSON mode that produces valid but unstructured JSON), Anthropic has no schema-less JSON mode. LangChain4j's Anthropic integration reflects this correctly by refusing the schemaless request rather than silently ignoring the constraint.

## Fix

Always pair `ResponseFormat.JSON` with a `JsonSchema` when using Anthropic:

```java
ResponseFormat responseFormat = ResponseFormat.builder()
    .type(ResponseFormatType.JSON)
    .jsonSchema(JsonSchema.builder()
        .name("MySchema")
        .rootElement(JsonObjectSchema.builder()
            .addStringProperty("field", "Description")
            .required("field")
            .build())
        .build())
    .build();
```

For a broad catch on provider-specific failures (including older Claude models that don't support structured output at all), wrap the `llm.chat(request)` call in `catch (Exception e)` and degrade gracefully:

```java
try {
    ChatResponse response = llm.chat(request);
    return Optional.of(parse(response.aiMessage().text()));
} catch (Exception e) {
    log.warn("Structured enrichment failed ({}), falling back to structural rendering", e.getMessage());
    return Optional.empty();
}
```

## Why this is non-obvious

The LangChain4j docs describe `ResponseFormat.JSON` as a valid type value. There is no public documentation on which providers support it with or without a schema. The `UnsupportedFeatureException` is thrown before any network call, so there is no HTTP error to debug — it looks like an in-process configuration error with no obvious connection to the Anthropic API's structured output requirements.

The `supportedCapabilities()` mechanism exists on `ChatModel` for high-level AI Services to check before using JSON schema, but `ClaudeMarkdownRenderer`-style code calling the low-level `ChatModel.chat(ChatRequest)` API bypasses that guard entirely.

### Why this fix

`ResponseFormat.JSON` with `JsonSchema` is the only valid combination for Anthropic. Adding a schema is not optional — it is the required API surface.

entries.title: @LookupIfProperty for conditional CDI bean activation via Instance<> — cleaner than inert-bean pattern
entries.body:
@LookupIfProperty for conditional CDI bean activation via Instance<> — cleaner than inert-bean pattern

### Context
A Quarkus application ships multiple provider implementations of an SPI (e.g. `DeviceProvider`) in one Docker image. Each provider should be independently enableable via config (`provider.enabled=true/false`). Disabled providers must be invisible to `Instance<DeviceProvider>` iteration — not just "present but returning empty results."

### What a skilled developer would normally do
Guard in `@PostConstruct`: check `enabled`, skip initialization if false. Make every method return a no-op result (`discover()` → empty list, `dispatch()` → FAILED, `status()` → DISCONNECTED). This is the "inert-bean" pattern — the bean exists but does nothing.

Problems with inert beans:
- The bean IS discovered by `Instance<DeviceProvider>` — callers see a broken provider
- `@PostConstruct` still runs (and may fail if config properties are missing)
- Every method needs guard logic
- SmallRye Config still validates all `@ConfigMapping` properties at startup (see GE-20260626-e0ecaf)

### Technique
Use `@LookupIfProperty` from Quarkus ARC:

```java
@ApplicationScoped
@LookupIfProperty(name = "casehub.iot.homeassistant.enabled", stringValue = "true")
public class HomeAssistantProvider implements DeviceProvider { ... }
```

When `enabled` is absent or `false`:
- The bean is never instantiated
- `@PostConstruct` never runs
- `Instance<DeviceProvider>` iteration skips it entirely
- No guard logic needed in any method

Combined with `Optional<String>` on all `@ConfigMapping` properties (GE-20260626-e0ecaf), this allows disabled providers to exist on the classpath without causing config validation failures or appearing in the provider registry.

### Why this is non-obvious
`@LookupIfProperty` is less well-known than `@IfBuildProperty` (which is build-time only and prevents runtime reconfiguration). The naming — "lookup if" vs "if build" — doesn't clearly convey the difference. Many developers reach for `@IfBuildProperty` first, discover it prevents runtime toggling in Docker images, and then fall back to the inert-bean pattern instead of finding `@LookupIfProperty`.

entries.body:
@All List<T> in Quarkus/ArC gives testable multi-bean injection without Instance<T>

## Context
When building a registry or routing layer that needs all CDI beans of a type
(e.g. routing to the right `Connector` by id), the natural CDI approach is
`Instance<T>`. But `Instance<T>` is a CDI interface with many abstract methods
— difficult to stub in plain JUnit tests without a full container.

## What developers normally do
Inject `Instance<T>`, iterate with `.stream()`, or use `@InjectMock` inside a
`@QuarkusTest` — both require a CDI container.

## The technique
Inject `@All List<T>` instead. ArC populates it at startup with all discovered
beans. In tests, pass `List.of(...)` directly to the constructor — no CDI
context, no mocking of `Instance<T>`, no `@QuarkusTest` needed.

```java
// Production: ArC populates this automatically
ConnectorService(@All List<Connector> connectors) {
    this.registry = connectors.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.toMap(Connector::id, Function.identity()));
}

// Test: plain JUnit, no CDI
new ConnectorService(List.of(new SlackConnector(), new TeamsConnector()));
```

## Why this is non-obvious
`Instance<T>` is the CDI standard; `@All` is ArC-specific and not prominently
documented for this use case. The standard guidance says to use `@QuarkusTest`
for CDI testing. `@All List<T>` sidesteps the container requirement entirely
for patterns where the bean set is static at startup.

## Constraints
Requires `io.quarkus.arc.All`. Only works when the bean set is consumed at
construction time (static registry). Not suitable if beans are added/removed
at runtime.

**See also:** [GE-20260604-2f0889](GE-20260604-2f0889.md) — @Alternative @Priority(N) stubs appear in @All List<T> alongside original bean — not as replacements (gotcha when combining these patterns)

**See also:** [GE-20260529-ab148d](GE-20260529-ab148d.md) — multiple CDI constructors without @Inject → UnsatisfiedResolutionException (related CDI injection gotcha)

**See also:** [GE-20260609-75e00d](GE-20260609-75e00d.md) — package-private test constructor + @PostConstruct null guard technique

Quarkus Arc resolves CDI cycles between @ApplicationScoped beans via client proxies — even with constructor injection
entries.body:
Quarkus Arc resolves CDI cycles between @ApplicationScoped beans via client proxies — even with constructor injection

### Symptom
Code review flags a CDI cycle between two `@ApplicationScoped` beans as Critical — "application will not start." The cycle exists in the injection graph: `A → B (constructor injection) → A`. But the full build and all `@QuarkusTest` suites pass without any startup error.

### Context
`MessageService` (`@ApplicationScoped`) was given a field-injected `ChannelGateway`. `ChannelGateway` (`@ApplicationScoped`) already constructor-injected `MessageService` for its inbound dispatch paths (`receiveHumanMessage`, `receiveObserverSignal`). The cycle: `MessageService → ChannelGateway → MessageService`.

### What was tried
Code reviewer flagged the cycle as Critical, citing CDI startup failure. Using `Instance<ChannelGateway>` (lazy injection) to break it was considered as a fix.

### Root cause
The concern is correct for **pseudo-scoped** beans (`@Dependent`) which cannot be proxied — CDI cannot create a client proxy for a dependent-scoped bean, so a cycle involving one causes startup failure.

For **normal-scoped** beans (`@ApplicationScoped`, `@RequestScoped`, `@SessionScoped`), CDI mandates that the container MUST be able to create a client proxy. Quarkus Arc honors this: when `ChannelGateway`'s constructor is called, it receives a client proxy for `MessageService` — not the actual instance. The proxy is valid immediately; the actual `MessageService` instance is only resolved on the first method call. Both beans initialize without needing the other to exist first.

### Fix
Ensure all beans in the cycle are normal-scoped. Add a comment explaining the deliberate cycle so reviewers don't flag it:

```java
// Deliberate CDI cycle: MessageService → ChannelGateway → MessageService
// (via ChannelGateway.receiveHumanMessage / receiveObserverSignal).
// Both are @ApplicationScoped (normal scope). Arc resolves via client proxies —
// verified by full build and @QuarkusTest suite.
@Inject
ChannelGateway channelGateway;
```

### Why this is non-obvious
Most developers associate "CDI cycle" with startup failure. The distinction — pseudo-scoped vs normal-scoped — is in the spec but rarely surfaced in error messages or tutorials. The symptom that triggered the concern (a code reviewer calling it Critical) is exactly what skilled developers would say if they didn't know about proxy-based cycle resolution.

### Why this fix
A client proxy is the CDI-correct solution. Using `Instance<T>` (lazy injection) also works but adds indirection and a `.get()` call at every use site. Proxy resolution is transparent — callers don't change. Only use `Instance<T>` when a pseudo-scoped bean is in the cycle and proxy creation isn't possible.

**See also:** [GE-20260422-53d0f7](GE-20260422-53d0f7.md) — JPA @EntityListeners can be @ApplicationScoped CDI beans in Quarkus

**See also:** [GE-20260530-385dbb](GE-20260530-385dbb.md) — @Provider @ApplicationScoped on ClientRequestFilter bypasses CDI injection in Quarkus @RegisterRestClient

entries.title: CDI 4.1 Instance.handles() returns Iterable not Stream — use Arc's InjectableInstance.handlesStream()
entries.body:
CDI 4.1 Instance.handles() returns Iterable not Stream — use Arc's InjectableInstance.handlesStream()

### What exists but isn't documented

`jakarta.enterprise.inject.Instance.handles()` (CDI 4.1) returns `Iterable<Instance.Handle<T>>`,
not a `Stream`. The CDI spec's `Handle` interface only exposes `get()`, `getBean()`, `destroy()`,
`close()` — no `stream()` method. To sort CDI beans by metadata (e.g. `@Priority`), you need
Arc's extension: `InjectableInstance.handlesStream()` returns `Stream<InstanceHandle<T>>`.

### Context

Quarkus applications that need to iterate CDI beans in a specific order — enricher pipelines,
ordered observers, sorted strategy lists.

### How to use it

Inject `InjectableInstance` instead of `Instance`, then call `handlesStream()`:

```java
import io.quarkus.arc.InjectableInstance;
import io.quarkus.arc.InjectableBean;
import io.quarkus.arc.InstanceHandle;

@Inject @Any InjectableInstance<MyBean> beans;

beans.handlesStream()
    .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(h ->
        (h.getBean() instanceof InjectableBean<?> ib) ? ib.getPriority() : Integer.MAX_VALUE))
    .map(InstanceHandle::get)
    .forEach(bean -> bean.doWork());
```

### Why not in docs

`InjectableInstance` is an Arc implementation detail, not part of the CDI 4.x standard.
The Quarkus user guide for CDI shows `Instance<T>` injection only. `handlesStream()` is
discoverable via Arc's JavaDoc but not mentioned in any getting-started or ordering guide.

**See also:** [GE-20260519-eb8340](GE-20260519-eb8340.md) — Instance<T>.handles() returns Iterable<? extends Instance.Handle<T>> — incompatible with Iterable<InstanceHandle<T>>

entries.title: Cross-repo SPI extends creates CDI bean displacement — standalone composition required
entries.body:
Cross-repo SPI extends creates CDI bean displacement — standalone composition required

### Symptom
CDI deployment fails with ambiguous bean resolution or unexpected bean displacement when
a neural-text module's `CbrCaseMemoryStore extends CaseMemoryStore` is on the classpath
alongside platform's `CaseMemoryStore` implementations (JPA, SQLite, inmem).

### Context
`GraphCaseMemoryStore extends CaseMemoryStore` works within casehub-platform because all
implementations share the same CDI bean archive. Cross-repo, the inheritance creates three
displacement paths:

1. `QdrantCbrCaseMemoryStore` (neural-text, `@ApplicationScoped`) also satisfies
   `CaseMemoryStore` injection points — displaces `JpaMemoryStore` by priority
2. `NoOpCbrCaseMemoryStore` (neural-text, `@DefaultBean`) also becomes a
   `CaseMemoryStore @DefaultBean` — conflicts with `NoOpCaseMemoryStore` (platform)
3. Any `@Alternative` on the subtype cascades to the parent type's injection sites

### Root cause
CDI bean type resolution includes all supertypes. A bean typed as
`CbrCaseMemoryStore extends CaseMemoryStore` is injectable at both
`@Inject CbrCaseMemoryStore` and `@Inject CaseMemoryStore`. When the SPI
and its extension live in different repos (different CDI archives), the
priority/default-bean resolution rules interact across archive boundaries
in ways that don't occur within a single archive.

### Fix
Make the extended SPI a **standalone interface** — do not extend the base SPI.
Use composition via delegation:

```java
// WRONG — causes displacement
public interface CbrCaseMemoryStore extends CaseMemoryStore { ... }

// RIGHT — standalone SPI, delegates internally
public interface CbrCaseMemoryStore {
    // own methods only — no CaseMemoryStore inheritance
}

// Implementation delegates to injected CaseMemoryStore
@ApplicationScoped
public class QdrantCbrCaseMemoryStore implements CbrCaseMemoryStore {
    @Inject CaseMemoryStore delegate;  // no priority conflict
}
```

### Why this is non-obvious
The `extends` pattern works within a single repo (`GraphCaseMemoryStore extends
CaseMemoryStore` in casehub-platform) because all beans share one CDI archive.
The failure only manifests when the extending SPI lives in a different repo,
which is exactly when composition-over-inheritance is architecturally correct
but not what developers reach for first.

### Alternatives considered
- `@Typed(CbrCaseMemoryStore.class)` annotation to restrict bean types — rejected because it
  must be applied to every implementation, is easy to forget on new implementations, and
  doesn't prevent the `@DefaultBean` dual-registration problem
- Qualifier annotation to distinguish CBR from base memory beans — rejected because it
  changes the injection site contract for all existing `CaseMemoryStore` consumers

entries.title: Two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → Quarkus AmbiguousResolutionException, not Unsatisfied
entries.body:
Two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → Quarkus AmbiguousResolutionException, not Unsatisfied

## What happened

Two `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` implementations of the same SPI type appeared on the CDI
classpath simultaneously (one from a platform mock library, one from a persistence testing module).
Quarkus reported **"Ambiguous dependencies"** and refused to start — even though both beans
explicitly said "I am a default, defer to anyone else".

## Why this is non-obvious

`@DefaultBean` is documented as "yield to any other bean of the same type". With two
`@DefaultBean` beans and no non-default implementation, neither bean yields — the contract
("yield to someone else") cannot resolve because there IS no "someone else" with higher
precedence. The error message is **Ambiguous** (same as two regular `@ApplicationScoped`
beans conflicting), not **Unsatisfied** (what you'd expect if both were supposedly yielding).
Developers often assume two `@DefaultBean` beans resolve cleanly because they both "opt in"
to being overridden.

## Root cause

CDI/ARC `@DefaultBean` semantics: a default bean is only eligible when no other bean at
the same or higher priority is eligible. With two `@DefaultBean` beans and no higher-priority
bean, the tie-break is undefined — ARC treats this as an ambiguous injection point.

## Fix

Exclude the unwanted `@DefaultBean` implementation via `application.properties`:
```properties
quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.platform.mock.MockCurrentPrincipal,\
  io.casehub.platform.mock.MockGroupMembershipProvider,\
  io.casehub.platform.mock.MockPreferenceProvider
```

This removes the conflicting bean from CDI discovery entirely, leaving the desired
`@DefaultBean` as the sole implementation. Prefer excluding the one that returns null or
uninitialized values rather than the one with correct sentinel behaviour.

### Why this fix

`@Alternative @Priority(N)` would also work, but requires activating it via
`selected-alternatives` — that is a heavier configuration change and makes the
intent less clear. `exclude-types` is surgical: "this specific class should not
participate in CDI at all in this context."

### Alternative — use `Instance<T>` with `isUnsatisfied()` to avoid the conflict entirely

Rather than excluding a conflicting bean after the fact, don't provide a competing `@DefaultBean` in the extension at all. Inject `Instance<T>` and check `isUnsatisfied()` at call time:

```java
@Inject Instance<PreferenceProvider> preferenceProviderInstance;

int threshold;
if (preferenceProviderInstance.isUnsatisfied()) {
    threshold = DEFAULT_VALUE;  // no provider on classpath
} else {
    threshold = preferenceProviderInstance.get().resolve(...).getOrDefault(KEY).value();
}
```

`Instance<T>` always satisfies its own injection point (the container injects the `Instance` holder, not `T` directly). When zero beans of type `T` exist, `isUnsatisfied()` returns `true`; when one is active, `.get()` returns it. No `@DefaultBean` is added to the extension, so no conflict can arise.

**Best for:** library/extension authors who control their own code and want to make a platform SPI optional without contributing a competing `@DefaultBean`.

**Limitation:** requires call-site guards (`isUnsatisfied()` before `.get()`); callers that inject `T` directly still get an ambiguous point if two `@DefaultBean` beans exist from other sources.

## Constraints

Applies when both `@DefaultBean` implementations reach the CDI container's scanning phase
(i.e. both are indexed via `quarkus.index-dependency` or are in the app's own sources).
In two-repo / multi-module projects, platform library JARs can silently contribute
`@DefaultBean` mocks that conflict with internal no-ops.

## Alternatives considered

- Mark one bean `@Alternative @Priority(1)` instead of `@DefaultBean` — works but changes
  the semantics of the "winning" bean and requires `selected-alternatives` configuration.
- Remove one of the `@DefaultBean` implementations from the classpath entirely — clean, but
  may not be possible if it comes from a third-party dependency.

## Invalidation triggers

Would change if Quarkus ARC adds a deterministic tie-break for two `@DefaultBean` beans
(e.g. favour the one in the current module's sources). Track Quarkus changelog for ARC
`@DefaultBean` resolution changes.

**See also:** [GE-20260515-fd3156](GE-20260515-fd3156.md) — @DefaultBean must be on @Produces method not on the class | [GE-20260529-ab148d](GE-20260529-ab148d.md) — multiple CDI constructors without @Inject → UnsatisfiedResolutionException | [GE-20260601-848232](GE-20260601-848232.md) — exclude-types silently does nothing for Jandex-indexed JARs

**See also:** [GE-20260604-2f0889](GE-20260604-2f0889.md) — @Alternative @Priority(N) stubs appear in @All List<T> alongside original bean

**See also:** [GE-20260609-26ffa5](GE-20260609-26ffa5.md) — @ApplicationScoped POJO + @Produces for same type causes CDI ambiguous bean resolution

**See also:** [GE-20260515-99cf39](GE-20260515-99cf39.md) — config-driven @Produces @DefaultBean for engine-internal strategy selection

**See also:** [GE-20260614-337397](GE-20260614-337397.md) — quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel, clashing with @DefaultBean fallback | [GE-20260604-b3d2ef](GE-20260604-b3d2ef.md) — quarkus-flow CDI extension already registers WorkflowApplication — adding @Produces causes ambiguity

**See also:** [GE-20260615-6c4767](../casehub-engine/GE-20260615-6c4767.md) — adding custom CDI qualifier to @ApplicationScoped removes @Default

**See also:** GE-20260627-51e402 — @Alternative totally suppresses @DefaultBean (not just deprioritized, gone from container)

entries.body:
Multiple CDI constructors without @Inject → UnsatisfiedResolutionException for the bean itself, not a constructor

### Symptom
Quarkus startup fails with:
```
UnsatisfiedResolutionException: Unsatisfied dependency for type io.example.MyBean and qualifiers [@Default]
```
The bean class exists on the classpath, all its constructor parameter types exist, and it is annotated with `@ApplicationScoped`. No warning about constructors appears.

### Context
The bean has two constructors: one for CDI injection (using `@All List<X>` or `Event<Y>`) and one package-private constructor for unit tests (accepting simpler types). Neither constructor is annotated with `@Inject`.

### Root cause
CDI requires exactly one constructor annotated with `@Inject` when a class has multiple constructors. If none is annotated, CDI falls back to looking for a no-arg constructor. When no no-arg constructor exists, CDI reports the failure as "Unsatisfied dependency for the bean type" — not as "no suitable constructor found." The error message points at the injection point in the *caller*, not at the bean's constructor, making it look like the bean is absent from the CDI context.

### Fix
Annotate exactly one constructor with `@Inject` — the one intended for CDI use:

```java
@ApplicationScoped
public class InboundConnectorService {

@Inject  // ← required when multiple constructors exist
    InboundConnectorService(@All List<InboundConnector> connectors,
                            Event<InboundMessage> messageEvent) {
        this(connectors, messageEvent::fire);
    }

// Test constructor — no @Inject
    InboundConnectorService(List<InboundConnector> connectors,
                            Consumer<InboundMessage> eventBus) { ... }
}
```

### Why this is non-obvious
The error message says the *bean* is unsatisfied, not that its constructor is unusable. A developer familiar with the technology checks: Is the bean annotated? Is it on the classpath? Is Jandex indexing it? All answers are yes. The actual cause — no `@Inject` on the right constructor — is invisible in the error. Debugging time is wasted checking classpath, module boundaries, and Jandex configuration before the constructor annotation is noticed.

### Why this fix
CDI's fallback to no-arg when `@Inject` is absent is documented behaviour, but the error emitted when no no-arg exists is a bean-level "unsatisfied dependency" rather than a constructor-level error. Adding `@Inject` is the minimal fix; the alternative (providing a no-arg constructor) would require CDI-unfriendly field injection or a proxy-unsafe no-op default.

### Alternatives considered
- Using field injection with `@Inject` — avoids the constructor problem but breaks testability (can't use constructor injection in pure JUnit tests without CDI)
- Adding a no-arg constructor — CDI would use it, but then there is no way to inject dependencies without field injection

**See also:** [GE-20260601-fcf0d9](GE-20260601-fcf0d9.md) — two @DefaultBean beans for same type → AmbiguousResolutionException

**See also:** [GE-20260604-2f0889](GE-20260604-2f0889.md) — @Alternative @Priority(N) stubs appear in @All List<T> alongside original bean

**See also:** [GE-20260607-3611a2](GE-20260607-3611a2.md) — Preferences is not a CDI bean — inject PreferenceProvider

**See also:** [GE-20260604-4bfd2c](GE-20260604-4bfd2c.md) — adding package-private test constructor to CDI field-injected bean removes implicit no-arg

entries.title: casehub-work IllegalStateExceptionMapper silently maps IllegalStateException to HTTP 409
entries.body:
casehub-work IllegalStateExceptionMapper silently maps IllegalStateException to HTTP 409

### Symptom

REST endpoint returns HTTP 409 Conflict instead of the expected 500 Internal Server Error.
Happens when application code throws `IllegalStateException` for an infrastructure failure
(poll timeout, misconfiguration, unresolvable dependency).

### Context

Any application that depends on `casehub-work` and throws `IllegalStateException` from a
REST-invoked code path.

### Root cause

`casehub-work` JAR ships `io.casehub.work.runtime.api.IllegalStateExceptionMapper` — a
`jakarta.ws.rs.ext.ExceptionMapper<IllegalStateException>` that maps every
`IllegalStateException` to HTTP 409 Conflict. The mapper is registered globally via CDI
and affects any `IllegalStateException` thrown during a REST request in the application,
not just ones thrown from casehub-work code itself.

### Fix

Use a different exception type for infrastructure failures that should produce 500:

```java
// ❌ Produces HTTP 409 — mapped by casehub-work's IllegalStateExceptionMapper
throw new IllegalStateException("Agent did not reply for correlationId=" + id);

// ✅ Produces HTTP 500 — no mapper for generic RuntimeException
throw new RuntimeException("Agent did not reply for correlationId=" + id);
```

Alternatively, register a `@Priority(1)` exception mapper that overrides casehub-work's
for specific exception subtypes, or use a custom exception class that extends
`RuntimeException` directly.

### Why this is non-obvious

The mapper is shipped inside a transitive JAR (`casehub-work-0.2-SNAPSHOT.jar`) and is
nowhere documented. The symptom (409 instead of 500) gives no hint that an exception
mapper is involved — 409 Conflict is semantically about resource state, so developers
naturally investigate their domain logic rather than exception infrastructure. The 5-second
delay before the 409 (from a poll timeout) makes the connection even harder to spot.

entries.body:
Hibernate named query gains a parameter in one repo — sibling repo call site silently unbound until runtime

### Symptom

```
org.hibernate.QueryParameterException: No argument for named parameter ':tenancyId'
  at ReactiveSqmQueryImpl.executeReactiveUpdate
```

All message dispatches fail with HTTP 500 when `casehub.ledger.hash-chain.enabled=true`.

### Context

`LedgerMerkleFrontier.deleteBySubjectAndLevel` is a `@NamedQuery` defined in `casehub-ledger`.
The ledger repo added a `:tenancyId` predicate to the query. `ReactiveLedgerEntryJpaRepository.save()`
in `casehub-qhorus` (a sibling repo) calls this named query but was never updated to bind the new parameter.
The call site compiled and deployed without error — the unbound parameter only surfaces at runtime
when the query executes.

### Root cause

JPA named queries are resolved by name at runtime, not by signature at compile time. When the
query definition in one repo gains a new parameter, every call site in every sibling repo that
uses the same named query must be manually updated. There is no compile-time or build-time
enforcement — neither the Java compiler nor the Maven build reports the mismatch.

### Fix

Bind the new parameter at every call site that uses the named query:

```java
session.createNamedQuery("LedgerMerkleFrontier.deleteBySubjectAndLevel")
    .setParameter("subjectId", e.subjectId)
    .setParameter("level", node.level)
    .setParameter("tenancyId", e.tenancyId)  // ← add when query gains this param
    .executeUpdate()
```

### Why this is non-obvious

The build succeeds. The CDI wiring is correct. The error only appears on a specific code
path (`hash-chain.enabled=true`) that may not be covered by standard CI tests. The exception
message names the parameter (`':tenancyId'`) but gives no indication of which call site is
missing the binding — a classpath-wide search is required to find the stale call site.

**See also:** [GE-20260617-54b75b](GE-20260617-54b75b.md) — Hibernate Reactive Panache repo.update() converts positional ?N params to named params — unbound at runtime

Static entity factory creates JPA child entities without multi-tenancy fields — NOT NULL INSERT fails
entries.body:
Static entity factory creates JPA child entities without multi-tenancy fields — NOT NULL INSERT fails

### Symptom

```
org.hibernate.exception.ConstraintViolationException: column "tenancy_id" violates not-null constraint
```

Entities persisted via a static factory or utility method fail on INSERT even though the owning
parent entity has `tenancyId` set correctly.

### Context

`LedgerMerkleTree.append(digest, currentFrontier, subjectId)` is a pure static utility that
builds new `LedgerMerkleFrontier` nodes. It has no knowledge of tenancy context. The caller
in `ReactiveLedgerEntryJpaRepository.save()` sets `tenancyId` on the `LedgerEntry` being saved
but forgot to propagate it to the frontier nodes returned by `append()`. The nodes go into
`session.persist()` with `tenancyId = null`, violating the NOT NULL constraint.

### Root cause

Static factory and utility methods that create JPA entities operate outside any tenancy context.
Multi-tenancy fields (`tenancyId`, `tenantKey`, etc.) are caller responsibilities, not factory
responsibilities. The omission is invisible until the `session.persist()` flush fires — and only
on code paths where the NOT NULL column is actually written.

### Fix

Propagate multi-tenancy fields from the parent entity onto all child entities immediately after
the factory call, before any `session.persist()`:

```java
final List<LedgerMerkleFrontier> newFrontier =
    LedgerMerkleTree.append(e.digest, currentFrontier, e.subjectId);
newFrontier.forEach(node -> node.tenancyId = e.tenancyId);  // ← propagate before persist
// ... then session.persist(node) for each
```

### Why this is non-obvious

The parent entity (`LedgerEntry`) has `tenancyId` set correctly and was used for all prior
operations. The factory method looks complete — it takes all the structural parameters it needs.
The tenancy propagation step is easy to forget because it is not part of the factory's contract
and there is no type system or annotation to enforce it.

Maven child POM missing snapshotRepository causes SNAPSHOT deploy to parent's registry (403)
entries.body:
Maven child POM missing snapshotRepository causes SNAPSHOT deploy to parent's registry (403)

## Symptom

`mvn deploy` on a SNAPSHOT version fails with `403 Forbidden` when deploying a child module. The error URL points to the *parent* POM's registry, not the child's. CI succeeds for release versions but fails for SNAPSHOTs.

```
Could not transfer artifact io.example:child-parent:pom:0.2-20260427.144117-1
  from/to github (https://maven.pkg.github.com/org/parent-repo): 403 Forbidden
```

## Context

Child POM has a `distributionManagement` block with `<repository>` (releases) but no `<snapshotRepository>`. Parent POM has both pointing to the parent's registry. The CI token only has write access to the child's registry.

## Root cause

Maven uses `<repository>` for release versions and `<snapshotRepository>` for SNAPSHOT versions. When `<snapshotRepository>` is absent from the child POM, Maven inherits it from the parent — which points to a different registry (the parent's). The token cannot write there → 403.

## Fix

Explicitly declare both elements in the child's `distributionManagement`:

```xml
<distributionManagement>
  <repository>
    <id>github</id>
    <url>https://maven.pkg.github.com/org/child-repo</url>
  </repository>
  <snapshotRepository>
    <id>github</id>
    <url>https://maven.pkg.github.com/org/child-repo</url>
  </snapshotRepository>
</distributionManagement>
```

## Why this is non-obvious

Maven's `<repository>` and `<snapshotRepository>` are independent settings that inherit separately. A child POM that defines `<repository>` still inherits `<snapshotRepository>` from the parent. The 403 error message shows the wrong URL (the parent's), which points to a permissions problem rather than a configuration problem — leading developers to investigate token scopes first.

**See also:** [GE-20260426-840309](GE-20260426-840309.md) — mvn deploy fails on first SNAPSHOT publish to GitHub Packages | [GE-20260426-ad8f5a](GE-20260426-ad8f5a.md) — root parent POM must be deployed even when maven.deploy.skip=true

**See also:** GE-20260428-1ad5c4 "GitHub Actions fork CI deploys to upstream registry using GITHUB_TOKEN — unconditional mvn deploy fails"
**See also:** GE-20260426-d58530 — GitHub Packages silently accepts uploads to non-existent repository paths
**See also:** [GE-20260426-3e6b29 — maven-deploy-plugin retryFailedDeploymentCount retries with zero delay — useless for GitHub Packages first-upload](GE-20260426-3e6b29.md)

**See also:** [GE-20260428-f94886](GE-20260428-f94886.md) — setup-java server-id only wires credentials for exact repository id | [GE-20260619-31e6e4](GE-20260619-31e6e4.md) — GitHub Packages Maven registry does not follow repo name redirects

entries.title: Hibernate bytecode enhancement strips @Transient fields from @MappedSuperclass — subclass @Entity gets NoSuchFieldError
entries.body:
Hibernate bytecode enhancement strips @Transient fields from @MappedSuperclass — subclass @Entity gets NoSuchFieldError

### Symptom

`NoSuchFieldError` at runtime when an `@Entity` subclass tries to access a field
declared `@Transient` (or Java `transient`) on its `@MappedSuperclass` parent.
The field exists in the source code and compiles fine. The error appears only at
runtime after Hibernate bytecode enhancement has run.

### Context

Occurs when:
1. A `@MappedSuperclass` declares a field marked `@Transient` or `transient`
2. Quarkus/Hibernate bytecode enhancement is active (default in Quarkus)
3. A subclass `@Entity` inherits and accesses that field

### What was tried (didn't work)

- `@Transient` annotation on the field — stripped by enhancer
- Java `transient` keyword — also stripped by enhancer
- Both together — still stripped

### Root cause

Hibernate's bytecode enhancer runs at build time on `@MappedSuperclass` classes.
It strips **all non-persistent fields** from the enhanced bytecode — including
those explicitly marked `@Transient`. The enhancer treats `@Transient` as "not
part of the persistence model" and removes the field entirely, rather than
preserving it as a normal Java field that happens to not be persisted.

The Java `transient` keyword doesn't help — the enhancer treats both identically.

### Fix

**Option A — Remove the field** if it's write-only or unused by subclasses.
This was the fix in casehub-ledger #168: the `ledgerEntry` back-reference on
`LedgerSupplement` (`@MappedSuperclass`) was never read, so removing it was clean.

**Option B — Move the field to the `@Entity` subclass.** If the field IS needed
at runtime (e.g. a transient cache, a computed value), declare it on the `@Entity`
class instead of the `@MappedSuperclass`. The enhancer does not strip fields from
`@Entity` classes in the same way.

### Why this is non-obvious

`@Transient` is documented as "this field is not persisted" — the universal
expectation is that it still exists in memory as a normal Java field. Nothing in
Hibernate's or JPA's documentation says "bytecode enhancement physically removes
the field from the class." The compile succeeds; the error is runtime-only with
no warning.

### Why this fix

Removing the field (Option A) is preferred over moving it to the subclass when
the field exists only for API convenience (e.g. a back-reference that `attach()`
sets but nothing reads). Moving it to the subclass (Option B) adds a field to
every `@Entity` that may not need it. Evaluate per case — the deciding factor is
whether any code path actually reads the field.

### Alternatives considered

- Wrapping access in a `Map<UUID, LedgerEntry>` lookup instead of a direct field
  reference — rejected as over-engineering for a field that was never read.

entries.title: Probe delete permission with a nonexistent resource ID — 404 means authorised, 403 means denied
entries.body:
Probe delete permission with a nonexistent resource ID — 404 means authorised, 403 means denied

## What It Is

To test whether a token has delete permission on a resource without actually deleting anything, send a DELETE request to a known-nonexistent resource ID. The response reveals the permission check result:

- **404 Not Found** — the API checked authorisation first, passed, then looked up the resource and couldn't find it. **Permission confirmed.**
- **403 Forbidden** — the API rejected the request at the authorisation layer before even looking up the resource. **Permission denied.**

## Context

Useful when writing diagnostic scripts that need to verify delete scope on a token without side effects, and when no safe "list my permissions" endpoint exists. Works for any REST API that performs authorisation before existence checks (GitHub, most well-designed APIs).

## Example — GitHub Packages

```bash
http_code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" \
  -X DELETE \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GH_TOKEN" \
  -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" \
  "https://api.github.com/orgs/$ORG/packages/maven/__probe_nonexistent__/versions/0")

if [ "$http_code" = "404" ]; then
  echo "✓ delete:packages — permission confirmed"
elif [ "$http_code" = "403" ] || [ "$http_code" = "401" ]; then
  echo "✗ delete:packages — permission denied"
fi
```

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

Most developers either (a) check permissions by trying a real delete and accepting the risk, (b) look for a permissions endpoint that often doesn't exist, or (c) inspect the token's OAuth scopes via response headers. This approach requires knowing that well-designed APIs check auth before existence — and that 404 therefore implies authorisation was granted.

ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent does not cache null — mapping function re-invoked on every call when absent
entries.body:
ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent does not cache null — mapping function re-invoked on every call when absent

## ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent does not cache null — mapping function re-invoked on every call when absent

**ID:** GE-20260612-f6362e
**Stack:** Java (all versions)
**Symptom:** Code using `computeIfAbsent` to cache an expensive lookup result keeps calling the mapping function on every get, even after the first call. No exception, no warning — the function just runs repeatedly.
**Context:** The mapping function returns `null` when the target resource is not found (e.g. a channel UUID that doesn't exist yet). The developer expects null to be cached so subsequent calls skip the lookup. It isn't.

### What was tried (didn't work)
- Trusting that `computeIfAbsent` would cache the null return value the same way it caches a non-null value

### Root cause
`ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent` is specified by Java to NOT store null mappings. From the Javadoc:

> "If the specified key is not already associated with a value, attempts to compute its value using the given mapping function and enters it into this map unless null."

The phrase "unless null" is easy to miss. If the function returns null, no entry is created and the map remains unchanged. The next call to `computeIfAbsent` for the same key invokes the mapping function again.

This is by design — `ConcurrentHashMap` does not permit null values at all (unlike `HashMap`).

### Fix
Two options depending on the desired semantics:

**Option 1 — Sentinel value (recommended when null means "not found"):**
```java
private static final UUID ABSENT = new UUID(0, 0); // sentinel

UUID channelId = channelIdCache.computeIfAbsent(tenancyId, tid ->
    channelService.findByName(name).map(ch -> ch.id).orElse(ABSENT));

if (ABSENT.equals(channelId)) {
    // channel not found — treat as absent
    channelIdCache.remove(tenancyId); // optionally invalidate to allow retry
    return;
}
```

**Option 2 — Re-invoke on miss (when re-querying until available is correct):**
```java
// computeIfAbsent with null return = always re-query on miss
// Use this when "not found now" is transient and the next call should retry
UUID channelId = channelIdCache.computeIfAbsent(tenancyId, tid ->
    channelService.findByName(name).map(ch -> ch.id).orElse(null));
// null → not cached → next call retries the lookup automatically
```

### Why this is non-obvious
`HashMap.computeIfAbsent` has the same behaviour, but `HashMap` allows null values elsewhere, so the distinction is less visible. Developers coming from `HashMap` usage patterns assume null is a valid cached value. The Javadoc mentions it but the "unless null" clause is easy to overlook when reading quickly.

**See also:** [GE-20260607-813a95](GE-20260607-813a95.md) — ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent() null return — use sentinel pattern (the fix)

casehub-work IllegalStateExceptionMapper silently maps IllegalStateException to HTTP 409
entries.body:
casehub-work IllegalStateExceptionMapper silently maps IllegalStateException to HTTP 409

### Symptom

REST endpoint returns HTTP 409 Conflict instead of the expected 500 Internal Server Error.
Happens when application code throws `IllegalStateException` for an infrastructure failure
(poll timeout, misconfiguration, unresolvable dependency).

### Context

Any application that depends on `casehub-work` and throws `IllegalStateException` from a
REST-invoked code path.

### Root cause

`casehub-work` JAR ships `io.casehub.work.runtime.api.IllegalStateExceptionMapper` — a
`jakarta.ws.rs.ext.ExceptionMapper<IllegalStateException>` that maps every
`IllegalStateException` to HTTP 409 Conflict. The mapper is registered globally via CDI
and affects any `IllegalStateException` thrown during a REST request in the application,
not just ones thrown from casehub-work code itself.

### Fix

Use a different exception type for infrastructure failures that should produce 500:

```java
// ❌ Produces HTTP 409 — mapped by casehub-work's IllegalStateExceptionMapper
throw new IllegalStateException("Agent did not reply for correlationId=" + id);

// ✅ Produces HTTP 500 — no mapper for generic RuntimeException
throw new RuntimeException("Agent did not reply for correlationId=" + id);
```

Alternatively, register a `@Priority(1)` exception mapper that overrides casehub-work's
for specific exception subtypes, or use a custom exception class that extends
`RuntimeException` directly.

### Why this is non-obvious

The mapper is shipped inside a transitive JAR (`casehub-work-0.2-SNAPSHOT.jar`) and is
nowhere documented. The symptom (409 instead of 500) gives no hint that an exception
mapper is involved — 409 Conflict is semantically about resource state, so developers
naturally investigate their domain logic rather than exception infrastructure. The 5-second
delay before the 409 (from a poll timeout) makes the connection even harder to spot.

Response.Status.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY doesn't exist in Jakarta EE 9 JAX-RS — use raw integer 422
entries.body:
Response.Status.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY doesn't exist in Jakarta EE 9 JAX-RS — use raw integer 422

## Symptom

Code compiles with a `Response.Status.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY` reference in a `WebApplicationException` or `Response.status()` call, but the IDE shows an error and the build fails:

```
error: cannot find symbol
  symbol:   variable UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY
  location: class Response.Status
```

## Root cause

`Response.Status.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY` (HTTP 422) was added in JAX-RS 3.1 / Jakarta EE 10. Projects targeting Jakarta EE 9 / JAX-RS 3.0 (which Quarkus 3.x may use depending on the BOM) don't have this constant.

## Fix

Use the raw integer `422` directly:

```java
// Wrong (JAX-RS 3.0 / Jakarta EE 9):
throw new WebApplicationException("Not valid", Response.Status.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY);

// Correct:
throw new WebApplicationException("Not valid", 422);
```

Or create a constant:
```java
private static final int HTTP_UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY = 422;
```

## Why this is non-obvious

The HTTP 422 status is well-established (WebDAV, RFC 4918) and commonly used for validation errors. Developers reasonably expect it to be in the `Response.Status` enum. The version split between EE 9 and EE 10 isn't surfaced by IDE autocomplete which may show UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY from a different JAR on the classpath.

entries.title: Quarkus REST client interface with @Path at class level silently registers as a server resource — shadows the real endpoint
entries.body:
Quarkus REST client interface with @Path at class level silently registers as a server resource — shadows the real endpoint

## Quarkus REST client interface with @Path at class level silently registers as a server resource — shadows the real endpoint

**Stack:** Quarkus 3.36.x, RESTEasy Reactive

**Symptom:** After adding a REST client interface (for programmatic use with `QuarkusRestClientBuilder`), existing REST endpoint tests break with wrong HTTP status codes. Endpoints that should return 400 return 200 with empty arrays. Domain-filtered searches return no results. No error messages, no warnings in logs.

**Context:** Creating a JAX-RS interface for use as a programmatic REST client (not `@RegisterRestClient`). The interface has `@Path("/search")` at the class level and `@GET` on the method — identical annotations to the server resource.

### What was tried (didn't work)

- Checked CDI wiring, federation config parsing, SearchResource code — all correct
- Verified the blank-query check was still in the `search()` method — it was
- Checked whether `quarkus-rest-client-jackson` dependency caused a conflict — it didn't

### Root cause

Quarkus REST discovers **any class or interface** annotated with `@Path` at the class level as a JAX-RS resource — including interfaces intended for client use only. When `RemoteGardenClient` (a public interface with `@Path("/search")` and `@GET`) was on the classpath, Quarkus generated a no-op implementation and registered it as a resource alongside the real `SearchResource`. The no-op implementation matched first for some requests, returning 200 with empty results instead of delegating to the real resource.

### Fix

Make the client interface **package-private** (not `public`) and move `@Path` to the method level:

```java
@Consumes(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
interface RemoteGardenClient {  // package-private — not discovered as a resource

@GET
    @Path("/search")  // method-level only
    List<SearchResult> search(
            @QueryParam("q") String query,
            @QueryParam("limit") int limit
    );
}
```

The `QuarkusRestClientBuilder.build(RemoteGardenClient.class)` still works — the builder reads method-level annotations for client-side request construction. It does not require class-level `@Path`.

### Why this is non-obvious

The symptom appears on the **real** endpoint, not the client interface. Nothing in the logs mentions a duplicate resource registration. The failure mode — wrong HTTP status codes on endpoints you didn't touch — gives zero indication that a client interface is involved. The natural debugging path (inspect SearchResource, check CDI, verify query parameter handling) leads nowhere.

### Why this fix

Making the interface package-private is cleaner than `@RegisterRestClient` (which would require CDI and config for a single-URL client) or removing class-level annotations entirely (which would require base URI to include the path). Package-private interfaces are invisible to Quarkus resource scanning while still usable by the programmatic client builder.

### Alternatives considered

- **`@RegisterRestClient`** — rejected because it creates a single CDI bean per interface, requiring `application.properties` config per URL. Programmatic creation via `QuarkusRestClientBuilder` is needed for N dynamic upstream URLs.
- **Removing all `@Path` annotations** — rejected because `QuarkusRestClientBuilder.build()` needs at least a method-level `@Path` to construct the request URL.

*Score: 12/15 · Included because: the symptom (wrong HTTP status on unrelated endpoints) is completely disconnected from the cause (a client interface being discovered as a server resource). Multiple debugging approaches fail before the root cause surfaces.*

**See also:** [GE-20260616-e15321](GE-20260616-e15321.md) — JAX-RS @Path annotation shadows io.casehub.platform.api.path.Path

entries.title: jakarta.ws.rs.core.Response does not implement AutoCloseable — try-with-resources fails to compile
entries.body:
jakarta.ws.rs.core.Response does not implement AutoCloseable — try-with-resources fails to compile

## Symptom

Compiler error when wrapping a REST client Response in try-with-resources:

```
incompatible types: Response cannot be converted to AutoCloseable
```

## Context

Using `jakarta.ws.rs.core.Response` as a return type from a `@RegisterRestClient`
method and attempting to auto-close it to avoid HTTP connection pool leaks:

```java
try (Response response = gatewayClient.invokeAgent(request)) {  // ← compile error
    ...
}
```

## Root cause

`jakarta.ws.rs.core.Response` declares `close()` (added in JAX-RS 2.0) but does **not**
implement `java.lang.AutoCloseable`. The concrete Quarkus/RESTEasy implementation
(`ClientResponse`) does implement `Closeable`, but the declared return type from a
`@RegisterRestClient` method is the abstract `Response` — so the compiler rejects the
try-with-resources block.

## Fix

Use `try-finally` with explicit `response.close()`:

```java
Response response = gatewayClient.invokeAgent(request);
try {
    // use response
} finally {
    response.close();
}
```

`response.close()` is safe to call — it is declared on the abstract `Response` class.
The method releases the connection back to the HTTP connection pool.

## Why this is non-obvious

`close()` is declared on `Response` since JAX-RS 2.0, which strongly implies try-with-resources
should work — that is exactly why `AutoCloseable` exists. Nearly every Java resource type that
declares `close()` implements `AutoCloseable`. The gap is intentional (the JAX-RS spec authors
chose not to add `AutoCloseable` to `Response`) but invisible from the API surface. A developer
who sees `close()` naturally reaches for try-with-resources and gets a compile error with no
hint about why.

**See also:** [GE-20260607-9cef08](GE-20260607-9cef08.md) — sequential try-catch for must-not-throw close() with multiple resources

entries.body:
# REST Adapter Module

## Rule

When a library exposes HTTP endpoints, the REST layer lives in a separate
opt-in module — never in the core library module. Consumers include it by
adding a dependency; consumers who only need the Java SPI pay no JAX-RS
coupling cost.

```
my-library/
  api/              ← SPIs, domain types (Tier 1 — no framework deps)
  runtime/           ← services, entities (Tier 2/3 — no JAX-RS)
  rest/              ← JAX-RS resources, DTOs, exception mappers (opt-in)
```

The REST module is a plain JAR with CDI beans that carry JAX-RS annotations.
It is not a Quarkus extension — no deployment module is needed. Quarkus
auto-discovers the resources via Jandex indexing.

## Rationale

REST is a transport adapter, not part of the domain. Embedding it in the
core module forces every consumer to accept auto-registered endpoints,
pulls JAX-RS into the dependency graph, and makes suppression awkward
(build-time exclusions, `@IfBuildProperty` gates). A separate module
inverts the default: REST is opt-in, not opt-out.

This is Ports & Adapters (Hexagonal Architecture) applied to HTTP: the
library's SPI is the port; the REST module is one possible adapter.

## What belongs in the REST module

- **JAX-RS resource classes** — `@Path`, `@GET`, `@POST`, etc.
- **DTOs** — request/response representations, decoupled from domain entities.
- **Exception mappers** — `@Provider` classes translating domain exceptions to HTTP responses.
- **OpenAPI annotations** — `@Tag`, `@Operation`, `@APIResponse` on resource methods.

## What stays in the core module

- SPIs, domain types, entities, repositories, services, CDI events — everything
  that works without an HTTP boundary.

## Conventions

### Dependency direction

The REST module depends on the core library. The core library never
references the REST module.

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.example</groupId>
  <artifactId>my-library</artifactId>
  <version>${project.version}</version>
</dependency>
```

### Path prefix

Each REST module owns a path namespace. Use a consistent prefix across
modules so composed applications have a predictable URL space.

### DTOs vs domain types

REST resources return DTOs (records), not domain entities. The DTO is the
API contract; the domain entity is an implementation detail. This allows
the domain model to evolve without breaking HTTP clients.

### Versioning

The REST module versions alongside the core library — same multi-module
build, same release. Use `${project.version}` to keep them locked.

## Composition pattern

A deployable application composes libraries and their REST modules:

```xml
<dependency>my-engine</dependency>
<dependency>my-engine-rest</dependency>      <!-- opt-in -->
<dependency>my-ledger</dependency>
<dependency>my-ledger-rest</dependency>      <!-- opt-in -->
<dependency>my-work</dependency>
<!-- skip work-rest — this app writes its own domain-specific endpoints -->
```

A reference deployment (starter app, scaffold) is simply the full
composition: all libraries + all REST modules + persistence + config.
It is the canonical runnable artifact, not the only place REST exists.

## Anti-patterns

| Anti-pattern | Why it fails | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| REST in core runtime | Auto-registers on every consumer; can't suppress without build-time exclusion | Separate module |
| Consumer reimplements generic REST | Duplicated boilerplate, inconsistent API surfaces, no shared tooling | Include the library's REST module |
| Scaffold as sole REST provider | Non-scaffold deployments get zero REST for the library | REST module in the library build; scaffold depends on it |
| DTOs that expose JPA entities directly | Hibernate proxies, lazy-load exceptions, schema leaks | Dedicated DTO records in the REST module |

## Relationship to module-tier-structure

This protocol extends the three-tier module structure
(`pure-Java SPI / core library / full extension`). The REST module is a
fourth tier — a transport adapter that depends on Tier 2/3 but is never
required by it. The tiers remain:

1. **Tier 1** — `api/` (pure Java, no framework)
2. **Tier 2/3** — `runtime/` (services, JPA, CDI)
3. **Adapter** — `rest/` (JAX-RS, opt-in)
4. **Adapter** — other transport adapters (gRPC, MCP, CLI) follow the same pattern

entries.body:
quarkus.arc.exclude-types does not gate JAX-RS @Path resources — REST scanner is independent of CDI

### What happened

`quarkus.arc.exclude-types` (and the build-time `ExcludedTypeBuildItem`) was used to
exclude `A2AResource` and `ReactiveA2AResource` from CDI to resolve a duplicate-endpoint
conflict. Both resources still registered their `@Path` routes, causing Quarkus to fail
at startup with duplicate route errors.

### Root cause

Quarkus uses two independent scanners: one for CDI beans (Arc) and one for JAX-RS
endpoints (RESTEasy Reactive). `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` removes a class from the CDI
container only. The JAX-RS scanner reads `@Path` annotations from all classes on the
Jandex index regardless of CDI exclusion — the class is still visible as a REST endpoint.

### Fix

Gate the resource class at the source using Quarkus build-time conditionals:

```java
// Reactive variant — only active when reactive datasource configured
@IfBuildProperty(name = "quarkus.datasource.qhorus.reactive", stringValue = "true")
@Path("/a2a")
public class ReactiveA2AResource { ... }

// Blocking variant — active by default (reactive flag absent or false)
@UnlessBuildProperty(name = "quarkus.datasource.qhorus.reactive", stringValue = "true",
    enableIfMissing = true)
@Path("/a2a")
public class A2AResource { ... }
```

Alternatively, exclude the class from Jandex entirely (prevents both CDI and JAX-RS
registration) using `quarkus.index-dependency` negation or by removing the class from
the classpath altogether.

### Why this is non-obvious

CDI exclusion sounds like it should prevent a class from being "seen" by the framework.
But in Quarkus, CDI and JAX-RS are registered through separate pipelines. Most users
discover this by noticing that excluded beans still serve HTTP traffic — which is alarming.

### Why this fix

`@IfBuildProperty`/`@UnlessBuildProperty` on the class itself is the correct Quarkus
pattern for build-time conditional registration of both CDI beans and JAX-RS resources.
It uses the same mechanism Quarkus extensions use internally, survives ahead-of-time
compilation, and keeps the intent visible at the class declaration site.

### Alternatives considered

- `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` — removes from CDI only; JAX-RS routes still register. Does not fix the problem.
- Removing from Jandex index entirely — works but is coarser; also removes the class from type-safe CDI injection lookups that may be needed elsewhere.
